title: Geographic Information Science
text:
Preface
This book is an open educational resource textbook designed for my course, GEOG 370, Geographic Information Science, built from the course lectures.

title: Geographic Information Science
text:
About this book
This is an interactive textbook written for GEOG 370. It’s designed for students who are new to GIS and to spatial data. Chapters explain the concepts behind geographic information and show how to put them into practice in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.

title: Geographic Information Science
text:
How to use this book
Read the book in order if you can. Each chapter builds on the ones before it, and later chapters assume you have met the ideas and terms introduced earlier. Each unit opens with a short page that says what its chapters cover, so you can see where you are going before you start.

What’s in each chapter
Most chapters follow the same pattern, so you know where to look:

Learning objectives at the top list what you should be able to do by the end of the chapter. They are a good checklist when you review for an exam.
Numbered sections teach the material, with maps, figures, and tables. Cross-references such as “Section 1.2” or “Figure 2.1” are links you can follow.
Think about it boxes pose a question to stop and consider before reading on. There is no grade attached: they are there to help the idea stick.
Did you know..? boxes and Trivia time questions add a fact or a quick puzzle that connects the idea to the world around you.
Check your understanding questions near the end let you test yourself. You can answer them as many times as you like, and they are not graded.
A Summary recaps the chapter’s main points, Exercises give you practice, and Further reading and online resources points you to books, websites, data, and tutorials that go deeper.



QGIS and ArcGIS Pro
This book teaches with two GIS programs: QGIS, which is free and open source, and ArcGIS Pro, made by Esri. Chapter 1 introduces both. The ideas in each chapter are the same whichever program you use, and the skills you learn in one carry over to the other.
Names you would type or see in the software, such as file names like roads.shp, field names, and expressions, are printed in a monospaced font.


Key terms and the glossary
Important terms are printed in bold where they are first explained.
In the chapters, a key term has a dotted underline the first time it appears in a section. Hover over it, tap it, or reach it with the Tab key to see a short definition. All of the terms and their definitions are collected in the Glossary at the end of the book.
The books, articles, and documentation the chapters cite are listed together on the References page at the end of the book.


Finding your way around
The sidebar on the left lists every unit and chapter, and the outline on the right lists the sections of the page you are reading. Use the search box at the top to find any word in the book. The Aa button beside the search box changes the font and text size (see Fonts and reading settings).

title: Geographic Information Science
text:
How this book is organized

The chapters are grouped into units. Each unit opens with a page that summarizes its chapters.
Unit 1: Data Models and Projections (Chapters 1–7) lays the foundation. It explains what a geographic information system is, the science behind it, the questions it can answer, and who uses it, then turns to how a GIS stores the world as data, puts it in the right place with datums, coordinate systems, and map projections, asks questions of its attribute tables, and combines layers with attribute and spatial joins.
Unit 2: Spatial Data Quality (Chapters 8–10) is about where data come from and how good they are. It covers census data and their margins of error, turning addresses and scanned maps into GIS layers with geocoding and georeferencing, and the quality of volunteered data in OpenStreetMap.
More chapters are being written now and will appear here as they are added.

title: Geographic Information Science
text:
Fonts and reading settings
The online version of this book sets its text in Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, and names you would type into the software in Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono. Both were designed by the Braille Institute of America for readers with low vision, and both are free to use. Many common letters and numbers look alike in ordinary fonts: a capital I, a lowercase l, and the number 1, or a capital O and a zero. Atkinson Hyperlegible gives each of these characters its own distinct shape, so they are hard to mistake for one another. That matters in a book full of coordinates, file names, and field names, where one misread character puts a point in the wrong place or points the software at a file that doesn’t exist. The zero in the monospaced font has a slash through it, so you can always tell 0 from O.
A font that is easy for one reader can be hard for another, so you can change it. Press the Aa button beside the search box at the top of any page to choose a font and a text size. The fonts are:

Atkinson Hyperlegible (the default), described above.
Lexend, a font designed to reduce visual stress and make reading easier and faster.
Cardo, a traditional book serif.
Standard sans-serif and Serif, which use the fonts already on your device.
OpenDyslexic, which gives each letter a heavier bottom so letters are harder to flip or rotate. Some readers with dyslexia find it easier to read.

Text size goes from one step smaller than normal to three steps larger. Your choices are saved in your web browser, so the book keeps your settings from page to page and the next time you visit. Monospaced text keeps Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono whichever font you choose, so it always lines up.

title: Geographic Information Science
text:
Acknowledgments

I’d like to acknowledge the hard work of my students, without whom this would not be possible.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 1: What Is GIS?
This unit lays the foundation for everything else in the book. It starts with the big picture: what a geographic information system is, the science behind it, and the questions it can answer. It then turns to how a GIS stores the world as data, and how coordinate systems and map projections put that data in the right place on a round Earth. By the end of the unit you can open, explore, edit, query, and join spatial data in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.
GIS helps people decide where: where a fire is spreading, where rescuers should search, and how to get help there. This chapter looks at GIS in recent events, the four questions that define a geographic problem, and the kinds of questions a GIS can answer. It defines a geographic information system and its five components, separates GISystems from GIScience, and traces the history of GIS, who uses it, and the ethical questions it raises. It ends with the tools used in this book, QGIS and ArcGIS Pro, and how to write a GIS question of your own.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 2: What Is Geographic Data?
How do you store a tree, a road, or a mountain in a computer? This chapter follows the steps that turn the real world into data: entities become features, and features are stored in a data model, a data structure, and finally machine code. It separates discrete objects from continuous data, and spatial data from attributes, then introduces the two main data models, vector and raster, with the vocabulary of each, from nodes and vertices to cell size and resolution. It ends with how data are stored in files such as the shapefile, why metadata matters, and how to choose between vector and raster.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 3: Location and Coordinate Systems
How do you say exactly where something is on the Earth? This chapter starts with relative and absolute location, then models the Earth’s shape: Eratosthenes’s measurement, the ellipsoid, and the geoid, with the three heights a GPS and a map report. It explains geodetic datums (NAD27, NAD83, and WGS84) and why the same coordinates can land 100 meters apart in two of them. It ends with latitude and longitude: how they are built, how to write and convert them, how precise they need to be, and why great circles and the graticule matter.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 4: Map Projections
Every flat map distorts the Earth. This chapter shows how a projection flattens latitude and longitude onto a plane, a cylinder, or a cone, and what each kind keeps and gives up: shape, area, distance, or direction. It explains why Greenland looks as big as Africa on a Mercator map, why web maps are for display and not measurement, and how scale error grows away from standard lines. It then covers the systems used most in North Carolina, UTM and State Plane, reads EPSG codes, and gives a practical method for choosing a projection.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 5: Attribute Data and Queries
Geometry says where; attributes say what. This chapter looks at the attribute table, its records and fields, the data types that store them and the binary limits behind them, and the levels of measurement that decide which questions make sense. It then teaches attribute queries in SQL, from simple comparisons to AND, OR, NOT, brackets, LIKE, BETWEEN, and IN, with a way to check any query using sets and Venn diagrams, and the trap of NULL values.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 6: Databases and Table Joins
Most GIS data live in databases. This chapter explains what a database management system does, how relational databases link tables with primary and foreign keys, and how codes such as FIPS codes and GEOIDs serve as keys. It then teaches table joins: the destination and source tables, inner, left, right, and full joins, and how cardinality decides what a join can do, with ways to handle one-to-many relationships. It ends with a census join in QGIS, and the problems that most often break a join.

title: Unit 1: Data Models and Projections
text:
Chapter 7: Spatial Joins
When two layers share no key, location can link them. This chapter explains spatial predicates such as intersects, within, and contains, and the four kinds of spatial join, from simple inside joins to summarized distance joins. Worked examples match North Carolina towns to their nearest airports and septic systems to the geology beneath them. It covers cardinality, why distances need a projected coordinate system, six questions to plan any spatial join, and the tools that do the work in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.



“A computer-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage,
analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information”
(Bolstad). Its five components are data, hardware, software, people, and
procedures.
A system of numbers, such as latitude and longitude, that gives every
location a unique position so layers line up with each other.
A mathematical method for flattening the round Earth onto a flat map.
Every projection distorts area, shape, distance, or direction in some
way.
Data tied to a location on or near Earth, such as the address of a
house, the outline of a county, or the elevation at a point.
A free and open-source desktop GIS that runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
Esri’s commercial desktop GIS, for Windows.
A problem that happens in specific places at specific times. It can be
described by its scale, time, space, and purpose.
The theory and methods behind GIS: research on analysis, data
representation, visualization, and GIS and society. Michael Goodchild
named the field in 1992.
A question whose answer depends on location, such as where something
clusters, how places differ, what factors explain a pattern, how a place
has changed, or how accessible a service is.
The way a GIS represents the real world as data, for example as points,
lines, and polygons (vector) or as a grid of cells (raster).
How a data model is laid out in a computer’s memory or files, for
example as lists of coordinate pairs linked by pointers.
A non-spatial fact about a feature, such as a building’s name or the
year it was built. Attributes are stored in a table with one row per
feature.
A data model that stores the world as points, lines, and polygons, each
defined by x, y coordinates and linked to its attributes. Best for
discrete objects.
A data model that stores the world as a regular grid of equal-sized
cells, each holding one value. Best for continuous data and imagery.
An intermediate point where a line or polygon boundary changes
direction.
The real-world length of one side of a raster cell, such as 30 meters.
Smaller cells give finer resolution and larger files.
A common vector format from Esri that stores one layer in several files
with the same name: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), and .dbf (attributes)
are required, and .prj holds the coordinate system.
Data about data: who made a dataset, when, how, in what coordinate
system, and how accurate it is.
A location given in a coordinate system that means the same thing to
everyone, such as 38° 53′ 52″ N, 77° 02′ 11″ W.
A smooth mathematical model of the Earth’s shape: an ellipse rotated
about its polar axis, wider at the equator than from pole to pole.
Examples are Clarke 1866, GRS 80, and WGS 84.
The surface of equal gravity that best matches global mean sea level. It
is lumpy, up to about 100 m above or below the ellipsoid, and elevations
are measured from it.
The Global Positioning System: U.S. satellites that let a receiver, such
as your phone, work out its location. GNSS is the general name for GPS
and similar systems from other countries.
A model that fixes an ellipsoid’s size, shape, and position relative to
the Earth, realized by a network of control points, so latitude and
longitude point to real places. Examples are NAD27, NAD83, and WGS84.
The North American Datum of 1927. It used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and
an origin at Meades Ranch, Kansas.
The North American Datum of 1983, an earth-centered datum on the GRS 80
ellipsoid, fixed to the North American plate. The datum of most U.S.
government GIS data.
The World Geodetic System of 1984, the global, earth-centered datum used
by GPS. It differs from NAD83 by about 1 to 2 meters in North America.
The angle north or south of the equator, from 0° at the equator to 90°
at the poles.
The angle east or west of the prime meridian, from 0° at Greenwich to
180° east or west.
A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the center. The shortest
route between two points follows a great circle.
The network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map.
A conformal cylindrical projection from 1569, made for navigation: lines
of constant compass bearing are straight. It greatly enlarges areas
toward the poles.
A line where the projection surface meets the Earth, so the scale is
exact. Standard lines that follow latitude are standard parallels.
A system of 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, each a secant
Transverse Mercator projection in meters. North Carolina spans zones 17N
and 18N.
A U.S. system of about 120 zones following state and county lines, built
for surveyors, with error held to 1 part in 10,000. North Carolina has
one zone (EPSG:32119 in meters, 2264 in feet).
A number that identifies a coordinate reference system in the EPSG
registry, such as 4326 for WGS84 or 32119 for North Carolina State
Plane.
How a field is stored, such as text, integer, double, or date. It limits
what the field can hold.
What kind of values an attribute holds, which decides what questions
make sense: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio.
Structured Query Language, the standard language for asking databases
questions. In a GIS you usually write only its WHERE clause.
A drawing of sets as overlapping circles, useful for checking what an
AND or OR query will select.
An organized collection of tables, usually stored and managed by a
database management system.
Software that stores data once and lets many programs and people query
and edit it, while it controls who may change what.
A database that stores data in tables and links them through key fields
that hold the same values.
A field that holds values of another table’s primary key. Its values can
repeat.
A numeric code the U.S. government assigns to each state, county, and
other area, such as 37 for North Carolina and 37135 for Orange County.
In a join, the table whose fields are appended to the destination.
How many records in one table match each record in another: one-to-one,
many-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.
One destination record matches many source records. Summarize the source
first, or use a relate.
A set of spatial data about one theme, such as roads, soils, or
elevation. Layers for the same area stack on top of each other to make a
map.
A rule that tests a spatial relationship between two geometries, such as
intersects, contains, within, or touches.
A join that matches the features of two layers by location instead of by
a shared key, then appends attributes from one to the other.
A spatial join that matches features that contain, lie within, or
intersect each other, such as points inside polygons.
A spatial join that matches each feature to the closest feature, or to
every feature within a set distance, and can record the distance.
A coordinate system that gives positions as x, y in meters or
feet, on a map projection built on a datum, such as UTM or State Plane.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.1 GIS in recent events
Before you read on, take a moment to answer a question: what do you think a GIS is? Write your answer down. You may think of an app on your phone, a map on the news, or software you have heard of at work. All of those are part of the answer, but none of them is the whole answer. We will come back to your answer at the end of the chapter.
This first chapter looks at the big picture. It starts with recent events where maps and spatial data mattered, then defines what a geographic information system is, the science behind it, and the people who use it. It ends with the tools you will use in this book, and the kinds of questions you will be able to answer by the end of it.
The easiest way to see what GIS does is to watch it at work. In each of the events below, people had to make fast decisions about where: where the danger is, where people are, and where to send help.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.1.1 Wildfires in Los Angeles, January 2025
On January 7, 2025, two wildfires broke out in Los Angeles County and spread quickly in strong Santa Ana winds. The Palisades Fire burned through Pacific Palisades on the west side of the city, and the Eaton Fire burned through Altadena and the hills above Pasadena. Together they destroyed more than 16,000 homes and other buildings (Figure 1.1), among the most destructive fires in California’s history.






Figure 1.1: The Palisades Fire seen from Palisades Drive in Pacific Palisades, January 7, 2025, the day it started. Photo: Ariam23, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0, cropped.



Think about how maps and spatial data would be used during an event like this:

Fire perimeters and spread forecasts. Firefighters map the edge of the fire several times a day, from aircraft and satellites, and models forecast where wind will push it next.
Evacuation zones and routes. Emergency managers divide the area into zones and tell each one when to leave, and which roads to take.
Shelters and resources. Maps show where shelters, water, fuel, and fire engines are, and how to get them where they are needed.
Damage assessment. After the fire passes, satellite and aerial imagery show which buildings were damaged or destroyed.

Damage assessment is a good example of GIS at work. Smoke and cloud block ordinary cameras, but radar satellites send out their own microwave signal, which passes through smoke. Researchers compared images from the European Space Agency’s Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar satellite taken before and after the Eaton Fire, and mapped which buildings in Altadena had changed. Each damaged building became a shape on a map, published within days by The New York Times and by NASA’s Disasters program. Insurers, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), utilities, residents, and rebuilding offices could all use maps like these to plan aid and recovery before crews could safely reach every street.


1.1.2 An earthquake in Tibet, January 2025
On the same day, January 7, 2025, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Dingri County in Shigatse, Tibet, close to the Nepal border. The shaking was felt in Nepal, Bhutan, and India, and the earthquake killed more than 120 people. In the first hours after an earthquake, rescue teams have one urgent question: where should we search first?
The region has been hit before. On April 25, 2015, the magnitude 7.8 Gorkha earthquake struck central Nepal, killing nearly 9,000 people and destroying or damaging hundreds of thousands of homes, temples, and historic buildings in and around Kathmandu (Figure 1.2).






Figure 1.2: Collapsed shrines in the Pashupatinath Temple area of Kathmandu after the April 2015 Nepal earthquake. Photo: Nabin K. Sapkota, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons license.



No single map answers that. You need to combine several layers of information: where the epicenter was and how strongly the ground shook in each place, where the buildings are and how they were built, how many people live in each village, and which roads through the mountains are still open. Putting layers like these together, to find the places that meet several conditions at once, is one of the oldest and most important things a GIS does. The U.S. Geological Survey publishes a ShakeMap and an estimate of likely losses (PAGER) for large earthquakes worldwide within an hour or so, for exactly this purpose.


1.1.3 Spacing pilgrims in Mecca, 2021
Not every geographic problem is a disaster. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Saudi Arabia limited the Hajj pilgrimage in 2021 to about 60,000 vaccinated residents, compared with more than two million pilgrims in a typical year. Pilgrims at the Grand Mosque in Mecca walked around the Kaaba on marked paths, spaced apart (Figure 1.3).






Figure 1.3: Pilgrims spaced apart around the Kaaba at the Grand Mosque in Mecca, July 2021, with barriers keeping the crowd small. Photo: AhmanElq, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons license.



Planning that spacing is a spatial problem. How many people fit safely in a space? Where should the markers and paths go? How do crowds move through the entrances and exits? The same questions come up when planning a football game, a graduation, or a concert on your own campus.


1.1.4 Hurricane Katrina, 2005: a problem in space and time
Hurricane Katrina made landfall on the Gulf Coast on August 29, 2005 (Figure 1.4). Its storm surge, ocean water pushed ashore by the storm, flooded the Mississippi coast and much of New Orleans, and the storm killed well over a thousand people. A satellite view of the storm in the Gulf shows before; a map of the flooded coast shows after. The same place looks completely different from one week to the next.






Figure 1.4: Hurricane Katrina in the Gulf of Mexico, August 2005. A geographic problem has a location, an extent, and a time. Image: NASA.



The storm, the surge, and the recovery all happened in specific places at specific times. That is what makes Katrina a geographic problem: it has a where and a when.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.2 Defining a geographic problem
Four questions help describe any geographic problem. Table 1.1 applies them to Katrina.



Table 1.1: Four questions that define a geographic problem, applied to Hurricane Katrina.










Question
What it asks
Katrina




Scale
Does the problem look different at different levels of geographic detail?
One flooded home, one county, the whole Gulf Coast


Time
Are the consequences short-term or long-term?
Hours of storm surge; years of rebuilding


Space
Does the problem affect a small area or a large one?
Damage stretched across several states


Purpose
Are we advancing scientific knowledge, or solving a practical problem?
Better storm surge models, or faster evacuations






Scale matters because a decision made for a whole region may be wrong for a single neighborhood, and the data you need change with it: a county-level flood map can’t tell a family whether their street will flood. Time matters because some problems last hours and others decades, and because the data you have describe one moment. Space matters because large problems need data from many sources that must fit together. Purpose matters because research and practice ask for different kinds of answers: a scientist wants to know why the surge reached so far inland, and an emergency manager wants to know who must leave now.






TipThink about it



Apply the four questions to the Los Angeles fires or the Tibet earthquake. At what scales does the problem matter? How long will its consequences last? How large an area does it cover? Who would use a map of it, and for what purpose?

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.3 What questions can GIS answer?
GIS helps answer a few broad kinds of questions. One way to remember them is: where things are, how much is there, how things change, and how to get there.

1.3.1 Where things are: the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, 2010
On April 20, 2010, the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers. Oil flowed from the well for 87 days, until it was capped in July, making it the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history. At its largest, oil on the surface covered tens of thousands of square miles of the Gulf.
The simplest GIS question is where is it? Agencies mapped the oil every day, from satellites, aircraft, and ships, and used those maps to close fishing areas in its path (at the peak, more than a third of the federal waters in the Gulf), to protect beaches and marshes, and to send cleanup crews where they were needed. Knowing where the oil was, and where currents would carry it next, drove almost every decision.


1.3.2 How much: where Americans live
GIS can also show how much of something is in each place. A map of U.S. population density, the number of people per square mile or square kilometer, shows at a glance that most Americans live in a few metropolitan areas: along the East Coast from Boston to Washington, around the Great Lakes, in Florida, Texas, and California. Large parts of the interior West are nearly empty (Figure 1.5). Maps like this are made from U.S. Census data, which you will map yourself in Unit 2.






Figure 1.5: Population density of U.S. counties. Each county is shaded by its number of people per square kilometer (the legend’s “km2”), from under 1 (white) to over 1,000 (darkest blue). Map: Austiger, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons license.





1.3.3 How things have changed: the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami
On December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia, set off a tsunami that crossed the Indian Ocean and killed about 230,000 people in more than a dozen countries. Satellite images of the same coastline before and after the tsunami show where beaches, buildings, roads, and trees were swept away (Figure 1.6).






Figure 1.6: The coast north of Phuket, Thailand, seen by satellite in 2000 (left), in 2002 (middle), and after the December 2004 tsunami (right), where red marks the land the tsunami flooded and damaged. Comparing images like these is change detection. Images: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.



Comparing images or maps of one place at two times is called change detection. It measures what was lost, and it guides rebuilding and planning for the next disaster. The same method tracks slower changes too: forests cut or regrown, cities spreading into farmland, glaciers retreating, and coastlines eroding.


1.3.4 How to get there: route optimization
Beyond mapping, GIS solves problems. Route optimization is one you probably use every day. When you ask your phone for the fastest route to Miami, the software treats roads as a network of lines and intersections, each road segment with a length and a travel time, and searches for the path with the lowest total cost. (Most routing software uses descendants of an algorithm that the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra published in 1959.)
What did your phone need to know to answer? The road network, which roads connect where, speed limits, turn restrictions, live traffic, and your own location from GPS. The same network analysis plans delivery routes that visit many stops, measures how long an ambulance or fire engine takes to reach each neighborhood, and helps choose where to put a new store, clinic, or fire station, a task called site selection.


1.3.5 Five kinds of GIS questions
A widely used list from the early GIS literature sorts the questions a GIS can answer into five kinds (Table 1.2).



Table 1.2: Five kinds of questions a GIS can answer.










Kind
The question
Example




Location
What is at this place?
Who owns the parcel at 123 Main Street?


Condition
Where is the place that meets these conditions?
Where is there flat, forested land within 1 km of a road and not in a floodplain?


Trends
What has changed here since then?
How much forest was lost in the Blue Ridge after Hurricane Helene?


Patterns
What spatial patterns exist?
Do cancer cases cluster near a particular factory?


Modeling
What if…?
What happens to traffic if this bridge closes? Where will the fire spread?

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.4 What is GIS?

1.4.1 Where geography meets computer science
So what is GIS? It sits where two fields overlap (Figure 5.8). Geography asks where things are, and why they are there. Computer science gives us the data structures, algorithms, and software to store and analyze large amounts of data. GIS is the overlap: using computers to capture, store, analyze, and display geographic data.






Figure 1.7: GIS is where geography and computer science overlap.





1.4.2 Does GIS mean…?
Ask a room of people what GIS stands for, and you’ll get more than one answer:

Geographic Information Systems: the tools. The software, hardware, and data for working with maps and spatial data. This is what most people mean.
Geographic Information Science: the theory and methods behind the tools.
Guaranteed Income Source: a joke, but with some truth in it. GIS skills are in demand in government, business, the environment, health, and planning (see Section 1.7).

This book covers the first two.


1.4.3 What is a GISystem?
There are many definitions of a geographic information system. One of the clearest comes from Paul Bolstad’s textbook, GIS Fundamentals (Bolstad 2022):

“A GIS is a computer-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage, analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information.”

Two parts of the definition are worth slowing down for. First, spatial data: data tied to a location on Earth, such as the address of a house, the outline of a county, or the elevation at a point. Second, the six verbs, collect, maintain, store, analyze, output, and distribute. They describe the whole life of spatial data, from the moment it is measured to the moment someone uses a map of it to make a decision. You will practice each of them in this book.
Other definitions stress different things. Esri, the company that makes ArcGIS, calls GIS a system that creates, manages, analyzes, and maps all types of data, connecting data to a map. Others stress that a GIS is a way of thinking about problems, not just software. All of them agree on the core: data with a location, and a computer to work with it.


1.4.4 Is a map a GIS? John Snow and cholera, 1854
In late August and September 1854, cholera killed more than 500 people within a few blocks of Broad Street, in the Soho district of London. Most doctors at the time believed that cholera spread through bad air, a “miasma”. The physician John Snow suspected contaminated water instead.
Snow marked each death at its home address on a street map, along with the locations of the public water pumps where people got their drinking water (Figure 1.8). The deaths clustered around the pump on Broad Street. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump’s handle on September 8, and the outbreak, already waning, ended. His map, published in 1855 (Snow 1855), became a classic example of spatial analysis, and Snow is remembered as one of the founders of epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations.






Figure 1.8: John Snow’s map of cholera deaths in Soho, London, 1854 (detail). Each dot is a death; each × is a public water pump. Map: John Snow, 1855, public domain.



So, is Snow’s map a GIS? It has spatial data (deaths and pumps, each at a location), it has analysis (comparing the pattern of deaths with the pumps), and it led to a decision (remove the handle). But it has no computer. By Bolstad’s definition, which says computer-based, it is not. By the spirit of the definition, it does everything a GIS does. Decide for yourself, and notice that the thinking behind Snow’s map, combining layers of information to find a pattern, is the same thinking you will use in GIS software.


1.4.5 The five components of a GIS
A geographic information system is more than software. It has five components, arranged around data (Figure 1.9).






Figure 1.9: The five components of a GIS, with data at the center.




Data are the center of every GIS. Without good data, nothing else matters. Data include the spatial features themselves and their attributes, the facts we know about each one, and metadata, the record of who made the data, when, and how.
Hardware can be as simple as pen and paper, or as complex as GPS units, drones, satellites, sensors, laptops, and servers in the cloud.
Software includes programs such as QGIS and ArcGIS Pro, but also the methods and analysis the programs carry out.
People are often the most important part, and the most overlooked: the analysts who build the data and maps, the users who read them, and the decision makers who act on them.
Procedures are the agreed methods and workflows that make results reliable and repeatable, so that two analysts given the same data and the same question get the same answer.



1.4.6 Geographic Information Science (GIScience)
Geographic information science, or GIScience, is the theory of GIS: the research behind the tools. The geographer Michael Goodchild coined the term in 1992, arguing that the hard problems of GIS were scientific questions in their own right, not just questions of software (Goodchild 1992). GIScience covers:

Analysis techniques: how to measure distance, find clusters, model surfaces, and predict change.
Data management, storage, and entry: how to represent the real world in a computer, and how to keep data accurate.
Visualization and cartography: how maps and graphics communicate, and how they can mislead.
GIS and society: ethics, privacy, equity, and who is and isn’t represented in the data.

GIScience asks how we can improve GISystems, so the tools of tomorrow come from the science of today.


1.4.7 GIScience or GISystems?
What is the difference, and what kinds of problems does each solve?



Table 1.3: GISystems and GIScience compared.











GISystems
GIScience




What it is
The tools that store, analyze, and display spatial data
The questions and methods behind the tools


Kind of problem
Practical tasks
Research questions


Wildfire example
Mapping today’s fire perimeter
Building a better model of where fires will spread


Hurricane example
Mapping evacuation routes
Improving storm surge forecasts






The two depend on each other. Every tool in a GISystem started as a research question in GIScience, and the practical problems people bring to GISystems raise new questions for GIScience.


1.4.8 Why “geographic”?
Why do we say geographic information, rather than just spatial information?

Spatial can mean any space. Computer-aided design (CAD) software is spatial: it measures shapes and distances in a drawing of a building or an engine part. But those drawings aren’t tied to places on Earth.
Geographic means locations on or near Earth’s surface. Geographic data come with coordinates, which place them on a round Earth, and map projections, which flatten it onto a screen or a page. Handling those is a big part of what makes GIS different from other graphics software, and it is the subject of later chapters.
Geospatial is often used to mean the same thing as geographic, especially in industry, the military, and government. The U.S. National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) is one example.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.5 A brief history of GIS
People have made maps for thousands of years, and overlaying maps to find patterns is much older than computers. But GIS as we know it began in the 1960s, when computers first became powerful enough to store maps (Table 1.4).



Table 1.4: Some milestones in the history of GIS.









When
What happened




1854
John Snow maps cholera deaths and water pumps in London.


1960s
Roger Tomlinson leads the Canada Geographic Information System (CGIS), built to inventory land across Canada. Tomlinson coins the term geographic information system and is often called the father of GIS.


1965
Howard Fisher founds the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics and Spatial Analysis, whose software and graduates shape the field for decades.


1969
Jack and Laura Dangermond found Esri in Redlands, California. Landscape architect Ian McHarg’s book Design with Nature (McHarg 1969) popularizes overlay analysis: stacking transparent maps of soils, slope, water, and land use to find the best places to build.


1972
The first Landsat satellite launches, beginning the longest continuous record of Earth from space.


1980s
Desktop and workstation GIS software spreads, including Esri’s ARC/INFO (1982) and the open-source GRASS GIS, first developed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.


1990
The U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER files put every street in the country into digital form for the 1990 census.


1992
Michael Goodchild names the field of geographic information science.


1995–2000
The Global Positioning System (GPS) becomes fully operational, and in 2000 the U.S. turns off the deliberate error that had limited civilian accuracy.


2002
Gary Sherman begins writing Quantum GIS, now QGIS.


2004–2005
OpenStreetMap is founded, and Google launches Google Maps and Google Earth, putting interactive maps in front of hundreds of millions of people.


2007 onward
Smartphones with GPS make nearly everyone a producer of location data.


2015
Esri releases ArcGIS Pro.


2020s
Cloud platforms, drones, and artificial intelligence (GeoAI) process satellite imagery and map features at a scale no team of people could.






Two threads run through this history. One is the move from expensive mainframes run by specialists to software on every laptop and maps on every phone. The other is the explosion of data: from a few hand-digitized maps to daily satellite images of the whole planet, and billions of location records from phones and cars.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.6 The GIS process
Using a GIS to solve a problem is a cycle that connects people, data, and the real world (Figure 1.10).







flowchart LR
  W(["The physical world"]) ==> P["Define protocols"]
  P --> C["Collect and edit<br/>spatial data"]
  C --> A["Analyze"]
  A --> R["Report results"]
  R --> D["Decide and act"]
  D ==> W




Figure 1.10: The GIS process as a cycle. Data come in from the physical world, and decisions go back out to it. Those two links are where GIS meets the real world.






Define protocols. Decide what to measure, how, where, and to what accuracy. Good procedures here save trouble later.
Collect and edit spatial data. Gather data from the field, from GPS, from imagery, or from existing sources, and clean it.
Analyze. Use the GIS to answer the question: overlay layers, measure distances, find clusters, or model change.
Report results. Make maps, tables, and reports that communicate what you found.
Decide and act. People use the results to make decisions, which change the physical world, and the cycle starts again.

The two links to the physical world (the thick arrows) are where GIS connects to reality: data come in from the world, and decisions go back out to it. Everything in between is an interaction between computers, people, and data.

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.7 Who uses GIS?
GIS is used in almost every sector of the economy (Table 1.5).



Table 1.5: Some of the sectors that use GIS.









Sector
Examples




Business
Banking, insurance, logistics, media, marketing, real estate, retail, economics


Government and safety
Politics, government, homeland security, military, emergency management, law enforcement


Health, education, and culture
Health care, public health, education, research, libraries, museums, archaeology


Environment and resources
Agriculture, forestry, conservation, restoration, biology, mining, energy exploration


Infrastructure and utilities
Transportation, engineering, electricity, gas, water, wastewater, telecommunications, surveying






A few examples of what that work looks like: a county planner checks a proposed subdivision against floodplain maps; a public health analyst maps which neighborhoods are more than 30 minutes by bus from a clinic; an insurer prices policies by wildfire risk; a retailer chooses where to open its next store; a utility tracks every pipe and valve in its water system; a conservation group maps habitat corridors for black bears; a newsroom maps where public money was spent.
Some people work as GIS analysts, technicians, or developers, but many more use GIS as one skill among others in a job with a different title: planner, epidemiologist, ecologist, engineer, or market analyst. The U.S. Department of Labor’s Geospatial Technology Competency Model describes the skills employers look for, and the GIS Certification Institute offers a professional certification, the GISP, for experienced practitioners.






TipThink about it



Find your own major, or the career you hope to have, in Table 1.5. If it isn’t there, how might location still matter in that field?

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.8 GIS and society
Maps are powerful, and they can do harm as well as good. GIScience takes this seriously, and so should anyone who makes maps.

Privacy. Your phone records where you go, and that data is bought and sold. A few location points are often enough to identify a person, find where they live and work, and reveal visits to a clinic, a place of worship, or a protest. Mapping individuals’ data, even with names removed, can expose them.
Equity and representation. Data describe some places and people better than others. Rural areas, poorer neighborhoods, and countries with fewer resources are often mapped in less detail, so they are easier to overlook in decisions. Volunteer projects such as the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team map buildings and roads in places that commercial maps miss.
Maps can be used to discriminate. In the 1930s, the federal Home Owners’ Loan Corporation drew maps grading city neighborhoods for lending risk, outlining many Black and immigrant neighborhoods in red. This practice, now called redlining, shaped where banks lent money for decades, and its effects can still be seen in home values, health, and tree cover in the same neighborhoods today.
Maps can mislead. Choices about color, classes, scale, and what to leave out can make the same data tell very different stories. A good analyst makes those choices honestly and explains them.

Professional organizations such as the GIS Certification Institute and URISA publish codes of ethics for GIS professionals. A simple test to start with: who could be helped by this map, who could be harmed by it, and who was left off it?

Many employers use ArcGIS Pro, so it is worth knowing both. The good news is that the skills transfer: layers, attribute tables, coordinate systems, and geoprocessing tools work the same way in both programs, and once you know one, you can learn the other quickly. When a chapter gives step-by-step instructions, it gives them for both.
GIS doesn’t stop at desktop software. You will also meet web maps (ArcGIS Online, Google Maps, OpenStreetMap), cloud platforms for satellite imagery (Google Earth Engine), and programming languages with GIS libraries (Python and R). The concepts in this book apply to all of them.

section: 1.10 What this book will teach you
text:
1.10 What this book will teach you
By the end of the book, you will be able to:

Use GIS software to design, develop, and carry out a GIS for a scientific spatial research project.

The book follows the course’s three units, each ending with a project (Table 1.7).



Table 1.7: The three units of the course.










Unit
Modules

Editing and querying spatial data

Unit 1 builds the foundation: how a GIS stores the world as data, and how coordinate systems and data models put that data in the right place. title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.11 What are GIS questions?
A GIS question is one where the answer depends on location. Here are five from North Carolina. The key word in each names the kind of question.



Table 1.8: Examples of GIS questions.










Question
Key word
Kind of analysis




Where are there higher clusters of theft and burglary in Chapel Hill?
Where
Mapping and finding clusters


Are incomes different between Durham and Raleigh?
Difference
Comparing places


What location factors contribute to housing prices in Charlotte?
Factors
Explaining a pattern


How has forest cover changed in the Blue Ridge Mountains after Hurricane Helene?
Change
Comparing data over time

Accessibility
Distance and travel time






Good GIS questions have a few things in common. They are specific about what is being measured and where. They can be answered with data that exist, or that you can collect. And the answer would be useful to someone: a planner, a business, a public health department, or the people who live there.






TipThought experiment: a GIScience project in your field



What is a geographic information science project related to your own area of study or interest? GIS is used in business, computer science, environmental science, geography, law, geology, real estate, public health, the social sciences, urban planning, communications and journalism, government, transportation, and much more.
Take two minutes and write down one idea. Then answer three questions about it: What is the location question? What data would you need? Who would use the answer? Ideas like this can grow into your final project in Unit 3.
If you’re stuck, here are three to start from. Public health: which neighborhoods can’t reach a clinic by bus in 30 minutes? Real estate: what explains differences in housing prices between neighborhoods? Journalism: where in the state was disaster relief money spent?

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.13 Summary

Maps and spatial data guide decisions in real events, such as wildfires, earthquakes, hurricanes, and crowd planning: where the danger is, where people are, and where to send help.
A geographic problem can be described by its scale, time, space, and purpose.
GIS answers questions about where things are, how much is in each place, how things change, and how to get there, and more generally about location, condition, trends, patterns, and “what if” models.
A geographic information system is “a computer-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage, analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information.” It has five components: data, hardware, software, people, and procedures.
GIScience is the theory and methods behind the tools. GISystems solve practical problems; GIScience asks research questions and improves the tools.
Geographic means tied to places on or near Earth’s surface, unlike other spatial data such as CAD drawings. Geospatial is a common synonym.
GIS grew from the Canada Geographic Information System and university labs in the 1960s to free software, GPS, and maps on every phone today.
GIS is used in almost every sector, and maps can harm as well as help: think about privacy, equity, and honesty whenever you make one.
This book uses QGIS and ArcGIS Pro. Their concepts and skills transfer to each other and to other GIS tools.

Now look back at the answer you wrote down at the start of the chapter: what do you think a GIS is? Has your answer changed?

title: 1  What Is GIS?
text:
1.14 Exercises

GIS in the news. Find a news story from the past year in which a map or spatial data played a role. What was the geographic question? Describe the problem using the four questions in Table 1.1.
Layers for a decision. An earthquake strikes a mountain region. List five layers of data you would want in order to decide where rescuers should search first, and say where you might find each one.
Is it a GIS? Is a paper road atlas a GIS? A weather app on your phone? A spreadsheet of customer addresses? Use Bolstad’s definition and the five components to argue each case.
The five kinds of questions. Write one question of each kind in Table 1.2 (location, condition, trends, patterns, modeling) about your hometown or campus.
Systems or science? For a topic you care about, give one example of a GISystem task and one example of a GIScience research question.
Ethics. Your phone’s location history for the past month is put on a map. What could someone learn about you from it? Who should be allowed to see it?
Your project. Write your idea from the thought experiment as one clear GIS question. Underline its key word (where, different, factors, change, accessibility, or another), list the data you would need, and say who would use the answer.

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.1 How a map represents the world
Start with a scenario. Your new GIS consulting firm has been hired to make a map of campus for new students. What data would you collect? How would you collect it? (And what would you name your firm?) Take two minutes and make a list. You might write down buildings, sidewalks, parking lots, bus stops, and the dining halls. Keep your list: we will come back to it several times in this chapter.
Whatever is on your list, you made choices. You didn’t list every tree, every bench, or every crack in the sidewalk, and you didn’t say how a building should be drawn. This chapter is about those choices: how we turn the messy, continuous real world into data a computer can store and analyze. It answers five questions. How does a map represent the world? What types of data do we use? How do data models describe geography? How is geographic data stored? And what are the advantages and disadvantages of each type?

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.1.1 Entities and features
Start with the real world. An entity is a real-world object: a tree, a building, a light post, a sidewalk, a lawn. A feature is how a map represents an entity, usually as a point, a line, or a polygon (Figure 2.1).






Figure 2.1: The same scene as entities in the real world (left) and as features on a map (right). The tree and light post become points, the sidewalk a line, and the building and lawn polygons.



Notice what the map leaves out. The building’s windows, the color of its bricks, the shape of the tree’s crown, and the people walking by are all gone. Every map is a set of choices about what to keep, what to leave out, and how to draw what is kept. Look back at your campus list: which entities made it onto your map, and which did you leave off without even thinking about it?


2.1.2 Data abstraction
A computer can’t store a tree. It can only store numbers, and in the end, only ones and zeros. Data abstraction is the chain of steps that turns the real world into something a computer can store (Figure 2.2):

The real world: the wetland, with its water, plants, and soggy edges.
A data model: the way people think about it in a GIS, such as polygons for each wetland and a table that gives each one an ID, an area, and a type.
A data structure: the way the model is laid out in a computer, such as a list of the x, y coordinate pairs around each polygon’s edge.
Machine code: the ones and zeros the computer actually stores.







Figure 2.2: Data abstraction. Each step to the right looks less like the world to a person and suits the computer better.



Humans work with data models; computers store data structures and binary code. The good news is that GIS software hides the right-hand steps. When you open a layer in QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, you see polygons and tables, not lists of coordinates, and certainly not ones and zeros. But knowing the steps are there helps you understand why files are organized the way they are, why some operations are slow, and why the same data can be stored in more than one way.


2.1.3 Geographic data models
A data model sits where human understanding and computer understanding overlap. People think about roads, rivers, and parcels; computers handle numbers and coordinates. The data model is the meeting point. Paul Bolstad, in GIS Fundamentals, describes a data model as the objects in a spatial database plus the relationships among them, and says its purpose is “to provide a formal means of representing and manipulating spatially-referenced information” (Bolstad 2022). Formal here means mathematical: a data model has exact rules, so a computer can follow them without guessing.
GIS uses four main data models (Figure 2.3):

Vector: points, lines, and polygons, each stored as coordinates.
Raster: a grid of cells, each holding a value.
TIN (triangulated irregular network): triangles that connect sampled elevation points into a surface.
Tabular: tables of attributes, linked to features.







Figure 2.3: The four main geographic data models: vector, raster, TIN, and tabular.



Most of this chapter is about vector and raster, the two models you will use most. A TIN is a special model for surfaces such as terrain: it puts more triangles where the ground is rough and fewer where it is flat, so it can be more efficient than a grid. Tables aren’t a picture of the world on their own, but they hold the attributes that make vector and raster data useful.

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
section: 2.2 What types of data do we use?
text:
2.2 What types of data do we use?

2.2.1 Discrete objects and continuous data
There are two ways of thinking about what is on a map (Figure 2.4).
Discrete objects exist in one place and not in another. They have clear boundaries, and at any location they are either present or absent: a road is either here or it isn’t. Roads, houses, lakes, and state boundaries are discrete objects.
Continuous data describe a quantity that exists across the whole map. It is always present, and its value changes from place to place. Every point on Earth has an elevation, a temperature, and an amount of rainfall, even if the value is zero. You can’t point to where elevation “ends.”






Figure 2.4: Discrete objects (left) are present or absent: roads, houses, and a lake. Continuous data (right) have a value everywhere: here, elevation in meters, with contour lines.



Some things can be thought of either way, and the choice depends on your question. Is a forest discrete or continuous? A forest boundary drawn as a polygon is discrete: you are either inside the forest or not. But the percent of tree canopy over each patch of ground is continuous, and it shades gradually from dense forest to open field. As you will see, this choice largely decides whether you use the vector or the raster model.






TipThink about it



Sort these into discrete objects and continuous data: fire hydrants, air pollution, county boundaries, snow depth, rivers, soil moisture, noise from an airport. Which ones could be either, depending on the question?




2.2.2 Points, lines, polygons, and annotation
Maps portray the world with four kinds of features (Figure 2.5):

A point is a location with no area, such as a school or a well.
A line has length but no area, such as a road or a stream.
A polygon encloses an area, such as a lake or a park.
Annotation is the text placed on a map, such as place names and street names.







Figure 2.5: The four kinds of map features: points, lines, polygons, and annotation.



The same entity can be any of these, depending on scale. A city is a point on a map of the United States, and a polygon on a map of its county. A river is a line on a state map, and a polygon on a detailed map of its banks. You will see this idea again in the vector model, below.


2.2.3 What is an entity?
Every entity carries five kinds of information. Take a lake as an example:

A spatial location: where it is, as an address or coordinates. The lake’s center is at a particular latitude and longitude.
An extent: how big it is, its size, boundary, and dimensions. The lake covers 40 hectares.
Non-spatial attributes: facts that describe it without saying where it is, such as a name, a number, a quality, or a color. The lake is called Lake Ridge, and it is 12 meters deep.
Time: when it existed, and when the data were collected. The shoreline was mapped from aerial photos taken in 2023, and a dry summer could move it.
A geometry: its shape. The lake is stored as a polygon.



2.2.4 Spatial and non-spatial data
Spatial data have a location that can be put on a map: the buildings on your campus, the rainfall measured across North Carolina, the U.S. highway network. Non-spatial data have no location of their own: the parts of a bicycle, a list of student ID numbers, your class grades.
When non-spatial information describes a spatial entity, we call it an attribute. A building’s name and the year it was built are attributes of the building’s polygon. Quick check: is a student’s home address spatial or non-spatial? On its own it is just text, but once software matches it to a location on a map (a step called geocoding), it becomes spatial.


2.2.5 Attribute data
Attribute data describe features. They have no location on their own; they borrow the location of the feature they are linked to. Attributes are usually stored in a table, with one row per feature and one column per attribute. Every feature in a layer has the same set of attributes, even if some values are blank.
Take a layer of fire hydrants (Figure 2.6). Each dot on the map is one hydrant, and each row of the table describes one of those dots: its ID, how many flanges it has (the outlets hoses connect to), its color, and its condition rating. Select hydrant 2 on the map, and its row lights up in the table; select the row, and the hydrant lights up on the map.






Figure 2.6: Fire hydrants as spatial data (left) and attribute data (right). Each row of the table describes one hydrant on the map.



That consistency, the same columns for every feature, is what lets a GIS query a layer (find every hydrant rated low) and symbolize it (color each hydrant by its rating).


2.2.6 Thematic layers
A layer groups similar features, such as all the roads, all the parcels, or all the hydrants. Stacking layers that cover the same area lets us compare themes and find where they meet (Figure 2.7). This is the overlay idea from Chapter 1, put into practice.






Figure 2.7: Thematic layers stacked over the same area, from the Earth’s surface at the bottom up through elevation, land cover, soils, and roads to political boundaries.



The two programs in this book organize layers slightly differently:

ArcGIS Pro: the layers you display together make up a map. A project (an .aprx file) can hold several maps, along with layouts and other items. (Older ArcMap called a map a data frame, and saved its work as a map document, an .mxd file.)
QGIS: layers belong to a project (a .qgz file), and are drawn in the map canvas. The Layers panel lists them, top to bottom, in the order they are drawn.

In both programs, a layer points to data stored somewhere else, in a file or a database. It does not hold the data itself. Deleting a layer from your map does not delete the data, and moving the data can break the layer. Keep that in mind when you move a project to another computer.






TipThink about it



Go back to your campus map list. Name three layers you would need. For each one, would its features be points, lines, or polygons? What attributes would you give them?

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
section: 2.3 How do data models describe geography?
text:
2.3 How do data models describe geography?

2.3.1 Vector and raster
The two main data models represent the world in very different ways (Figure 2.8; Table 2.1).
The vector model stores geometry as coordinates. A point is a single x, y pair; a line is an ordered list of pairs; a polygon is a list that closes back on itself. Vector suits discrete objects, and each feature carries its own attributes.
The raster model divides space into a regular grid of cells, each holding one value. Raster suits continuous data. How much detail it keeps depends on the size of the cells. (In an image, a cell is called a pixel, short for picture element.)






Figure 2.8: The same points, line, and area stored as vector (left) and raster (right). In the raster, each feature becomes a group of cells, and the line becomes a staircase.






Table 2.1: The vector and raster data models compared.











Vector
Raster




Stores
Points, lines, and polygons
A regular grid of cells


Best for
Discrete objects
Continuous data


Location
x, y coordinates
The cell’s row and column in the grid


Detail set by
The precision of the coordinates
The cell size


Attributes
Each feature has its own row of attributes
Each cell holds one value


Examples
Roads, parcels, wells, county boundaries
Elevation, satellite imagery, land cover, temperature






Before you read the examples in the table, try to think of your own: what would you store as vector, and what as raster?


2.3.2 The vector model: one entity, several features
The vector model gives you choices. The buildings in a neighborhood can be stored as points, as outlines (lines), or as filled areas (polygons) (Figure 2.9).






Figure 2.9: The same buildings stored three ways in the vector model: as points, as outlines, and as filled areas.



The right choice depends on scale and purpose. A citywide map of schools only needs points. A campus map for finding building entrances needs footprints. What is the difference between a line and an area? Enclosure: an area is a closed shape with an inside, so you can measure how big it is and ask whether something is in it. An outline drawn as a line has no inside, only a length.


2.3.3 Vector terms
A few terms describe the parts of vector features (Figure 2.10):

A point is a standalone location.
A node is the start or end point of a line.
A vertex (plural vertices) is an intermediate point where a line changes direction.
A line segment is the straight piece between two vertices or nodes.
A polygon is a closed line that encloses an area. Its corners are vertices.







Figure 2.10: The parts of vector features: a polygon and its vertices, a line with a node at each end and vertices between, its line segments, and a point.



Nodes matter for networks. Roads meet at nodes, so routing software, like the route optimization in Chapter 1, uses them to find paths from one road to the next.
When you edit vector data in QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, you will move, add, and delete vertices one at a time. The more vertices a line has, the more closely it can follow a curving river, and the larger its file.


2.3.4 The raster model: a grid of cells
A raster is rows and columns of equal-sized cells, laid on an x, y coordinate system (Figure 2.11). Four things define it:

Each cell holds one value. Most values are numbers, such as an elevation in meters. A value can also stand for a category, such as a land cover class (1 = water, 2 = forest, 3 = farmland), usually stored as a numeric code with a table that says what each code means. The cell marked N in the figure is a reminder that a value need not be a measurement.
The cell size is the real-world length of one side of a cell, such as 30 meters. It sets the raster’s resolution.
The coordinates of the lower-left cell anchor the grid to a place on Earth.
The number of rows and columns sets how far the grid extends.







Figure 2.11: A raster grid. Each cell holds one value, and the grid is located by the coordinates of its lower-left cell.



Because every cell is the same size, you don’t need to store the coordinates of each cell. You only need the coordinates of one corner and the cell size, and you can work out where every other cell is. That is a big part of why rasters are simple and fast to process.


2.3.5 Cell size and cell coordinates
Cell size is the ground distance covered by one side of a cell. Smaller cells mean more cells over the same area, which means finer resolution and larger files. Figure 2.12 shows the same 200-meter square at three cell sizes. Halving the cell size multiplies the number of cells by four: 4, then 16, then 64.






Figure 2.12: The same 200 m square at three cell sizes: (a) 100 m cells, 4 cells; (b) 50 m cells, 16 cells; (c) 25 m cells, 64 cells.



To find where a cell is, start from the lower-left cell and count. Number rows and columns from 0, starting at the lower-left cell. Then:
\[N_{cell} = N_{lower\text{-}left} + (\text{row} \times \text{cell size})\]
\[E_{cell} = E_{lower\text{-}left} + (\text{column} \times \text{cell size})\]
Here N is the northing, a distance north (the y coordinate), and E is the easting, a distance east (the x coordinate). You will meet eastings and northings again when we study coordinate systems.
For example, suppose the lower-left cell of a raster is at E 500,000 m, N 4,400,000 m, and the cells are 25 meters on a side. The cell in row 2, column 3 is at:

N = 4,400,000 + (2 × 25) = 4,400,050 m
E = 500,000 + (3 × 25) = 500,075 m







TipTrivia time: which cell size gives the best resolution?



Look at Figure 2.12 again. If you were buying a new TV, which of these would give you the best picture: (a) 100 m cells, (b) 50 m cells, or (c) 25 m cells?


Show the answer

(c), the 25-meter cells. Smaller cells mean more cells over the same area, so finer detail. A TV works the same way: more, smaller pixels on the same size screen give a sharper picture. The cost? Grid (c) has sixteen times as many cells as grid (a), so its file is larger and slower to process.









NoteDid you know..?



Each cell in an image from the Landsat satellites, which have photographed Earth continuously since 1972, is 30 meters on a side. That is about the size of a baseball infield, whose bases are 90 feet (27.4 meters) apart. A single cell can’t show you a house, but a grid of them covering every place on Earth, every 16 days for over 50 years, can show you forests being cut, cities growing, and lakes drying up.

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.4 How is geographic data stored?

2.4.1 Data structures
The data model is the concept; the data structure is how a computer actually stores it. Figure 2.13 shows one way a vector polygon can be stored. The polygon is built from three arcs (A1, A2, and A3), each a short line. Each arc is stored as an ordered list of coordinate pairs at particular addresses in the computer’s memory, and a pointer tells the computer which arc comes next.






Figure 2.13: A polygon stored as three arcs. Each arc is a list of coordinates in memory, and pointers link one arc to the next.



Notice that the last coordinate of each arc is the same as the first coordinate of the next. That shared point is what joins the arcs into a closed polygon. Storing shared edges once, and recording how they connect, is called topology. It saves space, and it guarantees that two neighboring polygons, like two counties, share exactly the same border, with no gaps or overlaps between them. You will meet topology again when you edit data.
You rarely need to think about data structures. But they explain things you will notice: why some file formats are larger than others, why a file can be corrupted if one part is missing, and why some tools need data in a particular format.


2.4.2 The Esri shapefile
The data structure you will use most often this semester is the shapefile, a vector format that Esri created in the early 1990s and published as an open specification in 1998 (Environmental Systems Research Institute 1998). Despite its name, a shapefile is not one file. It is a group of files that share a name and together store one vector layer (Table 2.2).



Table 2.2: The files that make up a shapefile named roads.










File
What it holds
Required?




roads.shp
The feature geometry: the coordinates of each point, line, or polygon
Yes


roads.shx
A positional index that links each shape to its record
Yes


roads.dbf
The attribute table, in dBASE format
Yes


roads.prj
The coordinate system and projection
No, but you almost always need it


roads.sbn, roads.sbx
A spatial index for faster searches
No


roads.cpg
The character set used for text in the .dbf
No


roads.shp.xml
Metadata for the layer
No






Three files are required: .shp, .shx, and .dbf. Without the .prj file, software can’t tell where on Earth the coordinates are, so the layer may show up in the wrong place, or not at all.
The most common student mistake is to email, upload, or move only the .shp file. The other files are left behind, and the shapefile won’t open. Always copy, move, and rename all of a shapefile’s files together, or zip the folder that holds them. Better yet, use the tools in QGIS (the Browser panel) or ArcGIS Pro (the Catalog pane), which treat the group of files as one layer.






NoteDid you know..?



The shapefile is over thirty years old, and it shows its age. Its attribute table is a .dbf file from dBASE, a database program from the early 1980s, so field names can be no more than 10 characters long (POPULATION_2020 becomes POPULATION), a table can have at most 255 fields, and the .shp and .dbf files can each be no larger than 2 GB. Each shapefile can also hold only one kind of geometry. Some GIS users run a website, Switch from Shapefile, that lists these limits and urges everyone to move to newer formats. The most popular replacement is the GeoPackage (.gpkg), an open standard from the Open Geospatial Consortium that stores many layers, rasters as well as vectors, in a single file. It has been QGIS’s default format since 2018. Yet the shapefile is still everywhere, because nearly every GIS program ever written can read it.




2.4.3 Metadata
Before you trust a dataset, read its metadata: data about the data. Good metadata answers questions like these:

Who created the data?
When were they created, and for what time period?
How were they created, and how accurate are they?
What coordinate system do they use?
Where can the data be found, and can I use them? Are there limits on how they may be shared or used?

Metadata is how you judge whether a dataset fits your purpose. A road layer made from 1990s paper maps may be fine for a state overview and useless for routing an ambulance. A land cover raster made with 30-meter cells can’t tell you how many trees are in your yard.
In the United States, many public datasets follow the metadata standard of the Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC); internationally, the ISO 19115 standard is common. In QGIS you can read a layer’s metadata in its Layer Properties, and in ArcGIS Pro in the Metadata tab of the Catalog pane or a layer’s properties.






TipThink about it



Your consulting firm has finished its campus map. What metadata would you write, so that a student three years from now could decide whether to reuse your data?

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.5 Vector or raster?
Neither model is better in general. Each has strengths and weaknesses (Table 2.3), and you choose the one that fits the data and the question.



Table 2.3: Advantages and disadvantages of the vector and raster models.










Model
Advantages
Disadvantages




Vector
Precise locations and boundaries
A more complex data structure



Compact storage for discrete features
Slower for overlay and surface analysis



Each feature carries its own attributes
A poor fit for continuous data



Looks good at any zoom level



Raster
A simple grid structure
Precision limited by cell size



Fast overlay and map algebra (math on grids, cell by cell)
Large files at fine resolution



A natural fit for continuous data and imagery
Lines and edges look blocky



Satellite and drone imagery is already raster
Each cell holds only one value






A memory aid that generations of GIS students have used for exams:

Vector is corrector, but raster is faster.

Vector keeps exact coordinates, so shapes and boundaries are more correct. Raster’s simple grid makes overlay and analysis faster. Here are a few choices to try:

Property parcel boundaries: vector. A parcel’s boundary is a legal line, and it needs to be exact.
A snow-depth map: raster. Snow depth is continuous; there is a value everywhere.
A city’s bus routes and stops: vector. Lines and points, with schedules and route numbers as attributes.
A satellite image of a wildfire: raster. Imagery is collected as a grid of pixels.
Land cover for a whole state: usually raster, because it covers everything, with no gaps.

Software can convert between the two. Turning vector data into a raster is called rasterizing, and turning a raster into vector features is called vectorizing. Each conversion loses some information: rasterizing loses precision, and vectorizing produces blocky, staircase-shaped lines that follow the cell edges.






NoteDid you know..?



The word raster comes, through German, from the Latin rastrum, a rake. Early television and computer screens drew their pictures as a set of parallel lines swept across the screen, like the lines a rake leaves in soil, and that pattern became known as a raster scan. Vector comes from the Latin vehere, to carry: in mathematics, a vector carries a point from one place to another, which is just what the line segments of a vector feature do.
