title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.7 Summary

A map abstracts the world. Real-world entities become features: points, lines, polygons, and annotation. Every map is a set of choices about what to keep.
Data abstraction runs from the real world to a data model (how people think about the data), a data structure (how a computer lays it out), and machine code.
Discrete objects are present or absent, with clear boundaries; continuous data have a value everywhere.
Every entity has a location, an extent, attributes, a time, and a geometry. Attributes are non-spatial facts that describe a spatial feature, stored in a table with one row per feature.
Layers group similar features, and stacked layers make a map.
The four main data models are vector, raster, TIN, and tabular. Vector stores points, lines, and polygons as coordinates, built from nodes, vertices, and line segments. Raster stores a grid of cells; the cell size sets its resolution, and every cell’s location can be worked out from the lower-left cell.
Shapefiles store a vector layer in several files (.shp, .shx, .dbf, and usually .prj) that must stay together. Metadata describes who made the data, when, how, and how accurate it is.
Vector is corrector, but raster is faster. Choose the model that fits the data and the question.

Now return to your campus map list from the start of the chapter. Which entities would you store as vector features, and which as rasters? What attributes and metadata would you record?

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.8 Exercises

Your campus map. For each item on the list you made at the start of the chapter, say whether you would store it as a point, a line, a polygon, or a raster, and why. List two attributes for each.
Five kinds of information. Pick an entity near you, such as your dorm, a bus stop, or a creek. Describe its location, extent, attributes, time, and geometry.
Discrete or continuous? Give three examples of discrete objects and three of continuous data from your own major or interests. Then find one thing that could be either, and explain when you would treat it each way.
Scale changes everything. Describe how a river, an airport, and a university could each be represented as a point, a line, or a polygon, depending on the scale of the map.
Cell arithmetic. A raster’s lower-left cell is at E 650,000 m, N 3,950,000 m, and its cells are 30 m. Find the easting and northing of the cell in row 4, column 7. How many cells would it take to cover a 3 km by 3 km square? How many with 10 m cells?
Read the metadata. Download a layer from NC OneMap (https://www.nconemap.gov) and open its metadata. Who made it, when, and how? What coordinate system does it use? Would you trust it for an ambulance routing system? For a state overview map?
Shapefile detective. Download a shapefile from the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line page, unzip it, and list every file in the folder. What does each one hold? Then open the layer in QGIS or ArcGIS Pro and look at its attribute table. Which field names look cut short to 10 characters?
Vector or raster? For each of these, choose vector or raster and explain why: hiking trails, wildfire burn severity, voting precincts, nighttime lights seen from space, the locations of cell towers, and annual rainfall.

title: 2  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
2.9 Further reading and online resources

2.9.1 Books and open textbooks

GIS Fundamentals: A First Text on Geographic Information Systems, by Paul Bolstad (Bolstad 2022). Chapter 2, “Data Models,” covers the vector, raster, and TIN models, topology, and data structures in depth.
Understanding GIS through Sustainable Development Goals, by Paul Holloway (Holloway 2023). Its chapters on spatial data introduce vector and raster data with worked examples.
Essentials of Geographic Information Systems, by Jonathan Campbell and Michael Shin. Chapter 4, “Data Models for GIS,” and Chapter 5, “Geospatial Data Management,” are free online: https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/67, also on LibreTexts at https://geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Geography_(Physical)/Essentials_of_Geographic_Information_Systems_(Campbell_and_Shin).
Intro to GIS and Spatial Analysis, by Manuel Gimond. See the chapters “Feature Representation” and “GIS Data Formats”: https://mgimond.github.io/Spatial/.
The Nature of Geographic Information, by David DiBiase and colleagues at Penn State. Chapter 1, “Data and Information,” and its sections on vector and raster representations: https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/.
GIS Commons: An Introductory Textbook on Geographic Information Systems, by Michael Schmandt. A free online text with a chapter on data models: https://giscommons.org.
Geographic Information Systems and Science, by Paul Longley, Michael Goodchild, David Maguire, and David Rhind. The chapters on representing geography and on data models are classics of the field.



2.9.2 Data models: vector, raster, and TIN

The GIS&T Body of Knowledge, from UCGIS, has short articles on this chapter’s ideas. Search it for “Vector Data Models,” “Raster Data Models,” “The Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN),” “Conceptual Models of Space,” and “Topology”: https://www.ucgis.org/site/gis-t-body-of-knowledge.
QGIS, A Gentle Introduction to GIS, the chapters “Vector Data,” “Vector Attribute Data,” and “Raster Data”: https://docs.qgis.org/latest/en/docs/gentle_gis_introduction/.
Esri, “Introduction to image and raster data,” in the ArcGIS Pro help: https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/help/data/imagery/introduction-to-raster-data.htm.
Esri, “TIN in ArcGIS Pro”: https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/help/data/tin/tin-in-arcgis-pro.htm.
National Geographic Education, “Vector and raster data” and related resources on GIS: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/geographic-information-system-gis/.
GIS Geography, “Vector vs Raster in GIS: What’s the Difference?”: https://gisgeography.com/spatial-data-types-vector-raster/.

2.9.3 File formats

2.9.4 Metadata

2.9.7 Where to find geographic data

USGS National Map Downloader, for elevation, hydrography, and other national layers: https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/.
Natural Earth, free vector and raster world data: https://www.naturalearthdata.com.
OpenStreetMap, the free, editable vector map of the world: https://www.openstreetmap.org.




A real-world object we want to store as data, such as a tree, a
building, or a lake. On a map, an entity is shown as a feature.
How a map or a GIS represents an entity, usually as a point, a line, or
a polygon, with attributes that describe it.
The chain of steps that turns the real world into something a computer
can store: real world, data model, data structure, and machine code.
The way a GIS represents the real world as data, for example as points,
lines, and polygons (vector) or as a grid of cells (raster).
How a data model is laid out in a computer’s memory or files, for
example as lists of coordinate pairs linked by pointers.
Something with clear boundaries that is either present or absent at a
location, such as a road, a house, or a state.
A quantity that has a value at every location and changes gradually from
place to place, such as elevation, temperature, or rainfall.
Data tied to a location on or near Earth, such as the address of a
house, the outline of a county, or the elevation at a point.
A non-spatial fact about a feature, such as a building’s name or the
year it was built. Attributes are stored in a table with one row per
feature.
A data model that stores the world as points, lines, and polygons, each
defined by x, y coordinates and linked to its attributes. Best for
discrete objects.
A data model that stores the world as a regular grid of equal-sized
cells, each holding one value. Best for continuous data and imagery.
One square in a raster grid. Each cell holds one value. In an image, a
cell is called a pixel (picture element).
A system of numbers, such as latitude and longitude, that gives every
location a unique position so layers line up with each other.
The real-world length of one side of a raster cell, such as 30 meters.
Smaller cells give finer resolution and larger files.
The level of detail in data. For a raster, it is set by the cell size:
the smaller the cells, the finer the resolution.
A common vector format from Esri that stores one layer in several files
with the same name: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), and .dbf (attributes)
are required, and .prj holds the coordinate system.
A set of spatial data about one theme, such as roads, soils, or
elevation. Layers for the same area stack on top of each other to make a
map.
Data about data: who made a dataset, when, how, in what coordinate
system, and how accurate it is.
“A computer-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage,
analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information”
(Bolstad). Its five components are data, hardware, software, people, and
procedures.
A vector feature with a location but no length or area, stored as a
single x, y coordinate pair, such as a well or a school.
A vector feature with length but no area, stored as an ordered list of
coordinates, such as a road or a stream.
A vector feature that encloses an area: a closed line whose first and
last points are the same, such as a lake, a park, or a county.
A free and open-source desktop GIS that runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
Esri’s commercial desktop GIS, for Windows.
A polygon for one piece of property, usually with its owner and address.
An organized collection of tables, usually stored and managed by a
database management system.
Triangulated irregular network: a surface model that joins sampled
elevation points into triangles, using more triangles where the ground
is rough.
Text placed on a map, such as place names, street names, and labels.
The angle north or south of the equator, from 0° at the equator to 90°
at the poles.
The angle east or west of the prime meridian, from 0° at Greenwich to
180° east or west.
How far something reaches: its size, boundary, and dimensions. A layer’s
extent is the rectangle that just encloses all its features.
Data with no location of their own, such as a list of grades. When
non-spatial data describe a spatial feature, they are its attributes.
The shape of a feature: a point, a line, or a polygon, stored as
coordinates.
Turning an address or place name into coordinates, so it can be put on a
map.
Stacking layers of data for the same area to find places that meet
several conditions at once, such as flat land near a road and outside a
floodplain.
The start or end point of a line. In a network, lines meet at nodes. In
OpenStreetMap, a node is any single point with a latitude and longitude,
standing alone or as a vertex of a way.
An intermediate point where a line or polygon boundary changes
direction.
The straight piece of a line between two vertices or nodes.
Finding the best path through a network, such as the fastest or shortest
route, or a delivery route that visits many stops.
A distance north from a starting line: the y coordinate in a projected
coordinate system.
A distance east from a starting line: the x coordinate in a projected
coordinate system.
A series of U.S. Earth-observing satellites, run by NASA and the USGS,
that have imaged the whole planet since 1972, mostly with 30-meter
cells.
A line stored as an ordered list of coordinates. Polygons can be built
from arcs that share their end points.
In a data structure, a stored address that tells the computer where the
next piece of data, such as the next arc, is found.
The recorded connections between features, such as which polygons share
an edge and which lines meet at a node. It keeps neighbors from having
gaps or overlaps.
The company that makes ArcGIS, founded in 1969 by Jack and Laura
Dangermond in Redlands, California.
A mathematical method for flattening the round Earth onto a flat map.
Every projection distorts area, shape, distance, or direction in some
way.
An open file format (.gpkg) from the Open Geospatial Consortium that
stores many vector and raster layers in a single file. It is QGIS’s
default format.
Math on rasters, cell by cell, such as adding two grids or finding every
cell where slope is under 10 percent.
To convert vector data into a raster.
To convert a raster into vector features.
The Census Bureau’s boundary files for states, counties, tracts, roads,
and other features.
Methods that use the locations of things, and the relationships among
them, to find patterns, explain them, or make predictions.
A free collection of short, peer-reviewed articles on geographic
information science and technology topics, from the University
Consortium for Geographic Information Science (UCGIS).
A common synonym for geographic, used especially in industry,
the military, and government.
Running a GIS tool on spatial data to make new data, such as buffering,
clipping, or overlaying layers.
Software whose source code anyone may read, change, and share, often
free of charge. QGIS and GRASS GIS are open source.
A free, editable map of the world built by volunteers, founded in 2004.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.1 Where are we?
Chapter 2 asked how a computer can store a tree, a road, or a mountain. The answer was coordinates: a point is an x, y pair, and a line or polygon is a list of them. This chapter asks the next question. What are those numbers measured from? A coordinate pair like 35.91, −79.05 means nothing until you know what the Earth’s shape is assumed to be, where that shape sits, and how the angles are counted. This is the first central problem of GIS: how do we represent a round, lumpy, spinning world in a computer?
Every GIS layer starts with location, and every location depends on three choices: a model of the Earth’s shape, a datum that pins that model to the ground, and a coordinate system for writing positions. This chapter builds those three layers from the ground up. Chapter 4 adds the fourth, the map projection that flattens it all onto a screen.
People describe where things are all the time, and most of the time they do it relative to something else. “You are here” on a mall map. “Ten paces north of the old oak” on a treasure map. A pile of stones, a cairn, that marks a trail above the treeline. “Third floor, past the elevators” on a building directory. Each is a relative location: it describes a place by its relation to a landmark. Relative locations work well, but only if you already know the landmark. Hand the treasure map to someone in another county, cut down the oak, and the directions are useless.
A street address is a step better. 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC, finds the White House for anyone who knows how Washington numbers its streets. But an address depends on a local naming system, and it doesn’t work in the ocean, in a national forest, or in a new subdivision whose streets haven’t been named yet.
An absolute location names a place in a system that means the same thing to everyone, everywhere. The White House is at 38° 53′ 52″ N, 77° 02′ 11″ W. Anyone with a GPS receiver, in any country, can go to that spot without knowing a single landmark in Washington. That is what a GIS needs: coordinates that resolve to the same spot no matter who reads them, so that layers made by different people at different times line up.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
TipThink about it



Write down three ways to tell a friend where your dorm or apartment is. Which are relative, which are absolute, and which would still work for a visitor from another country?

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
section: 3.2 Modeling the shape of the Earth
text:
3.2 Modeling the shape of the Earth

3.2.1 Geodesy
Before we can give anything a coordinate, we need a mathematical model of the Earth to measure against. Geodesy is the science of measuring the Earth’s size, shape, orientation in space, and gravity field. It is one of the oldest sciences, and it began with a clever bit of geometry.
Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes, the head of the great library at Alexandria, in Egypt, heard that at noon on the summer solstice the sun shone straight down a well at Syene (today’s Aswan), far to the south, so that it cast no shadow. At the same moment in Alexandria, a vertical pole did cast a shadow, at an angle of about 7.2°. Because the sun is so far away, its rays arrive at the Earth parallel to each other. So the shadow angle at Alexandria is the same as the angle between the two cities measured at the Earth’s center (Figure 3.1). And 7.2° is one-fiftieth of a full circle (360° ÷ 7.2° = 50). The distance from Alexandria to Syene, about 5,000 stadia, must therefore be one-fiftieth of the Earth’s circumference, which makes the circumference about 250,000 stadia.






Figure 3.1: How Eratosthenes measured the Earth. The sun’s rays are parallel, so the angle of a pole’s shadow at Alexandria equals the angle between Alexandria and Syene at the Earth’s center.



Nobody knows exactly how long Eratosthenes’s stadion was, so we can’t say exactly how close he came. Depending on which length you use, his answer is within roughly 2 to 15 percent of today’s value of about 40,075 km around the equator. Not bad for a stick, a well, and some geometry, more than 2,200 years ago.
Modern geodesy uses satellites, lasers, radio telescopes, and the Global Positioning System (GPS) to measure positions to the centimeter, and to watch the continents drift by a few centimeters a year. That precision is what makes modern datums possible.


3.2.2 Sphere or ellipsoid?
The simplest model of the Earth is a sphere, with one radius, about 6,371 km, everywhere. For a world map on a page, a sphere is good enough.
But the Earth spins, and spinning makes it bulge at the equator and flatten at the poles. Its shape is an oblate spheroid, or ellipsoid: an ellipse rotated about its short, polar axis (Figure 3.2). Two numbers define an ellipsoid:

The semi-major axis, a, is the equatorial radius: about 6,378 km.
The semi-minor axis, b, is the polar radius: about 6,357 km.

How squashed the ellipsoid is, its flattening, is
\[f = \frac{a - b}{a}\]
For the Earth, f is about 1/298. The equatorial radius is only about 21 km longer than the polar radius, a third of one percent, which is why the Earth looks perfectly round from space. But 21 km is a big error when you want positions to the meter, so detailed mapping always uses an ellipsoid.






Figure 3.2: A sphere (left) has one radius. An ellipsoid (right) has a longer equatorial radius, a, and a shorter polar radius, b. The flattening is greatly exaggerated here.



Over the years, surveyors have fitted many ellipsoids to the Earth, each from the best measurements of its day, and some fitted to one region rather than the whole planet. Three you will meet:



Table 3.1: Three common ellipsoids. GRS 80 and WGS 84 differ by only a fraction of a millimeter in b.











Ellipsoid
Semi-major axis a
Semi-minor axis b
Used by




Clarke 1866
6,378,206.4 m
6,356,583.8 m
NAD27, the older North American datum


GRS 80
6,378,137.0 m
6,356,752.3 m
NAD83


WGS 84
6,378,137.0 m
6,356,752.3 m
WGS84, the datum GPS uses












NoteDid you know..?



Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, at 8,849 m. But because the Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador just one degree south of the equator, is the point on Earth’s surface farthest from the Earth’s center: about 6,384 km, roughly 2 km farther out than Everest’s summit, even though Chimborazo is only about 6,263 m above sea level. Stand on top of Chimborazo, and you are the person on land closest to the stars.




3.2.3 The geoid
An ellipsoid is smooth and mathematical. The real Earth isn’t. Mountains, ocean trenches, and dense rock deep inside the planet make gravity a little stronger in some places and weaker in others, and water flows “downhill” toward the stronger pull.
Imagine the oceans perfectly still, with no tides, winds, or currents, and extended in canals under the continents. Their surface would settle along a surface of equal gravity. That surface is the geoid, and it is the best match to global mean sea level. Because mass inside the Earth is unevenly spread, the geoid is lumpy: relative to the WGS 84 ellipsoid, it sits as much as about 106 m below, in the Indian Ocean south of India, and about 85 m above, near New Guinea.
The geoid matters because it is what elevation is measured from. When a topographic map says a summit is 2,037 m above sea level, that height is measured from the geoid. Geodesists publish geoid models that give the geoid’s height everywhere: EGM2008 for the whole world, and GEOID18 for the United States.


3.2.4 Three heights
So every point on the ground has three related heights (Figure 3.3):

Ellipsoid height, h: the height above the ellipsoid. This is what a GPS receiver measures.
Orthometric height, H: the height above the geoid. This is the elevation printed on maps, the “height above sea level.”
Geoid height, N: the distance between the two surfaces at that spot, from the ellipsoid up to the geoid.

They are related by a simple equation:
\[h = H + N\]






Figure 3.3: Three heights at one point. GPS measures ellipsoid height, h. Maps show orthometric height, H, above the geoid. The geoid height, N, is the gap between the two surfaces.



In the lower 48 United States the geoid lies below the ellipsoid, so N is negative, roughly −30 m. In North Carolina it is roughly −30 to −35 m. Rearranging the equation, H = h − N, so elevation is about 30 m higher than the raw height a GPS receiver reports. That is why surveyors and GPS apps always apply a geoid model before they report an elevation.






TipThink about it



A GPS receiver on a hilltop in Chapel Hill reports an ellipsoid height of 120 m. The geoid height there is about −33 m. What is the hilltop’s elevation above sea level?


Show the answer

H = h − N = 120 − (−33) = 153 m. Subtracting a negative number adds it, so the elevation is higher than the GPS height.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.3 Geodetic datums

3.3.1 What is a datum?
An ellipsoid on its own is just a shape floating in space. A geodetic datum fixes an ellipsoid’s size, shape, and position relative to the real Earth: where its center is, and how it is oriented. Only then do latitude and longitude point to real places on the ground. A datum combines:

an ellipsoid,
an origin and orientation, which say where the ellipsoid sits, and
a network of control points on the ground whose coordinates have been measured precisely.

Those control points are how a datum is realized, made real on the ground. For two centuries surveyors measured them with instruments like the theodolite, a telescope that measures horizontal and vertical angles very precisely, and by triangulation: measuring the angles of a chain of triangles between hilltop stations, and from a few carefully measured baselines working out the distance to every other station, across a whole continent. At each station they set a bronze disk, a benchmark or survey marker, in rock or concrete, often with a witness post nearby warning people not to disturb it. You can find these disks on mountaintops, bridges, and courthouse steps all over the country, and the National Geodetic Survey publishes the coordinates of each one.
Today the control network is mostly satellites and permanent GPS stations, but the idea is the same. Every coordinate you collect is only meaningful relative to a particular datum.


3.3.2 NAD27
The North American Datum of 1927 (NAD27) used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid, which was fitted to North America rather than to the whole Earth. Its origin was a single survey station on Meades Ranch, in Kansas, near the middle of the contiguous United States. Its coordinates came from a huge adjustment of the triangulation networks of the day. Many older maps, including the classic USGS paper topographic quadrangles, use NAD27.


3.3.3 NAD83
The North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83) uses the GRS 80 ellipsoid and is earth-centered: the center of its ellipsoid is at the Earth’s center of mass. That made it compatible with satellite positioning. NAD83 is fixed to the North American tectonic plate, so the coordinates of a benchmark stay the same as the continent drifts.
NAD83 has been readjusted several times as measurements improved. Each version is a realization, written with its year in parentheses: NAD83(HARN), NAD83(2007), and NAD83(2011), the current one. A nationwide network of Continuously Operating Reference Stations (CORS), GPS receivers bolted to buildings and concrete piers that run around the clock, keeps it accurate.
NAD83 is the datum of most U.S. federal and state GIS data, including the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line files and North Carolina’s NC OneMap.


3.3.4 WGS84
The World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84) is a global, earth-centered datum maintained by the U.S. Department of Defense, and it is the datum GPS uses. Coordinates from your phone, from Google Maps, and from most websites are almost always WGS84.
In 1984, WGS84 and NAD83 agreed to within about a meter. But NAD83 moves with the North American plate, while WGS84 is tied to the whole Earth, so as the plate has drifted (and been realized again with better measurements) the two have separated. In North America today they differ by about 1 to 2 meters. For a statewide map, that is too small to see. For a survey of a property line, it matters a lot.


3.3.5 Datum shift
Here is the key point: the same latitude and longitude point to different places in different datums (Figure 3.4). The difference between where a coordinate lands in one datum and where it lands in another is a datum shift.






Figure 3.4: A datum shift. Two datums use different ellipsoids in different positions, so the same latitude and longitude land at two different places on the real Earth.



Between NAD27 and NAD83, the shift is anywhere from a few meters to over 100 meters across the United States. In one well-known USGS example from the Hayward, California, quadrangle, a single coordinate pair plotted in NAD27 and in NAD83 lands nearly 100 meters apart. That is a city block, plenty to put a well on the wrong side of a property line or a fire hydrant in the middle of a street.
This is one of the most common errors in GIS. Two layers that should line up, such as roads and parcels, are offset by a constant amount, because one is in NAD27 and the other in NAD83. The fix is a datum transformation: a set of equations, or a grid of measured shifts, that converts coordinates from one datum to another. QGIS and ArcGIS Pro apply datum transformations when you project or import data, and they will sometimes ask you to choose one. Before you combine layers, check each layer’s datum.






NoteDid you know..?



NAD83 is about to retire. The National Geodetic Survey is replacing it with a new set of datums, the modernized National Spatial Reference System. NATRF2022 (the North American Terrestrial Reference Frame of 2022) will replace NAD83 for latitude and longitude, and NAPGD2022 will replace NAVD 88 for elevations. Because NAD83’s center turned out to be about 2 meters off the Earth’s true center of mass, coordinates in the new datum will move by about 1 to 2 meters across the country, and elevations will change by up to a meter or more. Beta tools were released in 2026 and adoption is expected around 2027, so this is a datum change you will live through in your own career.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.4 Geographic coordinates

3.4.1 Building a coordinate system
With a datum in place, we can write positions as latitude and longitude. Let’s build that coordinate system from scratch.

The poles. The Earth spins around an axis. Where the axis meets the surface are the North and South Poles: two natural reference points.
The equator. Halfway between the poles is the equator, the natural zero line for north and south.
A prime meridian. For east and west there is no natural zero line, so we have to choose one. Many countries once used their own: Paris, Washington, Philadelphia, Cádiz. In 1884, the International Meridian Conference in Washington, DC, chose the meridian through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, England, as the prime meridian for the world.

With those reference lines in place (Figure 3.5):

Latitude is the angle north or south of the equator, measured at the Earth’s center. It runs from 0° at the equator to 90° N at the North Pole and 90° S at the South Pole.
Longitude is the angle east or west of the prime meridian. It runs from 0° at Greenwich to 180° east or west. 180° E and 180° W are the same line, which the International Date Line roughly follows.







Figure 3.5: Latitude (left) is an angle north or south of the equator. Longitude (right) is an angle east or west of the prime meridian, here seen from above the North Pole. Chapel Hill is at about 35.9° N, 79.05° W.



Strictly, on an ellipsoid the latitude angle is measured between the equator and a line perpendicular to the ellipsoid’s surface, which doesn’t pass quite through the center. This geodetic latitude is what GIS software and GPS use. The difference from the simple picture is at most about a fifth of a degree, at 45°.


3.4.2 Parallels and meridians
Now draw the grid (Figure 3.6).

Parallels are lines of equal latitude. They run east and west, they are parallel to the equator and to each other, and they get shorter toward the poles. They measure latitude.
Meridians are lines of equal longitude. They run north and south, from pole to pole, and all of them meet at the poles. They measure longitude.







Figure 3.6: Parallels (left) are lines of equal latitude; the equator is the parallel at 0°. Meridians (right) are lines of equal longitude; the prime meridian is the meridian at 0°.



The equator and the prime meridian are both zero lines, so a place on the equator is at 0° N, which is the same as 0° S, and a place on the prime meridian is at 0° E, which is the same as 0° W. Both answers are right.


3.4.3 How far is a degree?
Because the parallels are evenly spaced, one degree of latitude is always about the same distance: about 111 km, or 69 miles. (It varies a little, from 110.6 km at the equator to 111.7 km at the poles, because the ellipsoid is flatter there.)
A degree of longitude is different. The meridians come together at the poles, so the distance between them shrinks as you move away from the equator. One degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator, about 90 km at Chapel Hill’s latitude, 56 km at 60° N, and zero at the poles. (The rule is 111 km × the cosine of the latitude.) Remember this. It is why latitude and longitude are angles, not distances, and why you can’t measure distance or area in degrees.


3.4.4 Writing degrees
Latitude and longitude are angles, and there are two common ways to write them (Table 3.2).
Decimal degrees (DD) write the angle as one signed number. Positive numbers are north latitudes and east longitudes; negative numbers are south latitudes and west longitudes. Chapel Hill is at 35.9132, −79.0558. This is the format most GIS software and GPS units use, and the one you should type into a GIS.
Degrees, minutes, and seconds (DMS) split the angle the way we split an hour: there are 60 minutes (′) in a degree and 60 seconds (″) in a minute, so a second is 1/3,600 of a degree. Instead of a sign, DMS uses a letter for the hemisphere: N, S, E, or W. Chapel Hill is at 35° 54′ 48″ N, 79° 03′ 21″ W.



Table 3.2: Two ways to write the same longitude, a meridian that runs just east of Denver, Colorado.











Decimal degrees
Degrees, minutes, seconds




Example
−104.54°
104° 32′ 24″ W


Hemisphere
A sign: negative is south or west
A letter: N, S, E, or W


Used by
GIS software, GPS, spreadsheets, the web
Paper maps, nautical charts, surveys, deeds








3.4.5 Converting between them
Decimal degrees to DMS. Take −104.54°:

The whole number is the degrees: 104°.
Multiply the decimal part by 60 to get minutes: 0.54 × 60 = 32.4, so 32′.
Multiply the leftover decimal by 60 again to get seconds: 0.4 × 60 = 24″.
The sign becomes the hemisphere letter. A negative longitude is west: 104° 32′ 24″ W.

DMS to decimal degrees. Take the White House’s latitude, 38° 53′ 52″ N:
\[DD = D + \frac{M}{60} + \frac{S}{3600}\]
\[38 + \frac{53}{60} + \frac{52}{3600} = 38 + 0.8833 + 0.0144 = 38.8978°\]
It is north, so the number stays positive: 38.8978°. For a longitude west of Greenwich or a latitude south of the equator, put a minus sign in front.
Keep at least four to six decimal places when you convert, or the point will move. The next section shows how far.






TipThink about it



Convert Chapel Hill’s longitude, −79.0558°, to degrees, minutes, and seconds. Then convert 35° 54′ 48″ N to decimal degrees.


Show the answers

79°; 0.0558 × 60 = 3.348, so 3′; 0.348 × 60 = 20.88, about 21″. Negative, so west: 79° 03′ 21″ W.
35 + 54/60 + 48/3600 = 35 + 0.9 + 0.01333 = 35.9133°.





3.4.6 Precision and location
How many decimal places should a coordinate have? Each decimal place makes a coordinate ten times more precise (Table 3.3). Since a degree of latitude is about 111 km, each place you add divides that distance by ten.



Table 3.3: How precise is a decimal degree? Distances are for latitude, and for longitude at the equator; a degree of longitude covers less ground away from the equator.

A phone’s GPS is usually accurate to about 3 to 5 meters in the open, so five decimal places, about a meter, is already more than enough. Reporting eight decimal places claims millimeter precision that a phone doesn’t have. Extra decimals don’t make your data more accurate; they only make it look more accurate than it is. On the other hand, cutting coordinates to two or three decimal places, which spreadsheets sometimes do on their own, can move your points by a kilometer.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.5 Lines on the globe

3.5.1 Great circles
A great circle is the largest circle you can draw on a sphere. Its plane passes through the Earth’s center, and it cuts the globe into two equal halves. Any circle whose plane doesn’t pass through the center is a small circle.
Great circles matter for one big reason: the shortest route between two points on a sphere follows a great circle. That is why airline routes look curved on flat maps. A flight from New York to London heads northeast, passes near Newfoundland, and approaches Britain from the northwest. It looks like a detour on a flat map, but on the globe it is the straight path (Figure 3.7).






Figure 3.7: The great-circle route from New York to London (solid red) and a straight line on a flat Plate Carrée map (dashed). The great circle looks curved on the flat map, but it is the shortest path; the “straight” line is about 230 km longer.



Which parallels and meridians are great circles?


Show the answer

Every meridian, together with the meridian on the opposite side of the globe (180° away), makes a great circle, because its plane passes through the poles and the Earth’s center. Of the parallels, only the equator is a great circle. Every other parallel is a small circle, and the parallels get smaller toward the poles.



3.5.2 The graticule
The graticule is the network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map. It tells readers how the map has bent the globe to flatten it, and it lets them estimate the latitude and longitude of any place.
Choosing which lines to draw is a design decision (Figure 3.8). Too many lines clutter the map and compete with the data; too few, and the grid stops being useful. A common rule of thumb is every 15° or 30° on a world map, every 5° or 10° on a map of a continent, and every degree or less on a map of a state. Always ask what the reader needs the grid for. A world map of climate zones might only need the equator, the tropics, and the Arctic and Antarctic Circles.






Figure 3.8: The same world map with a graticule every 5°, every 15°, and every 30°. The 5° grid crowds the map; the 30° grid barely helps you read a location.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.6 From globe to flat map
Latitude and longitude are angles measured on a curved surface. They are not x and y distances on a flat plane. But a computer screen is flat, and so is a sheet of paper. So what happens if we simply pretend they are?
Plot longitude as x and latitude as y on an even grid, and you get the Plate Carrée, French for “flat square,” also called the equirectangular projection (Figure 3.9). Every 1° by 1° cell is a square on the map. It is what you see when you add a layer in latitude and longitude to a GIS without choosing a projection.






Figure 3.9: On the globe (left), each red circle covers the same area on the ground. On the Plate Carrée (right), where longitude is x and latitude is y, the circles stretch east to west more and more toward the poles.



The grid is simple, but the cells are only square on the map, not on the globe. On the Earth, a 1° cell at the equator is about 111 km on each side; at 60° N it is still 111 km tall but only 56 km wide. The Plate Carrée draws both as squares, so it stretches everything east to west more and more toward the poles. Greenland looks wide and squat, and Antarctica becomes a long band across the bottom of the map.
That raises the question for the next chapter: how do we represent a round Earth on a flat surface? Every answer, called a map projection, distorts something. Chapter 4 shows what each kind of projection keeps and what it gives up.






NoteDid you know..?



If you visit the Royal Observatory in Greenwich and stand astride the famous brass line of the prime meridian, a GPS app will tell you that you are not at 0°. It reads about 0.0015° W: the zero of longitude that GPS uses is about 102 meters east of the line. Nothing moved. The brass line marks the meridian astronomers defined in 1851 with a telescope that pointed along the local direction of gravity, which is tilted slightly by the local geoid. The modern earth-centered datums, WGS84 among them, define longitude from the Earth’s center of mass instead, and that small difference in the vertical becomes about 100 meters on the ground.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.7 Putting it together
Think of location in a GIS as a stack, with each layer built on the one below (Figure 4.1):

The Earth, the real, irregular surface, approximated by the geoid.
An ellipsoid, a smooth mathematical model of the Earth, such as GRS 80.
A datum, which pins the ellipsoid to the Earth and defines latitude and longitude, such as NAD83.
A map projection, which turns latitude and longitude into flat x, y coordinates, such as UTM.







Figure 3.10: From the Earth to a map. Each layer is built on the one below. This chapter covered the bottom three; Chapter 4 covers map projections.



A coordinate system that stops at the third layer, giving positions in latitude and longitude on a datum, is a geographic coordinate system (GCS). NAD83 and WGS84, used for latitude and longitude, are both geographic coordinate systems. A coordinate system that adds the fourth layer is a projected coordinate system, the subject of Chapter 4.
The most common point of confusion in this part of the course is the difference between a datum and a projection. A datum answers where is the Earth, and what shape is it? A projection answers how do I flatten it? Changing the datum moves your points on the ground. Changing the projection only changes how they are drawn on a flat map.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.9 Summary

A GIS needs absolute locations, coordinates that mean the same thing to everyone, rather than relative locations tied to landmarks.
Geodesy measures the Earth’s size and shape. Eratosthenes estimated its circumference around 240 BCE from shadow angles.
The Earth is modeled as an ellipsoid, defined by its semi-major axis a and semi-minor axis b, with a flattening of about 1/298. Common ellipsoids are Clarke 1866, GRS 80, and WGS 84.
The geoid is the surface of equal gravity that best matches mean sea level. Elevations are measured from it. Ellipsoid height (from GPS), orthometric height (elevation), and geoid height are related by h = H + N.
A geodetic datum fixes an ellipsoid to the Earth through control points. NAD27 used Clarke 1866 and an origin in Kansas; NAD83 uses GRS 80 and is earth-centered; WGS84 is the global datum GPS uses. The same coordinates land in different places in different datums, so check each layer’s datum and apply a datum transformation when needed.
Latitude is measured north and south from the equator, and longitude east and west from the prime meridian at Greenwich. Parallels are lines of latitude and meridians are lines of longitude; the network of both on a map is the graticule.
Coordinates can be written in decimal degrees (negative for south and west) or degrees, minutes, and seconds. Each decimal place makes a coordinate ten times more precise; five places is about a meter.
The shortest route between two places follows a great circle.
Treating latitude and longitude as x and y gives the Plate Carrée, which stretches the map toward the poles. Flattening the Earth well takes a map projection, the subject of Chapter 4.

title: 3  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
3.10 Exercises

Describe a place three ways. Pick a place on campus. Describe it with a relative location, a street address, and an absolute location in both decimal degrees and DMS. (Find its coordinates by right-clicking it in Google Maps or OpenStreetMap.)
Eratosthenes at home. Suppose that at noon a pole in your town casts a shadow at an angle of 5°, while at the same moment the sun is straight overhead in a town 550 km due south. What is the Earth’s circumference by Eratosthenes’s method? How close is it to 40,075 km?
Conversions. Convert to DMS: 35.2271, −80.8431 (Charlotte) and −33.8568, 151.2153 (the Sydney Opera House). Convert to decimal degrees: 40° 41′ 21″ N, 74° 02′ 40″ W (the Statue of Liberty).
Heights. Look up the elevation and the geoid height for your hometown with the NGS GEOID18 calculator (https://geodesy.noaa.gov/GEOID/GEOID18/computation.html). What ellipsoid height would a GPS receiver report there?
Find a benchmark. Use the NGS Data Explorer (https://geodesy.noaa.gov/NGSDataExplorer/) to find a survey marker near campus. What datum are its coordinates given in? When was it last recovered?
Datum detective. In QGIS, open the Layer Properties of any layer and find its coordinate reference system on the Information tab. In ArcGIS Pro, look in the layer’s Properties, on the Source tab. Which datum does it use? Find one layer from a state or federal source and one from a website or a phone app. Do they use the same datum?
Precision. A classmate collects tree locations with a phone and records them to ten decimal places. Explain, using Table 3.3, why that is misleading. How many decimal places would you keep, and why?
Great circles. Use the Great Circle Mapper (http://www.gcmap.com) to draw the route from Raleigh-Durham (RDU) to Tokyo (NRT). Which states and countries does it pass over? Why doesn’t it head due west?

above sea level,” printed on maps. h = H + N.

N. In the lower 48 United States it is negative, about −30 m.

by GPS. It differs from NAD83 by about 1 to 2 meters in North America.

Negative numbers are south latitudes and west longitudes.

and seconds (1/3,600 of a degree), with a hemisphere letter, such as 79°

at the poles.

y on an even grid. It stretches the map east to west toward the

values.

a. For the Earth, about 1/298.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.1 What is a map projection?
Chapter 3 built the bottom three layers of location in a GIS: the real Earth, an ellipsoid that models it, and a datum that pins the ellipsoid to the ground and gives us latitude and longitude. This chapter adds the top layer (Figure 4.1). A map projection converts latitude and longitude, angles on a curved surface, into flat x, y coordinates on a screen or a sheet of paper.
There is a catch, and it is the main idea of this chapter: every flat map distorts the Earth. You cannot flatten an orange peel without stretching or tearing it, and you cannot flatten the Earth without distorting shape, area, distance, or direction. Choosing a projection means choosing which errors you can live with. By the end of this chapter you will know how to make that choice for your own GIS work.
A map projection is a set of equations that converts latitude and longitude on the ellipsoid into x, y coordinates on a flat plane. Every projected map, every web map, and every measurement of distance or area in a GIS depends on one.
The classic way to picture a projection is with light. Put a light bulb inside a transparent globe, hold a screen against it, and the light casts the coastlines and the graticule onto the screen (Figure 4.2). Where the screen touches the globe, the image is exact. Farther away, the shadows stretch, and evenly spaced points on the globe spread farther and farther apart on the screen.
The light bulb is an analogy. Most modern projections are defined by equations, not by real shadows, but the analogy explains why distortion grows with distance from the place where the map surface touches the Earth.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
Figure 4.2: The light-bulb picture of a projection. A light at the globe’s center casts points onto a flat map plane. Near the point where the plane touches the globe there is no distortion; farther away, points that are evenly spaced on the globe spread apart on the map.










TipThink about it



Peel a clementine or an orange in as few pieces as you can, and try to press the peel flat on a table. Where does it tear? Where does it stretch? Every map projection makes the same kinds of compromises, just with mathematics instead of fingers.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.2 Every projection distorts something

4.2.1 Four properties
A map can preserve four properties of the globe, each one named for the kind of projection that keeps it:

Shape. A conformal projection keeps local angles true, so small shapes look right. A tiny circle on the globe is still a circle on the map, though it may be larger or smaller.
Area. An equal-area (or equivalent) projection keeps relative size true. A county twice as large as another on the ground is twice as large on the map.
Distance. An equidistant projection keeps true scale along certain lines, usually from one or two points. No projection keeps true distance between every pair of places.
Direction. An azimuthal projection keeps true directions, or bearings, from a center point.

No flat map keeps all four. In particular, no projection can be both conformal and equal-area. Some projections preserve none of the four exactly, but keep every error moderate: these are compromise projections.


4.2.2 Seeing distortion: Tissot’s indicatrix
How can you see what a projection does? In 1859, the French mathematician Nicolas Auguste Tissot came up with an elegant tool, now called Tissot’s indicatrix: draw identical small circles all over the globe, then project them. On the map, each circle becomes an ellipse whose size and shape show the distortion at that spot. If the circles stay round, shapes are preserved there; if they all cover the same area, area is preserved.
Figure 4.3 shows Tissot’s circles, each 500 km across on the ground, on four world maps.






Figure 4.3: Four projections of the same world, with identical circles (each 500 km across on the ground) drawn every 30°. On the conformal Mercator they stay round but grow toward the poles. On the equal-area Mollweide they keep their area but stretch. On an azimuthal equidistant map centered on Chapel Hill, distances from the center are true. On the Robinson compromise, no property is exact.





4.2.3 Mercator and reality
The most famous map projection is the one Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish mapmaker, published in 1569 for sailors. On a Mercator map, a line of constant compass bearing, called a rhumb line, is a straight line. A navigator could draw a straight line from port to port, read its angle, and steer that compass course the whole way. The Mercator is conformal, so small shapes and angles are right, which is what made it so useful at sea.
The price is area. To keep shapes right while the meridians stay parallel, Mercator stretches the map north and south as much as it stretches east and west, and that stretch grows with latitude. On a Mercator map, the scale at any latitude is the secant of the latitude (1 ÷ cos), and areas are enlarged by the square of that. At 60° north or south, a place looks four times larger than it is. Near the poles, the enlargement goes to infinity, which is why Mercator maps are always cut off before the poles.
The classic example is Greenland and Africa (Figure 4.4). On a Mercator map they look about the same size. In fact, Africa, about 30 million km², is roughly 14 times larger than Greenland, about 2.2 million km². Countries near the equator, like Brazil, Indonesia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, barely change size; countries far from it, like Canada, Russia, and Greenland, swell.






Figure 4.4: Greenland (blue) and Africa (green) on a Mercator map (left) and an equal-area map (right). The dashed red outline is Greenland at its true size, moved to the equator over Africa.



Use Mercator for navigation, not for comparing areas.






NoteDid you know..?



In 2017, the Boston Public Schools began replacing Mercator wall maps in their classrooms with the equal-area Gall-Peters projection. Teachers said the Mercator had shrunk Africa and South America in students’ minds for generations. The Gall-Peters itself is controversial: when the historian Arno Peters promoted it in the 1970s as a fairer map, cartographers pointed out that a Scottish clergyman, James Gall, had published the same projection in 1855, and that it badly stretches shapes near the equator. Many cartographers would rather see a good compromise projection on the wall. Either way, the choice of a map projection turns out to be a choice about how people picture the world.




4.2.4 Web Mercator: for display, not measurement
Look at almost any web map, such as Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, Bing Maps, or an Esri basemap, and you are looking at Web Mercator, code EPSG:3857. It treats the Earth as a sphere while using WGS84 latitude and longitude, which makes the math fast. Its great strength is that the whole world fits in a square, which can be cut into square tiles at every zoom level: one tile at zoom 0, four at zoom 1, sixteen at zoom 2, and so on (Figure 4.5). Your browser only downloads the tiles you are looking at, which is why web maps scroll and zoom so smoothly.






Figure 4.5: Web Mercator divides the world into square tiles. Each zoom level splits every tile into four.



To make the world square, Web Mercator cuts the map off at about 85.05° north and south, so the North and South Poles are not on the map at all. And it inherits all of Mercator’s area enlargement. Use it for:

web basemaps, and
smooth zooming and panning.

Avoid it for:

measuring area or distance,
comparing regions at different latitudes, and
anything near the poles.

If you collect data from a web map, reproject it to an equal-area or a local projection, such as UTM or State Plane, before you calculate areas or distances.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.3 How projections are made

4.3.1 Three developable surfaces
A developable surface is a shape that can be unrolled flat without stretching or tearing. Three are used for map projections: the plane, the cylinder, and the cone (Figure 4.6).

Planar (or azimuthal): a flat plane touches the globe at one point. Distortion grows in rings around that point, so planar projections suit the polar regions, or maps centered on one place.
Cylindrical: a cylinder wraps the globe. In its normal position it touches the equator, which suits the tropics, or a world map. Turned on its side, as in the Transverse Mercator below, it suits regions that run north to south.
Conic: a cone sits over one hemisphere like a hat and touches it along a parallel. Conic projections suit mid-latitude regions that run east to west, such as the contiguous United States.







Figure 4.6: The three developable surfaces (top) and the maps they make when unrolled flat (bottom): a polar azimuthal map, a cylindrical (Mercator) map, and a conic (Lambert Conformal Conic) map.



The line where a surface is sliced so it can be unrolled becomes the outer edge of the map.


4.3.2 Tangent and secant
A projection surface can touch the globe in one place or cut through it (Figure 4.7).

A tangent surface touches the Earth along one line, or at one point for a planar projection.
A secant surface cuts through the Earth along two lines, or along a circle for a planar projection.

Where the surface meets the Earth, scale is exact. These are the standard lines (or a standard point). When standard lines follow parallels of latitude, as on a conic projection, they are called standard parallels. The ratio of distance on the map to distance on the ground, compared with the map’s stated scale, is the scale factor: exactly 1 on a standard line, less than 1 where the map shrinks the Earth, and more than 1 where it stretches it.






Figure 4.7: Tangent (left) and secant (right) projection surfaces in cross-section. Scale is exact where the surface meets the Earth. Between a secant surface’s standard lines, map distances are a little too short (ab is shorter than AB); outside them, a little too long (de is longer than DE).



Why cut through the Earth on purpose? A secant surface spreads the error across a wider area. A tangent surface is perfect on one line and gets steadily worse everywhere else. A secant surface is slightly too small between its standard lines and slightly too large outside them, which keeps the largest error over the whole map much smaller. Good projection design puts the standard lines so that the area you care about stays close to zero error.


4.3.3 Projections are named for what they preserve
Putting it together, projections are grouped by the property they keep (Table 4.1).



Table 4.1: Projections are named for the property they preserve. No projection can be both conformal and equal-area.











Property preserved
Class
Examples
Typical use




Shape (local angles)
Conformal
Mercator, Lambert Conformal Conic, Transverse Mercator
Navigation, topographic and engineering maps


Area
Equal-area
Albers Equal-Area Conic, Mollweide
Thematic maps of density or land cover

Equidistant
Azimuthal Equidistant, Equidistant Conic
Distances from a city or an airport

Gnomonic, Azimuthal Equidistant

World maps for general reference






On a gnomonic projection, every great circle (Chapter 3) is a straight line. Navigators once used gnomonic charts to plot the shortest route between two ports, then copied it onto a Mercator chart as a series of short rhumb lines they could actually steer.






NoteDid you know..?



For most of the twentieth century, the National Geographic Society, whose wall maps hung in classrooms across the country, used the Van der Grinten projection, which enlarges the polar regions almost as much as Mercator. In 1988 it switched to the Robinson projection, which Arthur Robinson had designed in 1963 by eye, adjusting the shape until the world simply looked right, rather than starting from an equation. Ten years later, in 1998, National Geographic switched again, to the Winkel Tripel, which has even less overall distortion and is still its standard world map.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.4 Projections for the United States

4.4.1 Lambert Conformal Conic
The Lambert Conformal Conic projection, published by Johann Heinrich Lambert in 1772, uses a secant cone that cuts the ellipsoid along two standard parallels. Scale is exact on both, slightly too small between them, and too large outside them. For the contiguous United States, standard parallels at 33° N and 45° N keep the scale error within about 1 percent across most of the country (Figure 4.8, left).
On the map, meridians are straight lines that converge toward a point beyond the pole, and parallels are arcs of circles centered on that point, which gives the map its fan shape. Because it is conformal, Lambert Conformal Conic keeps local angles and shapes. That is why it is used for U.S. aeronautical charts, where pilots need true angles, and for the State Plane zones of states that are wider east to west than north to south, like North Carolina and Tennessee.


4.4.2 Transverse Mercator
The Transverse Mercator is the Mercator turned 90°. Instead of touching the equator, the cylinder touches the Earth along a chosen central meridian. Scale is true along that meridian, or along two lines parallel to it in the secant version, and error grows east and west of it (Figure 4.8, right). Like the Mercator, it is conformal.






Figure 4.8: Scale error across the contiguous United States on a Lambert Conformal Conic projection with standard parallels at 33° N and 45° N (left), and a secant Transverse Mercator with a central meridian at 96° W (right). Contours show the error in percent: 0% is a line of true scale, blue areas are shrunk, and red areas are stretched.



A single Transverse Mercator for the whole country would be too distorted at the coasts. But in a narrow strip along its central meridian it is very accurate. So it is used in narrow zones: the State Plane zones of north–south states such as Illinois and Vermont, and the sixty zones of UTM.


4.4.3 Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)
The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system divides the world, from 80° S to 84° N, into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide. The zones are numbered eastward from 180° longitude, so zone 1 runs from 180° W to 174° W. The contiguous United States falls in zones 10 to 19 (Figure 4.9). Each zone has a north and a south half, such as 17N and 17S, on either side of the equator.






Figure 4.9: UTM zones 10 to 19 across the contiguous United States. Each zone is 6° of longitude wide (solid lines), with its central meridian (dashed red) down the middle. North Carolina (green) straddles zones 17 and 18.



Each zone is its own secant Transverse Mercator projection:

The scale factor on the central meridian is 0.9996, so the two lines of true scale sit about 180 km on either side of it, and the error stays below about 1 part in 1,000 across the zone.
Coordinates are in meters: an easting and a northing.
The central meridian is given a false easting of 500,000 m, so every easting in the zone is positive. In the Northern Hemisphere, northings are measured from the equator; in the Southern Hemisphere, the equator is given a false northing of 10,000,000 m, so southern northings stay positive too.

A UTM coordinate needs its zone to make sense. Chapel Hill is at about 676,000 m E, 3,976,000 m N in zone 17N. The same numbers in zone 18N would land about 540 km farther east, in the Atlantic Ocean, because each zone measures its eastings from its own central meridian.
North Carolina spans two zones, split at 78° W: zone 17N to the west, including Asheville, Charlotte, Chapel Hill, and Raleigh, and zone 18N to the east, including Greenville, Wilmington, and the Outer Banks (Figure 4.10). Data that crosses a zone boundary is a common source of error. For a project that spans both zones, pick one zone for the whole study area, or use State Plane instead.






Figure 4.10: North Carolina’s coordinate system zones. The dashed line at 78° W splits UTM zones 17N and 18N. The orange lines are the two standard parallels of the state’s single State Plane zone, at 34° 20′ N and 36° 10′ N.





4.4.4 The State Plane Coordinate System
The State Plane Coordinate System (SPCS) was designed in the 1930s by the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, now the National Geodetic Survey, so that surveyors and engineers could work with flat x, y coordinates with very little distortion. It exists in two main versions, based on NAD27 and on NAD83.

Each state is covered by one or more zones, about 120 in all, whose boundaries follow state and county lines.
States that are wide east to west, like Tennessee, use Lambert Conformal Conic; states that are long north to south, like Illinois, use Transverse Mercator. The Alaska panhandle uses an oblique Mercator.
Zones are kept small enough that scale error stays at 1 part in 10,000 or better: no more than 1 meter in 10 kilometers.

North Carolina has a single State Plane zone, a Lambert Conformal Conic with standard parallels at 34° 20′ N and 36° 10′ N (Figure 4.10). In a GIS you will usually meet it as EPSG:32119, NAD83 / North Carolina in meters, or EPSG:2264, the same projection in U.S. survey feet. They are the same projection with different units, so always check which units a dataset uses. Most North Carolina state and county data, including NC OneMap’s, is in State Plane feet.






TipThink about it



Your project maps every stream in Dare County, on the Outer Banks. Which would you choose: UTM zone 17N, UTM zone 18N, or NC State Plane? What if your project covered the whole state?


Show the answer

For Dare County alone, UTM zone 18N or NC State Plane both work well; zone 17N would put the county outside its own zone. For the whole state, choose NC State Plane, which was designed to cover North Carolina in one zone.

title: 4  Map Projections
section: 4.5 Coordinate reference systems and EPSG codes
text:
4.5 Coordinate reference systems and EPSG codes
In software, a projection never travels alone. A coordinate reference system (CRS) bundles a datum, a projection with its parameters (the standard parallels, central meridian, scale factor, false easting, and so on), and the units.
There are two kinds of CRS:

A geographic coordinate system gives positions in latitude and longitude, in degrees, on a datum (Chapter 3).
A projected coordinate system gives positions in x and y, in linear units such as meters or feet, on a projection built on a datum.

Since there are thousands of coordinate reference systems, each is given a short numeric code. The EPSG registry, started by the European Petroleum Survey Group and now maintained by the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP), lists them all, and QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, PostGIS, and most web tools use its codes (Table 4.2).



Table 4.2: EPSG codes you will meet most often in North Carolina.

Two rules follow from this table:

Never measure distance or area in a geographic CRS. A degree of longitude is 111 km at the equator and 90 km in Chapel Hill (Chapter 3), so “square degrees” mean nothing on the ground. Measure in a projected CRS in meters or feet.
Never measure in Web Mercator (3857). It uses meters, but its meters are stretched, by about 24 percent in each direction at Chapel Hill’s latitude and more farther north.

When layers won’t line up, the first thing to check is whether each one has the correct CRS defined.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.6 Choosing a projection
So what is the best projection? There is no single answer. The best projection depends on two questions: where is your study area, and what will you measure?
1. Pick a projection designed for your area. A local system keeps distortion smallest.

Working in eastern North Carolina, east of 78° W? UTM zone 18N.
Working in Chapel Hill, or across North Carolina? North Carolina State Plane.
Working across North America or the contiguous United States? A North American Lambert Conformal Conic, or an Albers Equal-Area Conic if you are comparing areas.

2. Pick a projection that preserves the properties you need, where you need them.

Measuring area, or mapping density? Choose equal-area.
Measuring distance from a point? Choose equidistant, such as an azimuthal equidistant centered on that point.
Measuring direction from a starting point? Choose azimuthal, centered on that point.
Need shapes and angles to look right? Choose conformal. A conformal projection does not preserve area, so it is not a substitute for equal-area when you measure area.

3. Using elevation data? Pick a projection whose horizontal units match your elevation units. Slope and hillshade calculations divide a change in height by a distance across the ground. A digital elevation model with heights in feet on a projection in meters produces slopes that are off by a factor of about 3.3, the number of feet in a meter.
For a small study area, such as a county or a city, any good local projection works, and the differences among them are smaller than the errors in most data. The bigger your study area, the more the choice matters.

title: 4  Map Projections
section: 4.7 Projections in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro
text:
4.7 Projections in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro
Both programs reproject layers on the fly: each layer keeps its own CRS, and the software converts it to the map’s CRS as it draws. In QGIS, the project’s CRS is shown in the lower-right corner of the window; click it to change it. In ArcGIS Pro, the map’s CRS is set in the map’s Properties, on the Coordinate Systems tab. By default, both programs take the CRS of the first layer you add.
On-the-fly reprojection is convenient, but it can hide problems. Two tasks are easy to confuse:

Defining a projection tells the software what CRS a layer is already in, when that information is missing or wrong, for example when a shapefile has lost its .prj file (Chapter 2). The coordinates don’t change. In QGIS this is Assign Projection (or setting the CRS in Layer Properties); in ArcGIS Pro it is the Define Projection tool.
Projecting (or reprojecting) a layer converts its coordinates into a new CRS and saves a new layer. In QGIS this is Reproject Layer; in ArcGIS Pro it is the Project tool, or Project Raster for rasters.

Defining the wrong CRS is a classic mistake. A layer in latitude and longitude that is wrongly defined as State Plane feet is read as a few feet from the projection’s origin, so it shows up as a tiny speck far from where it belongs; in a world map, one wrongly defined in meters appears near 0° latitude and 0° longitude, in the ocean off West Africa. A layer in State Plane feet wrongly defined as degrees may not appear at all, because its numbers, in the millions, are far outside the range of latitude and longitude. If a layer shows up in the wrong place, check its defined CRS first. Project a layer, rather than relying on on-the-fly reprojection, before you measure lengths or areas, run overlay tools, or share the data.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.9 Summary

A map projection is a set of equations that converts latitude and longitude into flat x, y coordinates. It sits on top of an ellipsoid and a datum.
Every flat map distorts shape, area, distance, or direction. Conformal projections keep local shapes, equal-area projections keep area, equidistant projections keep distance from one or two points, and azimuthal projections keep direction from a center. No projection is both conformal and equal-area. Tissot’s indicatrix shows the distortion.
Mercator is conformal and great for navigation, but it enlarges areas toward the poles: four times at 60°. Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), the projection of web maps, is for display, not measurement.
Projections are built on three developable surfaces: the plane, the cylinder, and the cone. A tangent surface touches the Earth; a secant surface cuts it, spreading the error. Scale is exact on standard lines, and error grows away from them.
Lambert Conformal Conic suits mid-latitude regions that run east to west; Transverse Mercator suits regions that run north to south.
UTM divides the world into 60 zones, 6° wide, each a secant Transverse Mercator in meters. North Carolina spans zones 17N and 18N, split at 78° W.
The State Plane Coordinate System has about 120 zones, with error held to 1 part in 10,000. North Carolina’s single zone is a Lambert Conformal Conic, EPSG:32119 in meters or 2264 in feet.
A coordinate reference system bundles a datum, a projection, and units, and is identified by an EPSG code. Geographic systems are in degrees; projected systems are in meters or feet. Never measure in degrees or in Web Mercator.
Choose a projection designed for your area and one that preserves what you will measure. Define a projection to fix missing CRS information; project a layer to convert its coordinates.

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.10 Exercises

Tissot at home. Open QGIS, add a world countries layer (Natural Earth works well), and change the project CRS to Mercator, Mollweide, Robinson, and an azimuthal equidistant centered on Chapel Hill. Describe how Greenland, Antarctica, and Africa change on each.
True size. Use The True Size Of… (https://www.thetruesize.com) to drag North Carolina, Texas, and Greenland to the equator and to the Arctic. Describe what happens and explain why, using the word conformal.
Measure an area three ways. In QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, calculate the area of North Carolina’s counties in EPSG:3857, EPSG:32119, and EPSG:5070. Which answers agree? Which is far off, and by about how much? Why?
Find the zone. Which UTM zone are each of these in: Asheville, Wilmington, Denver, Seattle, and your hometown? (Zone number = the whole number part of (longitude + 180) ÷ 6, plus 1.)
Read a CRS. Look up EPSG:32119 at https://epsg.io/32119. Find its datum, projection, standard parallels, latitude of origin, central meridian, false easting, and units.
Choose a projection. For each project, choose a projection or CRS and explain why: (a) the area of every wetland in Orange County, NC; (b) a map of flight distances from RDU airport; (c) a world map of population density; (d) a map of the Arctic Ocean’s sea ice; (e) a statewide map of North Carolina for a highway department.
Wrong CRS. A classmate’s layer of North Carolina schools shows up as a tiny cluster in the ocean off West Africa, near 0° latitude and 0° longitude. What has gone wrong, and how would you fix it?
Units and slope. You have a digital elevation model with elevations in feet, in a projection in meters. What will happen to a slope calculation? How would you fix it?

title: 4  Map Projections
text:
4.11 Further reading and online resources

4.11.1 Books and open textbooks

GIS Fundamentals: A First Text on Geographic Information Systems, by Paul Bolstad (Bolstad 2022). Chapter 3, “Geodesy, Projections, and Coordinate Systems,” covers developable surfaces, UTM, and State Plane in depth.
Understanding GIS through Sustainable Development Goals, by Paul Holloway (Holloway 2023). Its chapter on coordinate systems and projections includes worked examples in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.
Map Projections: A Working Manual, by John P. Snyder (Snyder 1987), USGS Professional Paper 1395. The standard reference for the mathematics and use of dozens of projections: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/pp1395.
Flattening the Earth: Two Thousand Years of Map Projections, by John P. Snyder (University of Chicago Press, 1993), the history of map projections.
How to Lie with Maps, by Mark Monmonier (3rd ed., University of Chicago Press, 2018). Its chapter on projections shows how a projection can shape a message.
Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection, by Mark Monmonier (University of Chicago Press, 2004), on the Mercator and the Peters debate.
The Nature of Geographic Information, by David DiBiase and colleagues at Penn State. Chapter 2 covers plane coordinate systems, UTM, and State Plane: https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c2.html.
Intro to GIS and Spatial Analysis, by Manuel Gimond. The chapter “Coordinate Systems” includes a gallery of projections: https://mgimond.github.io/Spatial/chp09_0.html.

The GIS&T Body of Knowledge, “Map Projections,” “Map Projection Properties,” “Map Projection Classes,” and “Plane Coordinate Systems”: https://www.ucgis.org/site/gis-t-body-of-knowledge.

PROJ, the open-source library behind QGIS’s projections, with an illustrated list of every projection it supports: https://proj.org/en/stable/operations/projections/index.html.

xkcd, “What your favorite map projection says about you”: https://xkcd.com/977/.



4.11.3 Mercator, Web Mercator, and the true size of countries

The True Size Of…, drag countries around a Mercator map to see their real size: https://www.thetruesize.com.
