A mathematical method for flattening the round Earth onto a flat map.
Every projection distorts area, shape, distance, or direction in some
way.
A smooth mathematical model of the Earth’s shape: an ellipse rotated
about its polar axis, wider at the equator than from pole to pole.
Examples are Clarke 1866, GRS 80, and WGS 84.
A model that fixes an ellipsoid’s size, shape, and position relative to
the Earth, realized by a network of control points, so latitude and
longitude point to real places. Examples are NAD27, NAD83, and WGS84.
A shape that can be unrolled flat without stretching: a plane, a
cylinder, or a cone.
A projection surface that touches the Earth along one line or at one
point.
A projection surface that cuts through the Earth along two lines (or a
circle), spreading the error more evenly.
A line where the projection surface meets the Earth, so the scale is
exact. Standard lines that follow latitude are standard parallels.
A conformal cylindrical projection from 1569, made for navigation: lines
of constant compass bearing are straight. It greatly enlarges areas
toward the poles.
The Mercator variant used by nearly every web map (EPSG:3857). Good for
display, never for measuring distance or area.
A conformal conic projection with two standard parallels. It suits
mid-latitude regions that run east to west, and is used for North
Carolina State Plane.
A Mercator projection turned on its side, so the cylinder touches the
Earth along a central meridian. It suits regions that run north to
south.
A system of 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, each a secant
Transverse Mercator projection in meters. North Carolina spans zones 17N
and 18N.
A U.S. system of about 120 zones following state and county lines, built
for surveyors, with error held to 1 part in 10,000. North Carolina has
one zone (EPSG:32119 in meters, 2264 in feet).
A number that identifies a coordinate reference system in the EPSG
registry, such as 4326 for WGS84 or 32119 for North Carolina State
Plane.
A coordinate system that gives positions as latitude and longitude, in
degrees, on a datum. EPSG:4326 (WGS84) and 4269 (NAD83) are examples.
A set of spatial data about one theme, such as roads, soils, or
elevation. Layers for the same area stack on top of each other to make a
map.
“A computer-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage,
analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information”
(Bolstad). Its five components are data, hardware, software, people, and
procedures.
The angle north or south of the equator, from 0° at the equator to 90°
at the poles.
The angle east or west of the prime meridian, from 0° at Greenwich to
180° east or west.
A system of numbers, such as latitude and longitude, that gives every
location a unique position so layers line up with each other.
The network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map.
A projection that keeps local angles true, so small shapes look right.
Mercator and Lambert Conformal Conic are conformal.
A projection that keeps relative area true. Use one to measure or
compare areas, or to map density.
A projection that keeps true distance from one or two points, or along
certain lines.
A projection onto a plane that keeps true directions from its center
point.
A projection that preserves no property exactly but keeps every
distortion moderate, such as Robinson or Winkel Tripel.
Identical small circles drawn on the globe and then projected. Their
size and shape on the map show the projection’s distortion.
A line of constant compass bearing. It is straight on a Mercator map.
A line of equal longitude. Meridians run from pole to pole and meet at
the poles.
A line of equal latitude. Parallels run east and west and get shorter
toward the poles.
The parallel halfway between the poles, at 0° latitude. It is the only
parallel that is a great circle.
A free, editable map of the world built by volunteers, founded in 2004.
The company that makes ArcGIS, founded in 1969 by Jack and Laura
Dangermond in Redlands, California.
The World Geodetic System of 1984, the global, earth-centered datum used
by GPS. It differs from NAD83 by about 1 to 2 meters in North America.
To convert a layer’s coordinates from one CRS to another and save the
result. Defining a projection, by contrast, only labels what the
coordinates already are.
The ratio of scale at a place on a map to the map’s stated scale:
exactly 1 on a standard line, below 1 where the map shrinks the Earth,
above 1 where it stretches it.
An equal-area conic projection, the standard for measuring areas across
the contiguous United States (EPSG:5070).
An azimuthal projection on which every great circle is a straight line.
A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the center. The shortest
route between two points follows a great circle.
The meridian at the center of a projection or zone, such as the line
along which a Transverse Mercator cylinder touches the Earth.
A distance east from a starting line: the x coordinate in a projected
coordinate system.
A distance north from a starting line: the y coordinate in a projected
coordinate system.
A value added to every x coordinate so that none are negative,
such as 500,000 m in UTM.
The science of measuring the Earth’s size, shape, orientation in space,
and gravity field.
The North American Datum of 1927. It used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and
an origin at Meades Ranch, Kansas.
The North American Datum of 1983, an earth-centered datum on the GRS 80
ellipsoid, fixed to the North American plate. The datum of most U.S.
government GIS data.
The full description of how coordinates relate to the Earth: a datum,
plus a projection with its parameters, plus units.
A coordinate system that gives positions as x, y in meters or
feet, on a map projection built on a datum, such as UTM or State Plane.
A free and open-source desktop GIS that runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
Esri’s commercial desktop GIS, for Windows.
A free extension that adds geometry types and spatial functions to the
PostgreSQL database.
The Global Positioning System: U.S. satellites that let a receiver, such
as your phone, work out its location. GNSS is the general name for GPS
and similar systems from other countries.
Reprojecting layers as they are drawn, so layers in different CRSs line
up on the map without changing their stored coordinates.
A common vector format from Esri that stores one layer in several files
with the same name: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), and .dbf (attributes)
are required, and .prj holds the coordinate system.
A data model that stores the world as a regular grid of equal-sized
cells, each holding one value. Best for continuous data and imagery.
Stacking layers of data for the same area to find places that meet
several conditions at once, such as flat land near a road and outside a
floodplain.
The number of people per unit of area, such as people per square mile.
Data tied to a location on or near Earth, such as the address of a
house, the outline of a county, or the elevation at a point.
Methods that use the locations of things, and the relationships among
them, to find patterns, explain them, or make predictions.
A free collection of short, peer-reviewed articles on geographic
information science and technology topics, from the University
Consortium for Geographic Information Science (UCGIS).
The art and science of making maps.
Software whose source code anyone may read, change, and share, often
free of charge. QGIS and GRASS GIS are open source.

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.1 Attribute data
Chapters 2 to 4 were about where: how a GIS stores geometry, and how coordinates pin it to the Earth. This chapter is about the other half of GIS data, the half that says what. A polygon tells you where a county is. Its attributes tell you its name, how many people live there, how old they are, and how many homes stand empty. Most of the questions people bring to a GIS start with attributes: Which counties lost population? Which parcels are zoned commercial and larger than five acres? Which schools have no address?
To answer them, you need to know how attributes are stored, what kinds of values they hold, and how to write a query, a precise question the software can test against every record. We will finish with a way to check your own queries using sets, and with the trap of missing values.
Five terms carry the whole chapter:

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.1.1 Attribute tables
In Chapter 2, data abstraction turned a wetland into a data model: polygons for the geometry, and a table for everything else. That table is the attribute table, the non-spatial half of a vector layer. It follows three rules (Figure 5.1):

One row per feature. Every parcel on the map has exactly one record in the table, and every record has a parcel.
One column per attribute. Each column holds one kind of measurement, such as area or land use, for every feature.
The table and the map are linked. Select a record, and its feature lights up on the map; select a feature, and its record lights up in the table. The table is where you ask the question; the map is where the answer is drawn.







Figure 5.1: Seven parcels and their attribute table. A record is a row: everything known about one parcel, here parcel 5. An attribute is a column: one variable for every parcel, here Landuse. Selecting record 5 in the table also selects parcel 5 on the map. (The parcels are not drawn to scale.)



We will use these seven parcels throughout the chapter. Their attributes are:

ID, a number that identifies each parcel.
Area, in acres.
Landuse: Urban, Suburban, or Farm.
Municip, the kind of local government the parcel is in: City, Township, or County.
Density, in people per square mile.
MillRate, a property tax class from A to D.

Software uses several words for the same things. A column may be called an attribute, a field, or an item. A row may be called a record, a row, or (because each row is one feature) a feature. In this book, field and attribute mean the same thing, and so do record and row.
In QGIS, open a layer’s table by right-clicking it in the Layers panel and choosing Open Attribute Table. In ArcGIS Pro, right-click the layer in the Contents pane and choose Attribute Table. Click a column header to sort the table by that column; click again to sort the other way. Sorting a layer of world cities by population, largest first, is a quick way to explore a new dataset.


5.1.2 Data types
Every field has a data type, chosen when the field is created. The data type decides what a field can store and how much space each value takes. QGIS and ArcGIS Pro name their types a little differently (Table 5.1).



Table 5.1: Common field data types. Which types are available also depends on the format: a shapefile, a GeoPackage, a file geodatabase, or a database such as PostGIS. ArcGIS Pro’s Big Integer, Date Only, and Time Only types need version 3.2 or later.











What it stores
QGIS
ArcGIS Pro
Range or example




Text, any characters
Text (string)
Text
John Doe, 27514


Small whole numbers (16-bit)
(none)
Short Integer
−32,768 to 32,767


Whole numbers (32-bit)
Integer (32 bit)
Long Integer
−2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647


Large whole numbers (64-bit)
Integer (64 bit)
Big Integer
about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ in QGIS; ±9,007,199,254,740,991 in ArcGIS Pro


Decimal numbers, about 7 significant digits
(none)
Float
about ±3.4 × 10³⁸


Decimal numbers, about 15 significant digits
Decimal number (double)

about ±1.8 × 10³⁰⁸

(none; use Short Integer 0 or 1)
true, false


Dates and times
Date, Date & Time

12/31/2012 11:59:59 PM


A unique ID for each record
(fid)

The feature’s shape
(geometry)
Geometry (Shape)
point, line, polygon






Two terms describe numeric fields:

Precision is the total number of digits a field can hold.
Scale is how many of those digits fall after the decimal point.

A field with a precision of 6 and a scale of 2 can hold numbers up to 9,999.99. In ArcGIS Pro, you choose the type, and for some formats the precision and scale, when you create a field, and they can’t be changed later. To change a field’s type, you add a new field of the right type and calculate the values into it.
Some rules of thumb for choosing a type:

Store identifiers that are never used in arithmetic as text, even if they look like numbers. ZIP codes, FIPS codes, phone numbers, and parcel IDs all belong in text fields. Stored as a number, the ZIP code of Boston’s City Hall, 02201, becomes 2201, and Orange County’s FIPS code, 37135, can no longer be matched to another table that stores it as text.
Use an integer type for counts, such as population or number of rooms.
Use Double for measurements that need decimals, such as area or density. Float saves a little space, but it keeps only about 7 significant digits, so it can round large numbers.



5.1.3 Why fields have limits: binary
Why do field types have such strange limits, like 32,767 or 2,147,483,647? Because everything in an attribute table is ultimately stored in binary, as ones and zeros, and each field gets a fixed number of bits (binary digits).
In binary, each column is worth twice the one to its right: ones, twos, fours, eights, and so on (Figure 5.2). So the binary number 1101 means 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.






Figure 5.2: The binary number 1101. Each column is worth twice the one to its right, so 1101 is 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.



With n bits you can write 2ⁿ different values. If one bit is used for the sign, plus or minus, half of them are negative:

A 16-bit short integer has 2¹⁶ = 65,536 values, from −32,768 to 32,767.
A 32-bit integer has about 4.3 billion values, from about −2.1 billion to 2.1 billion.
A 64-bit integer has 2⁶⁴ = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 values, about ±9.22 × 10¹⁸.

Modern computers process data in 64-bit words: that is what “a 64-bit processor” means. It refers to how many bits the processor handles at once, not to how much memory the computer has. An integer field is only as wide as the bits behind it, so the population of a county fits easily in a 32-bit integer, but the population of the world, about 8.2 billion, does not.






NoteDid you know..?



In December 2014, the music video for PSY’s “Gangnam Style” became the first video on YouTube to be watched more than 2,147,483,647 times, the largest number a signed 32-bit integer can hold. YouTube’s engineers had seen it coming and had already switched the view counter to a 64-bit integer, which can count past nine quintillion. YouTube joked that it had never thought a video would be watched more times than a 32-bit integer could count. The same limit is behind the “Year 2038 problem”: many older computer systems count time as the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, in a signed 32-bit integer, which will run out on January 19, 2038.




5.1.4 Levels of measurement
The data type says what the computer can store. The level of measurement says what you may legitimately ask. They are different questions. The number 3 stored in an integer field could be a count of bedrooms, a rank, a temperature, or a code for “forest,” and the arithmetic that makes sense is different for each. The psychologist S. S. Stevens described four levels of measurement in 1946 (Stevens 1946), and they are still the standard way to sort attributes (Table 5.2).



Table 5.2: The four levels of measurement. Each level supports everything the levels above it support, and more.











Level
What it is
Examples
What you may ask




Nominal
Categories with no order. Two values are only ever the same or different.
Landuse, county name, land cover code
= and ≠. Counts and the most common value (the mode). No averages.


Ordinal
Ranked categories, but the distance between ranks is unknown.
MillRate (A, B, C, D), a hurricane’s category, “low, medium, high”
= ≠ < >. A median, not a mean.


Interval
Equal steps, but the zero point is arbitrary.
Temperature in °F or °C, calendar year
Differences. Sums and ratios mislead: 20 °C is not twice as hot as 10 °C.


Ratio
Equal steps and a true zero, so ratios hold.
Population, area, density, income, rainfall
Everything, including ratios and normalization, such as density = population ÷ area.






A few notes:

A nominal attribute can be stored as numbers, like land cover codes 11 for water and 41 for forest, but the average land cover code of a county is meaningless.
An ordinal attribute has an order, but not a size. A Category 4 hurricane is stronger than a Category 2, but it isn’t “twice as strong.”
An interval attribute’s zero doesn’t mean “none.” Zero degrees Celsius is not the absence of temperature, and the year 0 is not the beginning of time, so ratios of interval values make no sense.
A ratio attribute’s zero does mean “none”: zero people, zero acres. Only ratio data supports statements like “twice as many.”

The level of measurement also guides how you map an attribute: nominal data gets different colors or symbols for each category, while ordinal, interval, and ratio data get graduated colors or sizes. You will meet these ideas again when we make maps of census data.






TipThink about it



What level of measurement is each of these: a parcel’s zoning code, a restaurant’s health inspection grade (A, B, or C), median household income, the year a building was built, elevation in meters above sea level, and a student’s class rank?

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.2 Querying a table

5.2.1 What is a query?
A query is a written condition, not a click. It asks the table a question, such as which parcels are larger than 20 acres?, and four ideas follow from that:

The software tests every record separately, one at a time, against the condition.
The answer is a set of records, and therefore a set of features on the map.
The records that pass make up the selected set, or selection. They are highlighted in the table and on the map.
The logical operators AND, OR, and NOT decide how several conditions combine.



5.2.2 SQL
SQL, Structured Query Language, is the standard language for asking a database a question. A full SQL statement reads:
SELECT * FROM parcels WHERE "Area" > 20
In words: select all the columns (*) from the table named parcels, for the records where Area is greater than 20.
In a GIS you rarely type the whole statement. The layer you are working on supplies the FROM part, and the selection tool supplies the SELECT part, so you write only the WHERE clause, the condition:
"Area" > 20

In QGIS, use Select Features by Expression (on the attribute table’s toolbar, or under Edit > Select). Type the condition into the expression box, or build it by double-clicking fields and operators in the lists.
In ArcGIS Pro, use Select By Attributes (on the Map tab, or in the attribute table), which runs the Select Layer By Attribute tool. Build the clause with drop-down lists, or switch to SQL mode to type it.

A WHERE clause uses comparison operators (Table 5.3).



Table 5.3: Comparison operators.










Operator
Meaning
Example




=
equal to
"Landuse" = 'Urban'


<> or !=
not equal to
"Municip" <> 'City'


> and >=
greater than, greater than or equal to
"Area" > 20


< and <=
less than, less than or equal to
"Density" <= 100






Quoting is not decoration. It tells the software what kind of thing each part of the clause is:

Field names take double quotes: "Area", "Landuse".
Text values take single quotes: 'Urban'.
Numbers take no quotes: 20.

A number in quotes is text, and text sorts alphabetically, so '9' comes after '10'. A text value without quotes is read as a field name, which usually gives an error. Whether a text comparison cares about capital letters depends on the format: 'urban' may or may not match Urban, so match the capitalization in the data.


5.2.3 Simple and compound queries
A simple query uses one attribute and one comparison. "Area" > 20 tests each parcel’s area and selects four of the seven: parcels 2, 4, 5, and 6 (Figure 5.3, top).
A compound query joins two or more conditions with a logical operator. With AND, a record must pass both tests. "Landuse" = 'Urban' AND "Municip" = 'City' selects only parcels 1 and 5, the only ones that are both urban and in a city (Figure 5.3, bottom).






Figure 5.3: A simple query (top) selects parcels larger than 20 acres: four of seven. A compound query with AND (bottom) selects parcels that are both urban and in a city: two of seven.



AND narrows. Adding a condition with AND can never make a selection larger. Every extra condition is one more filter a record has to get through.


5.2.4 AND, OR, and NOT
There are three logical operators:

AND: both conditions must be true for the same record. The result is where the two sets overlap.
OR: either condition is enough. The result is everything in either set. OR widens: it can never make a selection smaller.
NOT: reverses a condition, and selects every record the condition doesn’t describe, its complement. It is written in front of the condition: NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban'), which is the same as "Landuse" <> 'Urban'.

Figure 5.4 shows OR and NOT on the same seven parcels, and Table 5.4 compares all three.






Figure 5.4: OR (top) selects parcels that are larger than 20 acres or in a city, or both: five of seven. NOT (bottom) selects every parcel that isn’t urban: four of seven.






Table 5.4: The three logical operators on the seven parcels.





Operator
Expression
Records selected
Count




AND
"Landuse" = 'Urban' AND "Municip" = 'City'
1, 5
2 of 7


OR
"Area" > 20 OR "Municip" = 'City'
1, 2, 4, 5, 6
5 of 7


NOT
NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban')
2, 3, 4, 6
4 of 7






Why does OR leave out parcels 3 and 7? Parcel 3 is 2.4 acres in a township, and parcel 7 is 4.4 acres in a county: each fails both tests.


5.2.5 Selecting rows also selects features
Selecting records in a table and selecting features on a map are the same act. That makes queries a powerful way to find places. Figure 5.5 shows a made-up county of forty townships. Each of the first three maps is one simple condition, and each selects a large, plausible-looking region. The fourth map ANDs all three together. Only the townships that pass all three tests remain, and there are far fewer of them than any one map suggests.






Figure 5.5: A made-up county of forty townships. Each of the first three maps selects townships that pass one condition. The fourth selects townships that pass all three: a AND b AND c.



Before you run a query like this, predict the result. If the answer is very different from what you expected, either the data or your query will teach you something.


5.2.6 Complex queries and brackets
A complex query mixes AND, OR, and NOT. Then the order in which the parts are evaluated matters, and brackets (parentheses) decide it. Each bracketed group is worked out on its own before the groups are joined (Figure 5.6):
("Landuse" = 'Urban' AND "MillRate" = 'B')
  OR (NOT "Municip" = 'City' AND "Density" > 200)
Read it in two groups. In the first, only parcel 5 is urban with a mill rate of B. In the second, only parcel 3 is outside a city with a density above 200 (it is a township with 237.5 people per square mile). The OR then joins the groups, so the query selects parcels 3 and 5.






Figure 5.6: A complex query with brackets selects parcels 3 and 5.



Without brackets, SQL evaluates NOT first, then AND, then OR. That happens to give the same answer here, but most of the time, removing brackets changes the answer. Always write the brackets, even when you think you don’t need them. They make the query say what you mean, and they make it easy for the next person to read.


5.2.7 Where you put NOT matters
The position of NOT can change a query’s answer completely (Figure 5.7).

NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban' AND "Municip" = 'County') negates the whole bracket. Only parcel 7 is both urban and in a county, so negating that selects everything else: six records.
NOT "Landuse" = 'Urban' AND NOT "Municip" = 'County' negates each condition, then joins them with AND. A parcel must be neither urban nor in a county. Only parcels 3 and 6 qualify: two records.







Figure 5.7: Where the NOT sits changes the answer. Negating the whole bracket (top) selects six parcels; negating each condition and joining them with AND (bottom) selects two.



This is De Morgan’s law, from logic: NOT (A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) OR (NOT B), not (NOT A) AND (NOT B). If you move a NOT inside a bracket, flip each AND to an OR, and each OR to an AND.


5.2.8 Beyond = and >
Four more operators make everyday queries shorter and clearer (Table 5.5).



Table 5.5: Four more operators.










Operator
Example
What it does




LIKE
"NAME" LIKE 'North%'
Matches a text pattern. % stands for any number of characters (including none), and _ for exactly one. This finds North Carolina, North Dakota, and Northampton.


BETWEEN
"Pop2020" BETWEEN 5000 AND 9000
Selects an inclusive range: both 5,000 and 9,000 are selected. It is a tidy way to write "Pop2020" >= 5000 AND "Pop2020" <= 9000.


IN
"Landuse" IN ('Urban', 'Suburban')
Tests membership in a list. It is a tidy way to write a chain of ORs on the same field.


IS NULL
"Pop2020" IS NULL
The only correct way to test for a missing value (see Section 5.4). IS NOT NULL finds records that have a value.






Watch BETWEEN when you divide data into classes. If one class is BETWEEN 0 AND 5000 and the next is BETWEEN 5000 AND 10000, a county with exactly 5,000 people lands in both. In QGIS, ILIKE works like LIKE but ignores capital letters.


5.2.9 What to do with a selection
A query only creates a selection. What you do next is what produces a result:

Zoom to the selection and look at it. This is the cheapest check there is. If the selected features are in implausible places, the expression is wrong, not the data. (QGIS: Zoom Map to Selected Rows in the attribute table. ArcGIS Pro: right-click the layer, Selection > Zoom To Selection.)
Read the summary statistics for the selected set: the count, sum, mean, and range. Read the count first. It tells you whether the query did what you meant. (QGIS: the attribute table’s title bar shows how many features are selected, and the Statistics panel summarizes a field for selected features only. ArcGIS Pro: the bottom of the attribute table shows the count, and right-clicking a field and choosing Statistics makes a chart and summary.)
Calculate a field for the selection. The field calculator writes values into an attribute, for the selected records only. For example, set a new field, Flag, to 1 for the selected parcels. That turns a query into a permanent category you can map and query again. (QGIS: Field Calculator, with Only update selected features checked. ArcGIS Pro: Calculate Field.)
Export the selection to a new layer or table, so it survives. (QGIS: right-click the layer, Export > Save Selected Features As. ArcGIS Pro: right-click the layer, Data > Export Features; with a selection, only the selected features are exported.)

A selection is temporary. Clearing it erases it, and so does closing the project, or sometimes a careless click on the map. If you will need the result again, calculate it into a field or export it.
When you want a layer to show only some features, all the time, use a filter instead of a selection: in QGIS, Filter (in the layer’s right-click menu), and in ArcGIS Pro, a definition query (in the layer’s Properties). A filter uses the same WHERE clause, but it hides the records that fail it until you remove it.






NoteDid you know..?



SQL was invented at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, to query the “relational” databases their colleague Edgar F. Codd had described in 1970 (Codd 1970). They first called it SEQUEL, for Structured English Query Language, but another company already had a trademark on that name, so it was shortened to SQL. That is why people still argue about whether to say “sequel” or “S-Q-L.” (Both are fine.) More than fifty years later, SQL is still one of the most widely used programming languages in the world, and every GIS program you will use speaks some form of it.

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.3 Thinking in sets

5.3.1 Every condition names a set
Here is a way to check a query before you trust it: think in sets. Each condition in a query selects a set of records.

AND keeps only the records in both sets: the intersection.
OR keeps the records in either set: the union.
NOT keeps the records outside a set: the complement.

A Venn diagram draws each set as a circle, inside a rectangle that holds every record. Sketching one before you write a query catches most logic mistakes. Try it with students. Let:

T = all students at the university (the whole table),
A = students from New York,
B = Geography majors, and
C = English majors.

The query "Home_State" = 'NY' AND "Major" = 'Geography' selects A AND B: students who are in both sets, the overlap of the circles. Change one word, "Home_State" = 'NY' OR "Major" = 'Geography', and it selects A OR B: everyone inside either circle, including the overlap (Figure 5.8).






Figure 5.8: AND is the intersection of two sets (left); OR is their union (right). T is every student; A is students from New York; B is Geography majors; C is English majors.



AND can never select more records than either condition alone; OR can never select fewer. If an OR query returns almost the whole table, check whether you meant AND. If an AND query returns nothing, check whether the circles can overlap at all.


5.3.2 What do you get?
Try these four before you look at Figure 5.9. For each, which students are selected?

"Major" = 'Geography' AND "Major" = 'English'
"Major" = 'Geography' OR "Major" = 'English'
"Home_State" = 'NY' AND "Major" = 'English'
"Home_State" = 'NY' OR "Major" = 'English'







Figure 5.9: The four queries as Venn diagrams. B AND C selects nothing, because in this table a student has only one major, so the circles don’t overlap.



The first is the surprise. Each record has only one value in the Major field, so no single student is both a Geography major and an English major in this table. The circles don’t overlap, and the query selects nothing. An AND on two different values of the same field always selects nothing.


5.3.3 Each feature is tested separately
That leads to the two most common mistakes in writing queries, both caused by forgetting that each record is tested on its own (Table 5.6).



Table 5.6: Two classic mistakes.










Wrong
Why it fails
Right




"Landuse" = 'Urban' AND "Landuse" = 'Farm'
No single parcel is both urban and farm, so nothing is selected.
"Landuse" = 'Urban' OR "Landuse" = 'Farm', or "Landuse" IN ('Urban', 'Farm')


"Pop2020" >= 5000 OR "Pop2020" < 9000
Every number is either at least 5,000 or below 9,000, so everything is selected.
"Pop2020" >= 5000 AND "Pop2020" < 9000






The rule of thumb: two values of one attribute take OR; two bounds on one attribute take AND.
The trouble comes from how we talk. “Show me the urban parcels and the farm parcels” uses and in English, but it means OR in SQL: you want a parcel if it is urban or if it is farm. Translate the question into “a parcel is selected if…” before you write the query.

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.4 Null values and missing data
One last trap. A NULL is not a value. It is the record telling you it doesn’t know.

NULL is not zero, and not blank. NULL means no value was recorded. Zero is a measurement, and an empty text string is a value. A Density of 0 says “nobody lives here”; a Density of NULL says “we never counted.”
NULL is equal to nothing, not even another NULL. So "Density" = NULL selects no records at all, even if half the table is NULL. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead.
NULL fails every comparison. A record with a NULL Pop2020 is selected by neither "Pop2020" >= 5000 nor "Pop2020" < 5000. Two queries that look like they split the table in two no longer add up to the whole table.
NOT doesn’t rescue it. NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban') drops the NULL records along with the urban ones. If you want them, say so: NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban') OR "Landuse" IS NULL (Figure 5.10).







Figure 5.10: Parcels 3 and 6 have no recorded land use. NOT (“Landuse” = ‘Urban’) selects only parcels 2 and 4; adding OR “Landuse” IS NULL brings back 3 and 6.



Shapefiles make this worse: the old dBASE format can’t store a true NULL in a numeric field, so missing numbers are often stored as 0, or as a code like −9999. Always read the metadata to find out how missing values are coded.
Build a habit: before you trust any count, query IS NULL on each field you used, and see how many records were never in the running.






TipThink about it



A table of 100 counties has 12 with a NULL median income. "MedIncome" > 50000 selects 40 counties. How many does "MedIncome" <= 50000 select? How many does NOT ("MedIncome" > 50000) select?


Show the answer

48 for both. The 12 counties with NULL income fail both comparisons, and NOT doesn’t bring them back: 40 + 48 + 12 = 100.

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.6 Summary

An attribute table stores one record (row) per feature and one attribute (field, column) per variable. Selecting a record selects its feature on the map.
A field’s data type limits what it can store. Integer types are only as wide as the bits behind them: a 32-bit integer tops out at 2,147,483,647. Store identifiers like ZIP codes and FIPS codes as text.
The level of measurement limits what you may ask: nominal (categories), ordinal (ranks), interval (equal steps, arbitrary zero), and ratio (a true zero).
A query is a WHERE clause the software tests against every record, one at a time. In SQL, field names take double quotes, text values single quotes, and numbers none.
AND narrows (the intersection), OR widens (the union), and NOT takes the complement. Brackets and the placement of NOT change the answer, so write them out.
LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, and IS NULL shorten everyday queries.
Draw a Venn diagram to check a query. Two values of one attribute take OR; two bounds on one attribute take AND.
NULL means no value was recorded. It fails every comparison, so run IS NULL before you trust a count.
A selection is temporary. Zoom to it, read its count, then calculate a field or export it to keep the result.

title: 5  Attribute Data and Queries
text:
5.7 Exercises

Explore a table. Download Natural Earth’s populated places layer (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) and open its attribute table. How many records does it have? Sort it by pop_max. What are the ten largest cities? Find a field with NULL values.
Data types. For each of these fields, choose a data type and explain why: a county FIPS code, the number of students in a school, a stream’s length in kilometers, whether a road is paved, a building’s construction date, and a phone number.
Levels of measurement. For each field in exercise 2, name its level of measurement. Which could you average?
Write the query. Using the seven parcels, write a WHERE clause for each, and list the parcels it selects: (a) farm parcels larger than 50 acres; (b) parcels in a township or a county; (c) urban parcels with a density over 1,000 or a mill rate of A; (d) every parcel that is not suburban.
Predict, then run. In QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, with the populated places layer, write one query with AND, one with OR, and one with IS NULL. Predict the count before you run each one. How close were you?
Find the mistake. Explain what’s wrong with each query, and fix it: (a) "STATE" = 'NC' AND "STATE" = 'SC'; (b) "POP" > 1000 OR "POP" < 5000; (c) "NAME" = Durham; (d) "INCOME" = NULL.
De Morgan. Rewrite NOT ("Landuse" = 'Urban' OR "Municip" = 'City') without a bracket after the NOT. Which parcels does it select?
Keep the answer. Select the North Carolina counties with more than 100,000 people. Calculate a field, Big, set to 1 for those counties, and export them to a new layer. Then clear the selection. Which of the two results survived?

text:
5.8 Further reading and online resources

5.8.1 Books and open textbooks

GIS Fundamentals: A First Text on Geographic Information Systems, by Paul Bolstad (Bolstad 2022). Chapter 8, “Attribute Data and Tables,” covers attribute tables, SQL queries, and Boolean logic.
Understanding GIS through Sustainable Development Goals, by Paul Holloway (Holloway 2023). Includes worked attribute queries in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.
Essentials of Geographic Information Systems, by Jonathan Campbell and Michael Shin. Chapter 5, “Geospatial Data Management,” covers attribute tables, data types, and queries: https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/67.
The Nature of Geographic Information, by David DiBiase and colleagues at Penn State. Chapter 3, “Census Data and Thematic Maps,” discusses levels of measurement: https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c3.html.
Intro to GIS and Spatial Analysis, by Manuel Gimond. The chapter “GIS Data Formats” covers attribute tables and data types: https://mgimond.github.io/Spatial/.
Getting Started with SQL, by Thomas Nield (O’Reilly, 2016), a short, friendly introduction to SQL.
PostGIS in Action, by Regina Obe and Leo Hsu (3rd ed., Manning, 2021), for when you are ready to query spatial databases directly.



5.8.2 Attribute data, data types, and measurement

QGIS User Guide, “Working with the Attribute Table”: https://docs.qgis.org/latest/en/docs/user_manual/working_with_vector/attribute_table.html.

Stevens, S. S., “On the Theory of Scales of Measurement,” Science (Stevens 1946), the original paper on levels of measurement: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.103.2684.677.
The GIS&T Body of Knowledge, “Scales of Measurement,” “Database Management Systems,” and “Structured Query Language (SQL) and Attribute Queries”: https://www.ucgis.org/site/gis-t-body-of-knowledge.



5.8.3 Queries and SQL

SQLite Tutorial, “SQLite NULL,” on how NULL behaves: https://www.sqlitetutorial.net/sqlite-is-null/.

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.1 Databases and keys
Chapter 5 asked questions of a single attribute table. Real projects rarely stop at one table. The census tract boundaries you download from the Census Bureau carry a code and a name, but no population. The population sits in a separate table, from a separate website, with no geometry at all. A county’s parcels live in one table, and its owners in another. A forest’s trails are in one table, and the forest’s size and ranger office in a second.
To map any of these, you have to bring the two tables together. That operation is a table join, and it is one of the most common and most error-prone steps in GIS work. This chapter starts with how databases store and link tables, then shows how joins work, how they fail, and how to check them.

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.1.1 From one table to many
An attribute table follows the rules from Chapter 5: one row per feature, and one column per attribute. A layer of Washington counties might have a FIPS code, a name, the 1990 population, the land area, and the population density, all in one table.
That works until the questions get bigger. Suppose you also track every county’s hospitals, every hospital’s doctors, and every doctor’s specialties. You could keep adding columns to the county table, but you would soon need a column for “hospital 1,” “hospital 2,” and so on, with most of them empty. A better design splits the data into several tables, each about one kind of thing, and links them through shared values. Storing and linking many tables is the job of a database.


6.1.2 What is a database management system?
A database management system (DBMS) is software that stores data once and lets many programs and many people query it. Common examples include:

Oracle and Microsoft SQL Server, large commercial systems used by governments and companies.
MySQL and PostgreSQL, free, open-source servers. PostGIS is an extension that adds geometry types and spatial functions to PostgreSQL.
SQLite, a small database that lives in a single file. SpatiaLite adds spatial functions to it, and a GeoPackage (Chapter 2) is a SQLite database laid out to a published standard. QGIS saves new layers as GeoPackages by default.

Without a DBMS, every program reads its own files directly (Figure 6.1, left). The mapping app reads one copy of the parcels, the permit office keeps another in a spreadsheet, and a reporting script reads last year’s export. The copies drift apart, and no one controls who edits what.






Figure 6.1: Left: without a DBMS, each program reads its own copies of the files. Right: with a DBMS, clients talk to an application tier, which talks to one stored copy of the data in the database tier.



A DBMS changes four things:

Client/server. Client programs such as QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, or a web browser send requests to a database server, which does the work and sends back the answer.
Multiple tiers. Large systems are usually built in three tiers (Figure 6.1, right): the client, an application tier (for example a web server or map server), and the database tier.
No direct write access. Users change data only through the DBMS, which checks their permissions first. A summer intern can be allowed to read the parcel table but not to edit it.
Concurrency. Many users can read and edit at the same time. The DBMS makes sure that two people editing the same record don’t overwrite each other’s work.







NoteDid you know..?



SQLite is probably the most widely used database engine in the world. It is built into every Android and iPhone, every major web browser, and many desktop programs, so a typical smartphone holds hundreds of SQLite databases. Every GeoPackage you save from QGIS is one more (SQLite Project 2024).




6.1.3 Relational databases
Most databases are relational databases: they store data in tables, and they link the tables through fields that hold the same values. The idea goes back to the paper by E. F. Codd that we met in Chapter 5 (Codd 1970).
Figure 6.2 shows a small example from North Carolina’s national forests. One table lists the four forests: each one’s name, ranger office, rough size, and an ID number. A second table lists trails, and each trail records the ID of the forest it is in. The two tables share no names, but they share the Forest_ID field, and that is enough to link every trail to its forest.






Figure 6.2: Two tables in a relational database. Each trail’s Forest_ID points to one row in the Forests table. Acreages are rounded.





6.1.4 Primary and foreign keys
A field that links tables is called a key. There are two kinds:

A primary key is a field whose values identify each row of a table uniquely. No value may repeat, and none may be missing. Forest_ID is the primary key of the Forests table: each forest has one ID, and no two forests share one.
A foreign key is a field in another table that holds values of that primary key. Forest_ID in the Trails table is a foreign key. Its values can repeat, because a forest can have many trails.

The names of the two fields don’t have to match. A Trails table could call the field FOREST and the Forests table could call it Forest_ID. What matters is that the values match, and that the two fields have the same data type.
Good keys are codes, not names. Names are spelled in different ways (“Pisgah,” “Pisgah NF,” “Pisgah National Forest”), and different places can share a name: about 30 states have a Washington County. In U.S. data, the most common keys are FIPS codes, the numeric codes the federal government gives each state, county, and census area. The Census Bureau’s GEOID strings these codes together, so that each place has its own code (Section 6.4).






TipThink about it



Your university gives you a student ID number (a PID at UNC). Why does the registrar’s database use that number as the key, rather than your name or your email address? What could go wrong with each of the other two?

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.2 Joining tables

6.2.1 What a join does
A table join appends the fields of one table to another, by matching the values in a key field. The two tables have names that tell you their role:

The destination table (ArcGIS calls it the target, or input, table) is the one that receives the new fields. Its rows are all kept, in their own order. In GIS, the destination is usually the layer with the geometry, because you want to map the result.
The source table (the join table) supplies the fields. Each of its values is copied to the destination row whose key matches.

It helps to picture the destination on the left and the source on the right. Figure 6.3 shows the trails joined to the forests: every trail now carries its forest’s name, ranger office, and acreage. Nantahala’s values appear twice, because two trails point to it.






Figure 6.3: The Trails table (destination) after a join with the Forests table (source). The purple fields came from Forests.



Three things about joins are easy to forget:

A join matches values, not positions. The two tables can be sorted in any order. The software looks up each destination key in the source.
A join is temporary. In QGIS and ArcGIS Pro, a join is a live link between two tables. Nothing is written to the files on disk. If you remove the join, or open the layer in a new project, the fields are gone. To keep them, export the joined layer to a new file.
A join changes neither table. The source table is not altered, and the destination only borrows the source’s fields while the join is in place.



6.2.2 Tables are bags, not sets
In Chapter 5 we treated the records a query selects as a set: a collection of distinct things, with no duplicates. A database table is not always a set. Unless a primary key forbids it, a table can hold two identical rows. A collection that can contain duplicates is called a bag (or a multiset).
That matters for joins. The table below, TAKES, records which students take which courses. Zhang appears twice, because Zhang takes two courses. When the TAKES table is joined to a table of students, Zhang’s row has two matches. A join does not choose between them: it either repeats Zhang’s row once for each match, or it keeps only the first one. We return to this problem under cardinality (Section 6.3).


6.2.3 Which rows does a join keep?
Here are two small tables from a student records system. STUDENT has one row per student. TAKES has one row per enrollment. One enrollment, for ID 33301, belongs to a student who has since left and is no longer in STUDENT.

Parr and McKeon have no enrollments. The student with ID 33301 has an enrollment but no row in STUDENT. A join has to decide what to do with records like these, which have no partner in the other table. There are four kinds of join, and they differ only in which unmatched records they keep (Figure 6.4):

An inner join keeps only rows that match in both tables. Here that is Zhang’s two enrollments and Shankar’s one.
A left join (or left outer join) keeps every row of the left table, the destination, and fills the source fields with NULL where there is no match. Here that adds Parr and McKeon, with NULL courses.
A right join keeps every row of the right table, the source. Here that is the three matched enrollments plus 33301’s enrollment, with a NULL name.
A full outer join keeps every row of both tables.

The left join of STUDENT to TAKES gives Table 6.3. Every student is there, once for each enrollment, and the two students with no enrollments are kept with NULL values.

The left join is the default in GIS. When you join a table to a layer in QGIS or ArcGIS Pro, every feature of the layer is kept, matched or not. That is what you usually want: a county with no data should still appear on the map, so that you can see the gap. To get an inner join instead:

In ArcGIS Pro, uncheck Keep All Target Features in the Add Join tool.
In QGIS, use the Join Attributes by Field Value tool from the Processing Toolbox, and check Discard records which could not be joined.

Right and full outer joins are rare in desktop GIS, because the extra rows they keep have no geometry to draw. You will meet them in SQL databases.

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.3 Cardinality

6.3.1 Four kinds of relationship
Cardinality describes how many records in one table match each record in the other. Name the destination first, and there are four possibilities (Figure 6.5):

One-to-one (1:1). Each destination record matches exactly one source record. States to governors: each state has one governor, and each governor runs one state.
Many-to-one (M:1). Many destination records match the same source record, but each destination record matches only one. Counties to states: many counties share a state, but each county is in one state.
One-to-many (1:M). One destination record matches many source records. States to counties: each state has many counties.
Many-to-many (M:M). Records on both sides match many records on the other. Students to classes: each student takes many classes, and each class has many students.







Figure 6.5: The four kinds of cardinality, with the destination table on the left of each panel and the source on the right.



The order matters. Counties to states is many-to-one; states to counties is one-to-many. The same two tables give a different cardinality depending on which one is the destination.


6.3.2 The rule of joining
One-to-one and many-to-one joins work directly. Every destination record finds at most one match, so there is exactly one value to copy into each field. In the Trails-to-Forests join (Figure 6.3), each trail is in one forest, so each trail gets one set of forest attributes. That many forest values are repeated doesn’t matter.
One-to-many and many-to-many joins break the rule of a GIS layer, that each record is one feature. Suppose the destination is a states layer and the source is a table of counties (Figure 6.6). North Carolina matches three counties here (and 100 in reality). Which county’s population should go in North Carolina’s row?






Figure 6.6: A one-to-many join. The North Carolina record matches three county records, so there is no single value to copy.



Software answers that question in different ways, and none of them is what you want:

QGIS copies the first matching record it finds and ignores the rest. You get one county’s value in each state, with no warning.
ArcGIS Pro’s Add Join tool also keeps only the first match by default (its Join Operation is set to one-to-first), so it too drops records without a warning.
A SQL database repeats the state’s row once for each county, so North Carolina appears 100 times. On a map, that means 100 copies of the North Carolina polygon stacked on top of each other.

There are three ways to handle a one-to-many relationship properly:

Summarize the source first. If you want the total county population in each state, use a summary tool (Aggregate or Statistics by categories in QGIS, Summary Statistics in ArcGIS Pro) to make a table with one row per state. Then join that table, which is now one-to-one.
Swap the tables. Make the counties the destination and the states the source. Counties to states is many-to-one, so each county gets its state’s attributes.
Use a relate. A relate (ArcGIS Pro) or a relation (QGIS) links the two tables without copying fields. Select North Carolina, and you can open all its counties in the related table. A relate never breaks the one-row-per-feature rule, because it never adds fields to the layer.

Many-to-many relationships need a third table. A linking table (a junction table) has one row for each pair: TAKES is a linking table between STUDENT and a COURSES table. Each of the two original relationships, students to enrollments and courses to enrollments, is then one-to-many.






TipThink about it



You have a layer of North Carolina’s 100 counties and a table of every hospital in the state, with the county each hospital is in. What is the cardinality of a join from counties to hospitals? How would you make a map of the number of hospital beds in each county?

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.4 Joining census data in QGIS

6.4.1 The task
The most common join in American GIS work is attaching census statistics to census boundaries. The Census Bureau publishes the two separately. Boundary files, called TIGER/Line shapefiles, have geometry and identifiers but almost no statistics. Statistics come as tables, downloaded from data.census.gov, with identifiers but no geometry. A join is the bridge (Figure 6.7). Chapter 8 covers the census itself; here we focus on the join.






Figure 6.7: A census join: the tract layer (destination) and the population table (source) share the GEOID key, and the join adds the POP field to each tract. The population values are made up for the example.





6.4.2 The key: GEOID
Each census tract has an 11-character GEOID made of three FIPS codes strung together:



Table 6.6: The parts of an 11-character tract GEOID, 37135010701.





Part
Digits
Example
Meaning




State
2
37
North Carolina


County
3
135
Orange County


Tract
6
010701
Tract 107.01 (the decimal is implied)






The GEOID is a code, not a quantity, so it must be stored as text (Chapter 5). Stored as text, California’s tract 06001400100 keeps its leading zero. Stored as a number, it becomes 6001400100, and it no longer matches anything.


6.4.3 Step by step
The steps below join 2020 tract populations to North Carolina’s census tracts. The same steps work for any state, and for counties or block groups.

Load the destination layer. Download the tract shapefile for your state from the Census Bureau’s TIGER/Line page, and add it to QGIS. Open its attribute table, and find the GEOID field. Check that it is a text field (Layer Properties > Fields shows the type).
Get the source table. On data.census.gov, find table P1 (Race) from the 2020 Decennial Census for all tracts in the state, and download it as a CSV. The GEO_ID column looks like 1400000US37135010701: the GEOID with a prefix in front. The total population is in the column P1_001N. (Older downloads, from before 2020, call the GEOID field GEO.id2.) Clean the table first if needed: delete the second header row, and make a column holding just the last 11 characters of GEO_ID.
Add the CSV as a table. Use Layer > Add Layer > Add Delimited Text Layer. Set the file format to CSV, check First record has field names, and under Geometry definition choose No geometry (attribute only table). Under Record and fields options, uncheck Detect field types, so that the GEOID stays text. Click Add.
Join. Open the tract layer’s Properties and go to the Joins tab. Click the green plus. Set Join layer to the CSV, Join field to its GEOID column, and Target field to GEOID. You can choose which fields to bring across, and set a short prefix for their names. Click OK.
Check the join. Reopen the tract layer’s attribute table. The joined fields appear at the right end, named with the CSV’s name or your prefix, such as pop_P1_001N. Sort by the joined field and look for NULL values. Every NULL is a tract that found no match. Never assume a join worked: always look.
Make it permanent. Export the joined layer (right-click > Export > Save Features As) to a new GeoPackage. The joined fields are now part of the new file.
Map it. Style the tracts with Graduated symbology on the population field. Chapter 11 covers how to choose the classes.

In ArcGIS Pro the steps are the same, except that you add the table with Add Data and join it with Add Join (right-click the layer, then Joins and Relates).






NoteDid you know..?



Spreadsheets cause so many join failures that scientists once renamed genes to avoid them. Excel turned gene symbols such as SEPT1 and MARCH1 into the dates 1-Sep and 1-Mar, and a 2016 study found the error in about a fifth of the genetics papers that came with Excel files (Ziemann et al. 2016). In 2020 the committee that names human genes gave 27 genes new symbols, such as SEPTIN1 and MARCHF1, partly to stop it. Opening a census CSV in Excel does the same thing to GEOIDs: it drops the leading zeros.




6.4.4 Why joins fail
When a join gives NULL for every record, or for some of them, the cause is almost always one of the four in Table 6.7.



Table 6.7: Common join problems and their fixes.










Problem
What you see
Fix




The key fields have different types (text and number)
The join fails, or every value is NULL
Convert one field so that both keys have the same type


Leading zeros were lost (06001 became 6001)
Many NULLs, often a whole state
Keep IDs as text. Don’t open the CSV in Excel; set the field types with a .csvt file, or turn off Detect field types


Extra spaces or different capitalization ('Wake ' vs. 'WAKE')
Some rows fail to match
Trim spaces and make the case the same before the join


Duplicate keys in the source
Wrong or missing values
The join is one-to-many: summarize the source first






Figure 6.8 shows the second problem, the most common of all. The tract layer stores GEOID as text, with the leading zero. The CSV was read as numbers, which have no leading zeros. Not a single key matches.






Figure 6.8: When a CSV’s GEOID field is read as a number, the leading zero disappears and no key matches.



A .csvt file fixes the field types of a CSV in QGIS and GDAL. It is a one-line text file with the same name as the CSV (for example pop.csvt next to pop.csv), which lists the type of each column in order, in quotes:
"String","Integer"


6.4.5 Attribute joins and spatial joins
Everything in this chapter is an attribute join: the tables are matched by the values of a shared key. Sometimes two layers share no key at all. A table of EMS calls has coordinates but no neighborhood code; a layer of neighborhoods has no call numbers. They can still be linked, by location, with a spatial join. That is the subject of Chapter 7.



Table 6.8: Attribute joins and spatial joins compared.











Attribute join
Spatial join

Location

Count the schools in each district


Needs

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.6 Summary

A database management system (DBMS) stores data once and controls who can read and change it. It works as a client/server system, often in three tiers, and lets many users work at the same time.
A relational database links tables through keys. A primary key identifies each row uniquely; a foreign key in another table points back to it and can repeat.
A table join appends the fields of a source table to a destination table by matching key values. The key fields can have different names, but their values and data types must match.
A join is temporary, matches on values rather than row order, and changes neither table. Export the result to keep it.
An inner join keeps only matched rows. A left join keeps every destination row, with NULL where there is no match; it is the default in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.
Cardinality is how many source records match each destination record. One-to-one and many-to-one joins work directly. For one-to-many, summarize the source first, swap the tables, or use a relate. Many-to-many needs a linking table.
Census statistics join to census boundaries on the GEOID, which must stay text so that its leading zeros survive.
Most failed joins come from mismatched types, lost leading zeros, stray spaces, or duplicate keys. Always check the result for NULLs.

title: 6  Databases and Table Joins
text:
6.7 Exercises

Design the keys. A city tracks parks, the playgrounds in each park, and the inspections of each playground. Sketch three tables. Give each a primary key, and show the foreign keys that link them.
Predict the join. Using the People and Cars tables, write out the result of an inner join, a left join, and a right join. How many rows does each have?
Name the cardinality. For each pair, name the destination and source and give the cardinality: (a) counties to a table of county unemployment rates; (b) ZIP codes to a table of businesses with their ZIP code; (c) census tracts to the counties they are in; (d) rivers to the counties they flow through.
Census join. Follow the steps in Section 6.4 for North Carolina’s census tracts. How many tracts are there? How many have NULL population after the join, and why? Export the result and make a graduated map.
Break it on purpose. Repeat exercise 4, but open the CSV in a spreadsheet program first and save it again. Then add it to QGIS with Detect field types checked. What happens to the join? For which state would this mistake do the most damage?
One-to-many. Join a table of North Carolina counties to a layer of the 50 states, with the states as the destination. What value does North Carolina get? Then summarize the county table by state and join it again. Compare the two results.
Relates. In QGIS, set up a relation between a layer of states and a table of counties (Project Properties > Relations). Use the identify tool on North Carolina. What do you see that a join could not show?

(Bolstad). Its five components are data, hardware, software, people, and

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.1 What is a spatial join?
Chapter 6 joined tables that share a key, such as a census table and census tracts that both carry a GEOID. Many questions involve two layers with no shared field at all:
In each case, the only thing linking the two layers is where their features are. A call belongs to the neighborhood it falls in; a school belongs to the district that contains it. A spatial join uses that location to match the records, and then appends attributes just like the joins in Chapter 6.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.1.1 Location instead of a key
An attribute join matches records whose key fields hold the same value (Figure 7.1, left). A spatial join matches features whose geometries have a spatial relationship (Figure 7.1, right). Instead of asking “does this FIPS code equal that one?”, the software asks “does this point fall inside that polygon?” or “which of these airports is closest to this city?”






Figure 7.1: Left: an attribute join matches rows by a shared key. Right: a spatial join matches features by location, here EMS calls (points) falling inside counties (polygons). The counties are made up.



Everything else about a join stays the same:

The destination layer (ArcGIS calls it the target features) is the one whose features you keep, and to which fields are added.
The source layer (the join features) supplies the fields.
The output is one table: every field of the destination layer, followed by the fields of the matching source feature. Destination features with no match are kept, with NULL in the new fields, unless you ask for matched features only.

Unlike an attribute join in the Joins tab, a spatial join usually writes a new layer. Your original layers are not changed.


7.1.2 Spatial relationships
Every spatial join needs a rule for deciding which source features match a destination feature. The rules come in two families:

Inside relationships test containment or overlap: a point inside a polygon, a line crossing a polygon, a polygon within another polygon. In this chapter we call a join that uses them an inside join.
Distance relationships test proximity: the closest feature, or every feature within a set distance. A join that uses them is a distance join.

The software calls these rules spatial predicates (QGIS’s geometric predicates, ArcGIS Pro’s match options). The names you will see in the tool dialogs are:



Table 7.1: Spatial predicates in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.









Predicate
True when the two geometries…




intersects
share any point at all (the most general test)


contains
one has the other entirely inside it


within (are within)
one lies entirely inside the other (the reverse of contains)


touches
share a boundary, but their interiors don’t overlap


overlaps
share some, but not all, of their area, and are the same kind of geometry


crosses
a line passes through a polygon or across another line


equals
are exactly the same geometry


disjoint
share no point at all


within a distance
are closer than a set distance


closest (nearest neighbor)
are the nearest pair






For points in polygons, intersects and within give almost the same answer. They differ only for a point that sits exactly on a boundary, which intersects counts and within does not.






NoteDid you know..?



To test whether a point is inside a polygon, most GIS software draws an imaginary line from the point out to infinity and counts how many times it crosses the polygon’s edge. An odd number of crossings means the point is inside; an even number means it is outside. The ray-casting test works for any polygon, however twisted, and it has been used since the earliest computer graphics in the 1960s.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.2 Four kinds of spatial join

7.2.1 Simple or summarized, inside or distance
Every spatial join can be described with two choices (Figure 7.2):

Inside or distance: is the relationship containment or proximity?
Simple or summarized: does each destination feature receive the attributes of one source feature, or a summary of many?







Figure 7.2: The four kinds of spatial join. In each panel, the destination is the layer the question asks about. The counties, hotels, and attractions are made up.



Reading the four panels:

Simple inside join (top left). Which county is each school in? The schools are the destination; the counties are the source. Each school gets the name and attributes of the one county that contains it.
Summarized inside join (top right). How many schools are in each county? Now the counties are the destination and the schools are the source. Each county gets a count of the schools inside it.
Simple distance join (bottom left). Which attraction is closest to each hotel, and how far away is it? Each hotel gets the attributes of its nearest attraction, plus a field holding the distance.
Summarized distance join (bottom right). How many attractions are closest to each hotel? Each attraction is assigned to its nearest hotel, and each hotel gets a count of the attractions assigned to it.

Notice that the same two layers can answer different questions. Schools-to-counties and counties-to-schools are both inside joins; which layer is the destination depends on what one row of the answer should be.


7.2.2 A simple distance join: cities and airports
Figure 7.3 shows a simple distance join with real data. The destination layer is North Carolina’s cities, and the source layer is the region’s major airports. Each city receives the code of its nearest airport and the distance to it. The cities are colored by their airport and sized by the distance.






Figure 7.3: A simple distance join: each North Carolina city in Natural Earth’s populated places layer joined to its nearest airport in Natural Earth’s airports layer, with distances measured in NC State Plane (EPSG:32119). The airports layer includes only larger airports, so Asheville’s own airport is missing and Asheville is matched to Knoxville, Tennessee.



Two things stand out. First, a distance join pays no attention to boundaries: Asheville’s nearest airport in this layer is across the state line in Tennessee. Second, the answer is only as good as the source layer. Asheville has a regional airport, but this small-scale layer leaves it out, so the join gives an answer that is correct for the data and wrong for the world. Always ask whether the source layer contains every feature that could be the right answer.


7.2.3 An inside join: septic systems and geology
A county health department wants to know the bedrock under every septic system, because septic systems on permeable rock can leak into groundwater. The destination is the septic systems (points), and the source is a geology map (polygons). Each septic system falls inside exactly one geology unit, so each receives exactly one rock type. The output table is the septic table with the geology unit’s name and symbol added to each row, ready for a query such as "ROCKTYPE" = 'Limestone'.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.3 Cardinality decides simple or summarized

7.3.1 The rule of joining, again
Chapter 6’s rule of joining applies to spatial joins too. Ask how many source features can match each destination feature:

One-to-one or many-to-one: a simple join. Each septic system lies in one geology unit; many septic systems can share a unit. Each city has one nearest airport; many cities can share one. There is never more than one set of attributes to copy, so a simple join copies them directly.
One-to-many or many-to-many: a summarized join. Each county contains many schools. Each river flows through many counties. There is no single set of attributes to copy.

A summarized join solves the one-to-many problem by collapsing all the matches into statistics. It finds every source feature that matches each destination feature, summarizes them, and appends one row of summary values. Every summarized join reports a count of matches (ArcGIS Pro names the field Join_Count). You can also ask for the sum, mean, minimum, maximum, and other statistics of any numeric field in the source. Summing an enrollment field over the schools in each county gives the number of students in each county, which answers the school district question from the start of the chapter.


7.3.2 Which layer is the destination?
The surest way to choose the destination is to picture the answer. What should one row of the output represent? That row is a feature of the destination layer.

“Which county is each school in?” One row per school: schools are the destination.
“How many schools are in each county?” One row per county: counties are the destination.
“Which volcano is closest to each city?” One row per city: cities are the destination.

Most failed spatial joins come from picking the wrong destination layer, or from running a simple join where several features match. In the second case, the software quietly keeps one match (usually the first it finds) and throws the rest away.






TipThink about it



A summarized distance join counts the attractions closest to each hotel. If you drew a boundary around all the land closer to each hotel than to any other, what shape would each hotel’s area be? (Hint: look up Thiessen polygons, also called Voronoi polygons.)








NoteDid you know..?



One of the most famous maps in history is a summarized distance join done by hand. After the 1854 cholera outbreak in London, John Snow mapped the homes of the people who died, then drew a line around the area closer, by walking distance, to the Broad Street pump than to any other pump. Most of the deaths fell inside that area (Snow 1855). Chapter 1 tells more of the story.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.4 Coordinate systems and distance joins

7.4.1 Distances come out in the data’s units
A distance join reports distances in the units of the source data’s coordinate system. If the layers are projected in meters, the distances are in meters. If the layers are stored in a geographic coordinate system (GCS), such as WGS84 (EPSG:4326) or NAD83 (EPSG:4269), the distances are in decimal degrees. The software does not warn you. You simply get a Distance field full of numbers like 0.47.
Degrees cannot be turned into miles or kilometers with one conversion factor. As Chapter 3 showed, a degree of latitude is always about 111 km (69 miles), but a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles: about 111 km at the equator, 90 km at Chapel Hill, 79 km at 45° N, and 56 km at 60° N (Figure 7.4, left). A distance in degrees mixes two different scales.






Figure 7.4: Left: the ground length of one degree of latitude and one degree of longitude, by latitude, on the WGS84 ellipsoid. Right: at 45° N, attraction B is closer to the hotel in degrees, but attraction A is closer on the ground.



The units are not just a labeling problem. They can change which feature is nearest. At 45° N, an attraction 0.9° east of a hotel is 71 km away, and one 0.8° north is 89 km away (Figure 7.4, right). In degrees, the northern attraction looks closer (0.8 < 0.9). On the ground, the eastern one is closer by 18 km. A distance join run on unprojected data would match the hotel to the wrong attraction.
The fix: before a distance join, project both layers into a coordinate system that preserves distance well for your study area, such as the right UTM zone or State Plane zone (Chapter 4). The distances then come out in meters or feet, and the nearest feature is the nearest on the ground.






NoteGeodesic distances



Some newer tools can measure distances on the ellipsoid even when the data are in a GCS. ArcGIS Pro’s Spatial Join, for example, has geodesic match options such as Within a distance geodesic and Closest geodesic. QGIS’s Join Attributes by Nearest does not: it measures in the layer’s own units. Unless you know what the tool does, projecting first is the safe habit.




7.4.2 Projecting on the fly is not enough
QGIS and ArcGIS Pro project layers on the fly (Chapter 4). If the map is set to NC State Plane, layers stored in WGS84 are drawn in State Plane too, and the map looks correct.
But the join tools read the coordinates stored in the layers, not the coordinates on the screen. Changing the map’s coordinate system changes the picture, not the data. If the data on disk are still in degrees, the distances will be too.
To fix it, make projected copies of the layers and run the join on those:

In QGIS, use Vector > Data Management Tools > Reproject Layer, or Export > Save Features As with a new CRS.
In ArcGIS Pro, use the Project tool.

Then check the layer’s properties to confirm the new CRS, and run the join again.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.5 Spatial joins in practice

7.5.1 Six questions to answer first
Before opening any tool, work through these questions on paper:

Sketch the layers. What kinds of geometry are they: points, lines, or polygons?
What should the output look like? What does one row represent, and which fields should it have?
Which layer is the destination? The layer whose features you keep and add fields to: the one that one row of the output represents.
Inside or distance? Inside when one feature lies within, or crosses, another; distance when they don’t touch.
What is the cardinality? Can a destination feature match more than one source feature?
Simple or summarized? One-to-one or many-to-one: simple. One-to-many or many-to-many: summarized, with the statistics you need.

And for a distance join, a seventh: are both layers in a projected coordinate system with sensible units?


7.5.2 Spatial joins in QGIS
QGIS splits spatial joins into separate tools, all in the Processing Toolbox and under Vector > Data Management Tools:

Join Attributes by Location is the simple inside join. Join to features in is the destination layer. The Features they check boxes set the predicates. By comparing to is the source layer. The Join type sets the cardinality: Create separate feature for each matching feature (one-to-many) repeats a destination feature for every match, and Take attributes of the first matching feature only (one-to-one) keeps one. Check Discard records which could not be joined to drop unmatched features.
Join Attributes by Location (Summary) is the summarized inside join. Choose the fields to summarize and the statistics (count, sum, mean, min, max, and others).
Join Attributes by Nearest is the distance join. Set the maximum number of nearest neighbors (1 for the closest) and, optionally, a maximum distance. It adds fields with the distance and the neighbor’s position.
Count Points in Polygon is a shortcut for the most common summarized join: it adds a count of points to each polygon.



7.5.3 Spatial joins in ArcGIS Pro
ArcGIS Pro does every kind of spatial join with one Spatial Join tool, in the Geoprocessing pane, or from the layer’s Data tab under Add Spatial Join. The kind of join depends on its settings:

Target features is the destination layer; Join features is the source.
Join operation: Join one to one gives one output row per target feature. When several join features match, it adds a Join_Count field and combines their values with the merge rules in the field map (first, sum, mean, minimum, maximum, and others). Join one to many writes one output row for each match.
Keep all target features: checked, unmatched targets are kept (a left join); unchecked, they are dropped.
Match option: the predicate, such as Intersect, Completely contains, Within a distance, or Closest.
Search radius: for Within a distance and Closest.
Distance field name: for Closest, the field that will hold the distance.

For example, to count the motorcycle crashes within 30 feet of each road, set Roads as the target, the crashes as the join features, Join one to one, Keep all target features, and Within a distance with a 30-foot radius. The Join_Count of each road is the number of crashes near it (Figure 7.5).






Figure 7.5: A “within a distance” join: every crash inside the road’s search distance (the dashed outline) counts toward the road’s Join_Count. The road and crashes are made up.



Table 7.2 summarizes which tool to use for each kind of join.



Table 7.2: Tools for each kind of spatial join, as named in QGIS 3 and ArcGIS Pro 3.










Join
QGIS
ArcGIS Pro Spatial Join




Inside, simple
Join Attributes by Location, first matching feature only
Match option Intersect or Within; Join one to one


Inside, summarized
Join Attributes by Location (Summary), or Count Points in Polygon
Join one to one with merge rules (Sum, Mean); adds Join_Count


Distance, closest

Match option Closest; set a distance field name
