Match option Within a distance; Join one to one








7.5.4 Reading the output
Open the attribute table of the output layer. The destination’s fields come first, then the source’s. Then check three things:

The row count. A simple join with every destination feature kept should have exactly as many rows as the destination layer. More rows means a one-to-many join repeated some features; fewer means unmatched features were dropped.
NULLs. Rows with NULL in the joined fields had no match. Is that what you expect? A point in the ocean, outside every county, has no county.
Distances. If there is a distance field, are the values sensible? Numbers below 1 for features kilometers apart mean the data were in degrees.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.6 Worked examples
For each example, answer the six questions before reading the solution.

7.6.1 Example 1: congressional districts with more than 10 earthquake deaths
Find every congressional district that has had more than 10 earthquake deaths. You have earthquake points with a DEATHS field, and congressional district polygons.






TipSolution






Output: one row per district, with total deaths.
Destination: congressional districts. Source: earthquakes.
Relationship: inside (points in polygons).
Cardinality: one-to-many; a district can contain many earthquakes.
Join: summarized, with the sum of DEATHS.
Then select the districts with an attribute query (Chapter 5), such as "DEATHS_sum" > 10 (QGIS names the summed field this way).






7.6.2 Example 2: a pollution risk index for rivers
Score each river by the total number of people living in the counties it flows through. You have river lines and county polygons with a population field.






TipSolution






Output: one row per river, with the total population.
Destination: rivers (lines). Source: counties (polygons).
Relationship: inside, using intersects (a river crosses each county it flows through).
Cardinality: one-to-many; each river crosses many counties.
Join: summarized, with the sum of population. Rivers that flow past more people score higher.






7.6.3 Example 3: the closest volcano to each U.S. city
Make a table of the volcano closest to each city in the United States, and how far away it is.






TipSolution






Output: one row per city, with its nearest volcano and the distance.
Destination: cities. Source: volcanoes.
Relationship: distance (closest feature).
Cardinality: many-to-one; each city has one closest volcano, though many cities can share it.
Join: simple distance join.
Coordinate system: project both layers first, using an equidistant or equal-area projection for the whole country (such as USA Contiguous Albers, EPSG:5070) so that the distances are in meters, not degrees. Better still, use a tool that measures geodesic distances.

text:

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.8 Summary

A spatial join attaches the attributes of a source layer to a destination layer by location, when the two share no key field.
An inside join matches features that contain, lie within, or intersect each other. A distance join matches the closest feature, or every feature within a set distance, and can record the distance.
The rules are called spatial predicates: intersects, contains, within, touches, overlaps, crosses, equals, disjoint, within a distance, and closest.
A simple join copies one source feature’s attributes to each destination feature. Use it for one-to-one and many-to-one relationships.
A summarized join counts and summarizes all the matching source features. Use it for one-to-many and many-to-many relationships. It always adds a count, and can add sums, means, minimums, and maximums.
Choose the destination layer by asking what one row of the output should represent.
A distance join reports distances in the stored units of the data. Project the layers before a distance join; projecting the map on the fly changes the display, not the data.
QGIS has a tool for each kind of join; ArcGIS Pro’s Spatial Join tool does them all through its settings. Check the output’s row count, NULLs, and distances.

title: 7  Spatial Joins
text:
7.9 Exercises

Name the join. For each question, name the destination and source layers, the relationship, the cardinality, and the kind of join: (a) Which watershed is each well in? (b) How many fast-food restaurants are within 1 km of each school? (c) What is the total length of streams in each county? (d) Which fire station is closest to each house? (e) How many houses does each fire station serve as the closest station?
Count points in polygons. Download Natural Earth’s populated places and country boundaries. In QGIS, count the populated places in each country, and sum their pop_max. Which country has the most places? Does that match the country with the largest summed population?
Simple inside join. Join the countries to the populated places, so that each place gets its country’s name and continent. How many places fall in no country, and why?
Degrees versus meters. Using Natural Earth’s populated places and airports, run Join Attributes by Nearest on the layers as downloaded (EPSG:4326). Then project both into a suitable projected CRS for your study area and run it again. Compare the distance fields. Did any place get a different nearest airport?
Within a distance. Using North Carolina road and crash data from NC OneMap or NCDOT, count the crashes within 30 meters of each road segment. Which segments have the most? What would change with a 100-meter radius?
Plan before you click. Work through the six questions for the earthquake, river, and volcano examples in Section 7.6, then run one of them with data from the USGS and Natural Earth.

title: Unit 2: Spatial Data Quality
text:
Chapter 8: Census Data
Every dataset has a source, a method, and limits. This unit is about where spatial data come from and how good they are. It starts with the largest source of free data about people and places in the United States, the census, and how to read its estimates honestly. It then turns to two ways of making new GIS layers from things that aren’t yet spatial data, addresses and scanned maps, and how to measure the error each one adds. It ends with data made by volunteers, in OpenStreetMap, and the ways the crowd checks its own work. By the end of the unit you can find, join, create, and judge spatial data in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.
The U.S. Census Bureau decides how many members of Congress each state gets and where trillions of federal dollars go. This chapter separates authoritative from asserted data and describes the decennial census, the American Community Survey, and the Economic Census. It explains the hierarchy of census geography, from states to blocks, and the GEOIDs that identify each area. It shows how to choose between decennial, ACS 1-year, and ACS 5-year data, how to read a margin of error, and how to join a census table to its boundaries in ArcGIS Pro.

title: Unit 2: Spatial Data Quality
text:
Chapter 9: Geocoding and Georeferencing
Many records describe a location without coordinates: a street address, or a place on an old paper map. This chapter covers both ways of giving them coordinates. Geocoding matches addresses against reference files, from ZIP Code centroids to parcels, and interpolates positions along streets; match scores and match rates tell you how well it worked. Georeferencing ties a scanned map to the ground with control points and a transformation, and residuals and RMSE measure its error. Both are shown step by step in ArcGIS Pro and QGIS.

title: Unit 2: Spatial Data Quality
text:
Chapter 10: OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
What makes geographic data good enough to use? This chapter defines spatial data quality by its seven elements, from lineage to completeness, then looks at volunteered geographic information, Big Data, and the FAIR principles. It explains how OpenStreetMap works, from its license to its nodes, ways, and tags, and how its quality is measured against authoritative data and from its own history. It ends with crisis mapping, from Haiti in 2010 to the 2015 Nepal earthquake, where thousands of new volunteers mapped a country in weeks.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.1 Population and place data
Chapter 6 joined a census table to census tracts to learn how joins work. This chapter turns to the data itself. The U.S. Census Bureau is the largest source of free, consistent information about people and places in the country. Its numbers decide how many members of Congress each state sends to Washington, where trillions of federal dollars go, where companies open stores, and how public health workers turn case counts into rates.
Census data are also easy to misuse. The same variable can come from three different products, published for eight levels of geography, and many values are estimates with sizable errors. This chapter is about choosing the right product and geography for a question, reading the numbers honestly, and getting them onto a map.
This chapter starts the unit on spatial data quality. Every dataset has a source, a method, and limits. The census documents all three unusually well, so it is a good place to learn to ask about them.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.1.1 Authoritative and asserted data
Data about people and places come from two very different kinds of source:

Authoritative data come from official agencies, such as the Census Bureau or the U.S. Geological Survey. They are collected under documented standards, and they ship with metadata that describe their sources, methods, dates, and accuracy.
Asserted data, also called volunteered geographic information, are contributed by the public. OpenStreetMap is the best-known example (Chapter 10). Their accuracy is undocumented and uneven, and they often have little or no metadata. Busy, popular places tend to be mapped well; quiet ones may be sparse. Where contributors are active, asserted data can be more current, and even more accurate, than old official data.

Neither kind is always better. Before using any dataset, ask who made it, how, when, and whether there is metadata that tells you how accurate it is.


8.1.2 Four kinds of population and place data
Most data about people and places fall into four groups:

Demographic data describe who lives in a place: counts of people and households, and their age, sex, race and ethnicity, and household type. The main sources are the decennial census, the ACS, and the Census Bureau’s annual population estimates.
Socioeconomic data describe economic and social conditions: education, income, employment, poverty, and housing costs. They are often used to characterize neighborhoods, for example in deprivation indices, and as stand-ins for health, because they track health outcomes closely. The main source is the ACS, so every value is an estimate.
Environmental and neighborhood data describe the places themselves: air and water pollution, flood zones, temperature, the habitats of disease-carrying insects, and amenities such as parks, grocery stores, and sidewalks. They usually come from outside the Census Bureau (the EPA, NOAA, and local governments), and are linked to census geography to describe the people exposed.
Health data include vital statistics (births and deaths), morbidity (illness), and the locations of hospitals, clinics, and doctors. They are often published only for counties or states, to protect privacy. Census counts supply the denominators that turn health counts into comparable rates, such as deaths per 100,000 residents.

A rule runs through all of them: the finer the geography, the fewer variables are published, and the less precise they are. A state has thousands of detailed census tables; a block has a handful of counts.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.2 The U.S. Census

8.2.1 The constitutional count
The census is written into the U.S. Constitution. Article I, Section 2 requires an “actual Enumeration” of the population every ten years, to divide the seats in the House of Representatives among the states. The first census was taken in 1790; the 2020 Census was the 24th, and the next is in 2030.
The decennial census counts every resident, whatever their age, citizenship, or housing status. Since 2010, it has asked only a short list of questions: age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, each person’s relationship to the householder, and whether the home is owned or rented. Everything else, from income and education to commuting and home values, now comes from a separate survey, the ACS.






NoteDid you know..?



Your individual census answers are sealed for 72 years. Until then, the Census Bureau may publish only statistics, and it cannot share your answers with any other agency, including the police, immigration authorities, or the IRS. In April 2022, the National Archives released the individual records of the 1950 census, and the 2020 records will be opened in 2092. Genealogists wait for each release eagerly.




8.2.2 The big three surveys
The Census Bureau runs dozens of surveys, but three matter most for mapping (Table 8.1).



Table 8.1: The three Census Bureau surveys used most in GIS.











Survey
How often
What it covers
Kind of numbers




Decennial census
Every 10 years (2010, 2020, 2030)
Every resident: age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, household relationship, owning or renting
Counts of the whole population


American Community Survey (ACS)
Every year, published as 1-year and 5-year estimates
About 3.5 million addresses a year: income, education, employment, commuting, housing costs, language, disability, and much more
Estimates from a sample, each with a margin of error


Economic Census
Every 5 years, in years ending in 2 and 7
Businesses: number of firms, employees, payroll, and sales, by industry
Counts and totals for businesses






Most of the socioeconomic variables you will map come from the ACS. The Bureau also publishes annual population estimates between censuses, built from the last census plus records of births, deaths, and migration.


8.2.3 Why census data matter
Census numbers drive decisions in three arenas:

Political power. The decennial count divides the 435 seats in the House among the states (apportionment), and states use the census to redraw congressional and legislative districts (redistricting).
Money. In fiscal year 2021, 353 federal programs, including Medicaid, SNAP, and Head Start, used census data to distribute more than $2.8 trillion (U.S. Census Bureau 2023).
Business, planning, and health. Companies use census demographics to choose store sites and gauge labor markets. Planners use commuting times to plan transit, and the age and tenure of housing to plan for growth. Health departments use census counts to compute rates and to find groups that are hit harder by disease. Emergency managers use them to find residents, such as older adults or households without a car, who may need help to evacuate.



8.2.4 The census is not perfect
Three limits are worth knowing:

Undercounts and overcounts. Some groups are missed more than others. After each census, the Bureau runs a Post-Enumeration Survey to measure the errors. For 2020, it estimated that the census missed about 5 percent of Hispanic residents and 3.3 percent of Black residents, and an even larger share of American Indians living on reservations, while overcounting non-Hispanic White and Asian residents (U.S. Census Bureau 2022). Young children are also undercounted, census after census.
Differential privacy. For 2020, the Bureau began adding carefully calibrated statistical noise to its published tables, so that individuals cannot be identified by combining them. Totals for states are exact, but counts for small areas, especially blocks, can look odd: a block with houses but no people, or a few children with no adults.
Change. Boundaries, questions, and methods change from census to census. Comparing 2010 and 2020 tract data, for example, requires care, because many tracts were split or redrawn.

The Census Bureau’s Vintage 2025 population estimates, released in January 2026, are a reminder that the population itself keeps changing: U.S. growth slowed to about half a percent between 2024 and 2025, mostly because fewer people moved to the country from abroad. Estimates like these are revised every year, so always check which vintage you are using.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.3 Census geography

8.3.1 The spine
Census data are published for a hierarchy of areas (Figure 8.1). The main line, called the spine, runs from the nation through regions, divisions, states, counties, census tracts, and block groups, down to blocks. Each level nests completely inside the one above. A block is always inside one block group, which is inside one tract, which is inside one county. Because of that, you can add up the blocks in a tract to get the tract, or the tracts in a county to get the county.






Figure 8.1: The hierarchy of census geography. The levels on the spine nest inside each other; the areas off the spine are built from blocks or counties but cross the spine’s boundaries. Redrawn after the Census Bureau’s “Standard Hierarchy of Census Geographic Entities.”



Other areas sit off the spine. They are built from blocks (or, for metropolitan areas, from counties), but they don’t fit neatly inside the spine’s levels:

Places: incorporated cities and towns, and census-designated places for unincorporated communities.
ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs): approximations of ZIP Code areas built from blocks. ZIP Codes are mail routes, not areas, so a ZCTA is never an exact match.
Metropolitan and micropolitan statistical areas: groups of counties tied together by commuting.
School districts, and congressional and state legislative districts.
American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian areas, which can cross state lines.

Off-spine areas cross the spine’s boundaries: a city can spill across two counties, and a ZCTA can cross tracts. You can’t get a ZCTA’s value by adding up tracts.


8.3.2 Tracts, block groups, and blocks
Three small levels are used most in local studies (Figure 8.2):

Census tracts are relatively permanent subdivisions of a county, with 1,200 to 8,000 people and about 4,000 on average. There are about 85,000 of them. They are updated each decade as the population changes, by splitting tracts that grew and merging ones that shrank. Tracts are the usual unit for neighborhood and health studies.
Block groups are clusters of blocks within a tract, usually with 600 to 3,000 people. There are about 240,000. They are the smallest areas with ACS estimates, and those estimates often carry large errors.
Blocks are the smallest areas, bounded by streets, streams, rail lines, and other visible features. The 2020 Census had more than 8 million of them, many with no one living there at all. Blocks get decennial counts only, with no ACS estimates.







Figure 8.2: A census tract (left) is divided into block groups (middle), which are divided into blocks (right). Each level nests completely in the one above. The boundaries are made up.





8.3.3 GEOIDs
Every census area has a GEOID, made by stringing together the FIPS codes of the levels above it (Chapter 6). The GEOID is the key that links census tables to boundaries.



Table 8.2: GEOID structure for the spine’s main levels.

8.4 Census products and variables

8.4.1 What is published where
Smaller geographies get fewer tables (Table 8.3). The decennial census publishes the same few thousand variables for every level, down to the block. The ACS publishes far more, but not for every area.



Table 8.3: Approximate number of variables published for each geography. Counts vary by year.

8.4.2 ACS 1-year and 5-year estimates
The ACS samples addresses every month, and pools them into two products (Figure 8.4):

1-year estimates use 12 months of data. They are the most current, but because the sample is small, they are published only for areas with 65,000 or more people, and they are the least reliable. No tract or block group has 1-year estimates.
5-year estimates pool 60 months of data. They are published for every area down to block groups, and they are the most reliable, but the least current: the 2020–2024 estimates describe the average over five years, not 2024.







Figure 8.4: ACS 1-year and 5-year estimates released in 2025. The 1-year estimates cover 2024 alone; the 5-year estimates pool 2020 through 2024.



Use 1-year estimates for large areas when timeliness matters, such as tracking a state’s income after a recession. Use 5-year estimates for small areas or small population groups. Never compare a 1-year estimate with a 5-year estimate, and don’t compare 5-year estimates whose periods overlap (2015–2019 with 2017–2021, for example), because they share years of data.


8.4.3 Counts and estimates
Decennial counts are full counts: everyone was asked. ACS values are estimates from a sample of about one household in 40 each year, and every one comes with a margin of error (MOE).
A margin of error works like the one on an opinion poll. If a poll finds that 55 percent of people prefer Coffee A, with a margin of error of ±3 points, the true share is probably between 52 and 58 percent. The Census Bureau’s margins of error use a 90 percent confidence level: if the survey were repeated 100 times, about 90 of the ranges would contain the true value.
Figure 8.5 shows five tract estimates of median household income. Tract D’s estimate, $39,800, looks lower than Tract A’s $48,200. But D’s margin of error is $15,300, so its true value could be anywhere from about $24,500 to $55,100. The two ranges overlap widely, so the data can’t tell you which tract has the lower income.






Figure 8.5: Made-up ACS estimates of median household income for five tracts, with their 90 percent margins of error. Green marks a coefficient of variation (CV) under 12 percent; orange, 12 to 40 percent.



A common way to judge an estimate is its coefficient of variation (CV), the standard error as a percentage of the estimate:
\[
\text{CV} = \frac{\text{MOE} / 1.645}{\text{estimate}} \times 100
\]
The 1.645 turns a 90 percent margin of error into a standard error. A widely used rule of thumb treats a CV under 12 percent as reliable, 12 to 40 percent as usable with caution, and over 40 percent as unreliable. When many of your estimates are unreliable, combine them: use larger areas (tracts instead of block groups), or broader categories (all people under 18 instead of each age).
When you add estimates together, the margin of error of the sum is approximately the square root of the sum of the squared margins of error:
\[
\text{MOE}_{\text{sum}} = \sqrt{\text{MOE}_1^2 + \text{MOE}_2^2 + \cdots}
\]
So combining two tracts with MOEs of 300 and 400 people gives an MOE of 500, not 700.






TipThink about it



You are mapping the share of households without a car in each block group of Durham County, to plan bus service. Half the block groups have a CV over 40 percent. What could you do instead? What would you lose by doing it?




8.4.4 Choosing a product and a geography
Put the pieces together like this:

What do you need to measure? If it’s a basic count (people, age, race, housing units), the decennial census has it, down to blocks. If it’s income, education, commuting, or anything else social or economic, you need the ACS.
How small are your areas? Blocks get decennial counts only. Tracts and block groups get ACS 5-year estimates. Areas of 65,000 or more people also get ACS 1-year estimates.
How current must it be? For large areas, 1-year estimates are newer. For everything else, use the latest 5-year estimates.
Do your areas nest? Stay on the spine when you add up areas or compare levels. If you need ZCTAs or school districts, download them directly rather than building them from tracts.
Are the estimates reliable enough? Check the margins of error before you map.







NoteDid you know..?



The 2020 Census was the first in which most households could answer online. About two-thirds of the households that responded on their own did so, and about 80 percent of those used the internet. The rest were counted by mail, by phone, or by census takers who visited the homes that didn’t respond.

title: 8  Census Data
section: 8.5 Getting census data into a GIS
text:
8.5 Getting census data into a GIS

8.5.1 Where to get the data

data.census.gov is the Census Bureau’s main site for tables. Search by topic, place, or table ID (such as S1901, income in the past 12 months), filter by geography, year, and survey, and download the table as a CSV.
The Census Data API (api.census.gov) returns any table for any geography from a URL. Packages for R and Python use it to download tables with their boundaries in one step.
IPUMS NHGIS (nhgis.org) offers census tables back to 1790, with boundary files for each year, and tables already adjusted to consistent boundaries over time.
TIGER/Line shapefiles are the official boundaries for every census geography, with the GEOID in every record. The Bureau also publishes cartographic boundary files, simplified and clipped to the shoreline, which are better for small-scale maps.



8.5.2 Tutorial: a census join in ArcGIS Pro
This tutorial attaches median household income from the ACS to North Carolina’s 100 counties, in ArcGIS Pro. The QGIS steps were covered in Chapter 6 (Section 6.4).

Get the data. Download a county boundary layer for North Carolina (for example the TIGER/Line or cartographic boundary file for U.S. counties, selected to STATEFP = '37'). On data.census.gov, find table S1901 (Income in the Past 12 Months) from the latest ACS 5-year estimates, filter to all counties in North Carolina, and download it as a CSV.
Start a project, add the data. Create a new map project and add the county layer and the CSV. The CSV appears under Standalone Tables in the Contents pane.
Check the key fields. Open the county layer’s fields view (right-click > Data Design > Fields). The county layer’s GEOID is text, 5 characters. Open the CSV: ArcGIS Pro reads its ID column, after you clean it to the 5-digit code, as a number (Long integer). The two key fields must have the same type, so one has to change.
Match the types. A CSV is read-only in ArcGIS Pro, so add a field to the county layer instead. In the county attribute table, click Add, name the field fips5, set its type to Long, and save. Right-click the new column and choose Calculate Field, with the expression fips5 = !GEOID!. Each text code is converted to a number. (Because both keys are now numbers, the missing leading zeros don’t matter.)
Join. Right-click the county layer, choose Joins and Relates > Add Join. Set the Input Join Field to fips5, the Join Table to the CSV, and the Join Table Field to its ID column. Click Validate Join to check how many records match: it should be all 100. Click OK.
Check and make it permanent. Open the attribute table and look for NULLs in the joined fields. Then right-click the layer and choose Data > Export Features to save a new feature class with the joined fields.
Map it. Symbolize the counties with Graduated Colors on the median household income field. Add the margin of error to the pop-up, so that readers can see how precise each estimate is.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.7 Summary

Authoritative data follow documented standards and come with metadata; asserted data are contributed by the public and their accuracy is undocumented.
Population and place data are demographic, socioeconomic, environmental, or health data. The finer the geography, the fewer variables and the larger the errors.
The decennial census counts everyone every ten years with a short form. The American Community Survey samples about 3.5 million addresses a year for social, economic, and housing data. The Economic Census profiles businesses every five years.
Census data apportion the House, guide trillions of federal dollars, and serve business, planning, and public health. The census also has limits: uneven undercounts, differential privacy noise in small areas, and changing boundaries.
Census geography has a spine (nation, regions, divisions, states, counties, tracts, block groups, blocks) whose levels nest, and off-spine areas such as places and ZCTAs that don’t.
A GEOID strings FIPS codes together: 2 digits for a state, 5 for a county, 11 for a tract, 12 for a block group, 15 for a block. Keep it as text.
ACS 1-year estimates are current but cover only areas of 65,000+ people. ACS 5-year estimates cover every area down to block groups and are more reliable.
Every ACS value has a margin of error at 90 percent confidence. Check the coefficient of variation, and combine areas or categories when estimates are unreliable.
Join census tables to boundaries on the GEOID, with matching field types, and check the result for NULLs.

title: 8  Census Data
text:
8.8 Exercises

Authoritative or asserted? Classify each source, and say what metadata you would look for: the 2020 Census, OpenStreetMap, a county’s parcel layer, a crowd-sourced map of potholes, and the USGS National Hydrography Dataset.
Pick the product. For each question, choose the product (decennial, ACS 1-year, or ACS 5-year) and the geography: (a) the number of children under 5 in each block of Chapel Hill; (b) median rent in each tract of Wake County; (c) the poverty rate in North Carolina in the latest year; (d) the share of commuters who walk to work in each block group of Orange County.
Read a GEOID. What does the GEOID 371830541091 identify? Which state, which county, which tract, and which level of geography?
Margins of error. Download median household income (table B19013) for every tract in Orange County, NC, from the latest ACS 5-year estimates, including the margins of error. Compute the CV of each tract. How many are over 12 percent? Over 40 percent?
County join. Follow the ArcGIS Pro tutorial in Section 8.5 (or the QGIS steps in Chapter 6) to map median household income for North Carolina’s counties. Which county has the highest income, and which the lowest? Are their margins of error small enough to be sure?
Rates. Download county population from the 2020 Census and a count of something by county (for example, hospitals, or COVID-19 cases from the state health department). Compute and map a rate per 100,000 residents. Why is a map of the raw counts misleading?

title: 9  Geocoding and Georeferencing
text:
9.1 Geocoding and address matching
Most information doesn’t arrive with coordinates. A table of patients has street addresses. A list of restaurant inspections has addresses. A historic map of Chapel Hill is a scan: a grid of pixels that knows its rows and columns, but nothing about where on Earth it belongs. Before any of these can be mapped with other layers, they have to be given a location.
This chapter covers the two most common ways to do that. Geocoding turns descriptions of places, most often street addresses, into coordinates. Georeferencing ties an image or scanned map to a coordinate system. Both are estimates, and both have errors you can measure. The thread running through the chapter: the reference data you choose, and how carefully you use them, decide how accurate the result is.

title: 9  Geocoding and Georeferencing
text:
9.1.1 An everyday example
Every time you type an address into a map app, the app geocodes it. The text “201 E Franklin St, Chapel Hill, NC 27514” has to become a latitude and longitude before the app can put a pin on the map or draw a route. That everyday step is the same one a health department uses to map thousands of disease cases, or a city uses to map every 911 call.
Geocoding is assigning geographic coordinates to data that describe a location in some other way. It is a form of data capture. The most common kind is address matching: placing an address at a point or in an area by comparing it with a reference file whose features already carry address information. The output is a point layer that keeps all the original attributes, ready to be mapped and analyzed with other layers.


9.1.2 How U.S. addresses are structured
U.S. addresses are street-based: a house number, a street name and type, a city, a state, and a ZIP Code. Two conventions make them easy for a GIS to place:

House numbers increase along each street, usually in blocks of 100. The 1100 block of Main Street comes after the 1000 block.
Odd numbers are on one side of the street, and even numbers on the other.

That ordered, ranged numbering is what lets software place an address along a street line. Not every country works this way. Some historic British houses had names rather than numbers, and many villages numbered houses in any order.






NoteDid you know..?



In most of Japan, streets have no names. A traditional Japanese address names a district, then a numbered block, then a building number, and the buildings on a block were often numbered in the order they were built, not their order along the street. Finding a house by its address alone can be hard even for locals, which is why Japanese police boxes keep detailed neighborhood maps for giving directions.




9.1.3 Reference files
Address matching compares each address with a reference file. There are three common kinds:



Table 9.1: The three common kinds of reference file for address matching.










Reference file
Each feature holds
Example




Point or polygon
One discrete address
Land parcels, address points


Point or polygon
A group of addresses
ZIP Code areas, ZIP+4 segments


Line
A range of addresses along a street segment
TIGER/Line roads, local street centerlines






Each kind places an address differently, with a different accuracy:

ZIP Code centroids. Every address in a five-digit ZIP Code is placed at the same point, the ZIP Code’s center. It matches almost every address, and quickly, but it is the least precise option: in a large rural ZIP Code, the error can be several kilometers. (Remember that ZIP Codes are mail delivery routes, not areas. The Census Bureau’s ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, Chapter 8, approximate them.)
ZIP+4 and ZIP+2. The four extra digits of a ZIP+4 identify a short piece of a delivery route: one side of a block, a single building, or a large mail recipient. The address is placed at the center of that segment. A ZIP+2 (the first two of the four digits) groups several segments.
Street centerlines. Each street segment stores the range of addresses on its left and right sides. The address is placed by interpolation along the segment (Section 9.1.4). The Census Bureau’s free, nationwide TIGER/Line files make this the most common method in the United States.
Parcels. Each parcel polygon is one property with its own address, so a match finds the exact lot. The point can be placed at the parcel’s centroid, inside the property rather than on the street. Parcels are the most accurate reference, but counties maintain them, so coverage and quality vary from place to place.
Address points. Many states and counties, including North Carolina, now keep a point for every address, often on the rooftop or the building entrance. Where they exist, address points are as accurate as parcels.

Figure 9.1 shows how the same address lands in four different places, depending on the reference file.






Figure 9.1: One address placed with four reference files: at the ZIP Code’s centroid, at the center of its ZIP+4 block face, interpolated along the street centerline, and at the parcel’s centroid. The streets and parcels are made up.



The trade-off is summarized in Table 9.2. Moving down the table, matching gets easier and cheaper, and the locations get less precise.



Table 9.2: Accuracy and effort of address-matching reference data.

9.1.4 Linear interpolation along a street
Street centerline matching takes three steps (Figure 9.2):

Attribute query. Find the street segment whose name, type, and address range include the address: for 1147 Main St, the segment of Main Street that holds 1100 to 1199.
Choose the side of the street. The segment stores a range for each side. Here the left side holds 1100 to 1198 (even), and the right side 1101 to 1199 (odd). 1147 is odd, so it is on the right.
Interpolate. Assume the addresses are spaced evenly along the segment, and find how far along it 1147 falls.







Figure 9.2: Linear interpolation along a TIGER street segment. 1147 is odd, so it is on the right side, 47 percent of the way from 1101 to 1199.



The share of the way along the segment is
\[
A\% = \frac{A_\# - A_{\text{from}}}{A_{\text{to}} - A_{\text{from}}}
\]
where \(A_\#\) is the target house number and \(A_{\text{from}}\) and \(A_{\text{to}}\) are the house numbers at the segment’s two ends, on that side of the street. The coordinates are then
\[
X_\# = X_{\text{from}} + A\% \times (X_{\text{to}} - X_{\text{from}}), \qquad
Y_\# = Y_{\text{from}} + A\% \times (Y_{\text{to}} - Y_{\text{from}})
\]
For 1147 Main St:

Address difference: 1147 − 1101 = 46.
Address range: 1199 − 1101 = 98.
Share along the segment: 46 ÷ 98 = 0.47, or 47 percent.
Change in X: 52 − 42 = 10.
Interpolated X: 42 + (0.47 × 10) = 46.7.

Y is found the same way. Software then moves the point a small offset distance (often 5 to 10 meters) to the correct side of the centerline, so that houses on opposite sides of the street don’t land on top of each other.
Interpolation is an estimate. It assumes the lots are equal in size, that every number in the range is used, and that the street is straight. A long rural driveway, a big lot at one end of a block, or a range of 1100 to 1199 with only six houses can each put the point tens of meters from the building.






TipThink about it



Where is 1184 Main St, on the same segment? Which side of the street is it on, what is A%, and what is its interpolated X? (Answer: the left side, since 1184 is even; A% = 84 ÷ 98 = 0.86; X = 42 + 8.6 = 50.6.)




9.1.5 Geocoding in practice
Individual and batch mode. Online tools geocode one address at a time. The Census Geocoder (geocoding.geo.census.gov) returns the coordinates of an address and the census tract, block group, and block it is in, and it can match a batch of up to 10,000 addresses from a CSV. GIS software geocodes a whole table at once in batch mode: ArcGIS Pro’s Geocode Table tool, or plugins and processing tools in QGIS such as MMQGIS.
Standardization. Before matching, the software parses each address into parts (number, prefix, name, type, suffix, unit) and standardizes them, so that “201 East Franklin Street” and “201 E Franklin St” are treated alike.
Match scores. Each candidate gets a match score, often from 0 to 100, measuring how closely the address agrees with the reference. Spelling differences (“Fraklin”), a missing street type, or a wrong ZIP Code lower the score. The software accepts the best candidate above a minimum score, and reports each address as:

Matched: one good candidate.
Tied: two or more candidates with the same score, such as “Main St” in two towns.
Unmatched: no candidate good enough.

Match rate. The match rate is the share of addresses that were matched. A 70 percent match rate means three addresses in ten are missing from your map, and they are rarely missing at random: rural route and PO Box addresses, new subdivisions not yet in the reference file, and addresses typed carelessly all fail more often. Review unmatched and tied addresses by hand (ArcGIS Pro’s Rematch Addresses pane does this), and always report the match rate with your results.






TipThink about it



A health department geocodes the home addresses of people with a disease, and posts a map of the points online. What could go wrong? How might the department show the pattern while protecting people’s privacy? (Look up geomasking and aggregation.)

title: 9  Geocoding and Georeferencing
text:
9.2 Georeferencing

9.2.1 Why georeference?
A scanned map, an aerial photo, or a raw satellite image is a raster that knows only its own file coordinates: pixel columns and rows, counted from the top-left corner. Its features don’t sit at their true positions on the Earth. To overlay it on other layers, measure on it, or digitize from it, you have to give it map coordinates (Figure 9.3).
Georeferencing transforms a raster from file coordinates to map coordinates in a coordinate system and projection. It is a kind of image rectification. Common uses include:

Overlaying historic maps on modern data, to see how a city, coastline, or forest has changed.
Digitizing features from a scanned paper map, such as old property lines or the boundaries of redlined neighborhoods.
Aligning a drone image or a scanned air photo with other layers.







Figure 9.3: Building outlines on a scanned image in file coordinates (left), and the same outlines after georeferencing, in UTM coordinates (right). The buildings are made up.





9.2.2 Five steps
Georeferencing follows five steps:

Get to know the data. What does the image show, what is its scale and date, and what reference layers cover the same area?
Set up ground control points (GCPs): features you can find on both the image and a reference layer.
Transform the raster. This has two parts. A coordinate transformation (spatial interpolation) works out where each cell belongs on the map. Resampling (intensity interpolation) then gives each output cell a value.
Validate the result with the residuals and the root mean square error (RMSE).
Rectify: save the georeferenced raster.



9.2.3 Ground control points
Ground control points (GCPs) are features that can be identified on the image and located accurately on a reference layer, such as a basemap, an orthophoto, or a road layer. Good GCPs are:

Easy to identify on both: road intersections, building corners, bridges, and dams.
Spatially accurate in the reference data.
Evenly distributed across the whole image, including near the corners and edges. GCPs bunched in one area leave the rest of the image unconstrained.
Stable. Avoid features that move or change: shorelines, river channels, vehicles, shadows, and trees. On a historic map, a church or a road junction that still exists is better than a field boundary.



9.2.4 Transformations
A transformation is a set of equations that converts each image position \((x', y')\) into map coordinates \((x, y)\). Its coefficients are solved from the GCPs, usually by least squares, which finds the coefficients that make the errors at the GCPs as small as possible overall.
First-order (affine) transformation. For moderate distortion over a small area, a first-order polynomial with six coefficients is enough (Jensen 2015):
\[
x = a_0 + a_1 x' + a_2 y', \qquad y = b_0 + b_1 x' + b_2 y'
\]
The six coefficients model the distortions in Figure 9.4: a shift in x and y (translation), a change of scale in x and in y, skew, and rotation. An affine transformation keeps straight lines straight and parallel lines parallel. It needs at least 3 GCPs.






Figure 9.4: The distortions an affine transformation corrects. Dashed: the original square.



Higher-order polynomials. Nonlinear distortions, such as those from terrain relief, lens curvature, or a paper map that has shrunk unevenly, need a higher-order polynomial, which lets the image bend (Figure 9.5). Each order needs more GCPs:



Table 9.3: Polynomial transformations and the minimum number of GCPs.





Order
Can model
Minimum GCPs




1st (affine)
Shift, scale, skew, rotation
3


2nd
Simple curves
6


3rd
More complex bends
10












Figure 9.5: Fitting the same GCPs with 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-order polynomials. Higher orders bend to fit the curve. The distortion and GCPs are made up.



Two rules follow:

Collect more than the minimum. With exactly 3 GCPs, an affine transformation fits them perfectly, and you have no way to measure the error. Ten or more well-spread GCPs are a good habit.
Use the lowest order that fits. A high-order polynomial bends to fit the GCPs, but it can warp badly in areas between and beyond them, as the right edge of the third panel in Figure 9.5 shows. Try first order, and move up only if the error is too large.

Software offers other transformations too. A Helmert (similarity) transformation allows only shift, rotation, and uniform scale. A spline (thin plate spline or rubber sheeting) fits every GCP exactly and stretches the image between them; it is useful for badly distorted historic maps, but it hides errors at the GCPs, because their residuals are all zero.


9.2.5 Resampling
After the transformation, the output grid doesn’t line up with the input pixels. Each output cell is traced back to its position in the input image, and given a value by resampling:

Nearest neighbor takes the value of the closest input cell. It keeps the original values, so use it for categorical rasters such as land cover.
Bilinear interpolation averages the four closest cells, weighted by distance. It gives a smoother look for continuous images such as air photos and scanned maps.
Cubic convolution uses the 16 closest cells. It is sharper than bilinear, but slower.



9.2.6 Residuals and RMSE
How good is the fit? After the transformation is solved, it is applied to each GCP’s image position, and the result is compared with where the GCP really is on the reference layer. The distance between the two is the GCP’s residual (Figure 9.6):
\[
R_i = \sqrt{(x_i - X_i)^2 + (y_i - Y_i)^2}
\]
where \((X_i, Y_i)\) are the reference coordinates of GCP \(i\), and \((x_i, y_i)\) are the coordinates the transformation gives it. A residual much larger than the others flags a GCP that may be misplaced, such as a click on the wrong intersection.






Figure 9.6: Residuals at six ground control points. Each arrow runs from a GCP’s true position to where the transformation puts it. GCP 6’s residual is more than twice the others, which suggests it was placed on the wrong feature. The GCPs are made up.



The root mean square error (RMSE) combines all the residuals into one number, in map units:
\[
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i^2}
\]
Square each residual, average the squares, and take the square root. For four GCPs with residuals of 56.81, 92.94, 0.96, and 35.17 meters:



Table 9.4: Computing the RMSE from four residuals.

Lower is better. A common target is an RMSE smaller than the cell size of the raster: for an air photo with 1-meter cells, under 1 meter. For a historic map, the target depends on the map’s scale and condition, and a larger RMSE may be the best that is possible. Either way, report the RMSE and the transformation order with the result, so users know how far to trust it.
The RMSE measures the fit at the GCPs only. A low RMSE from a few bunched GCPs, or from a high-order polynomial, can hide large errors elsewhere. The best check is to hold back a few check points that are not used to fit the transformation, and measure their errors too.






NoteDid you know..?



Between 1867 and the 1960s, the Sanborn Map Company drew detailed fire insurance maps of about 12,000 American cities and towns, showing the outline, building material, and number of stories of almost every building. The Library of Congress has scanned tens of thousands of these sheets, including many of North Carolina towns, and historians and planners georeference them to trace how neighborhoods have changed.




9.2.7 Georeferencing in ArcGIS Pro

Open the georeference tools. Add the scanned map to a map that already has reference layers, such as a basemap or orthophoto. Select the image in the Contents pane, and on the Imagery tab, click Georeference.
Bring the image into view. Zoom the map to the area the scan covers, and click Fit to Display on the Georeference tab. The image is stretched over the current extent, a rough starting position.
Add control points. Click Add Control Points. Click a feature on the scan, then the same feature on the reference layer. Repeat across the whole image.
Check the control point table. Open the Control Point Table to see each GCP’s residual and the total RMS error. Re-place or delete points with large residuals, and recheck. Change the transformation (1st Order Polynomial by default) only if the fit isn’t good enough.
Save or export. Save stores the transformation with the original raster in an auxiliary file, without changing its pixels. Save as New writes a new, rectified raster: choose the resampling method (nearest neighbor for categories, bilinear or cubic for images) and an output cell size close to the source’s. Export Control Points keeps a text file of the GCPs, so the work can be checked or repeated.



9.2.8 Georeferencing in QGIS
QGIS has a built-in Georeferencer (Layer > Georeferencer). Open the raster in the Georeferencer window, and click Add Point to place GCPs: click a feature on the image, then click From Map Canvas to pick its location on the main map. Under Transformation Settings, choose the transformation type (Linear, Helmert, Polynomial 1 to 3, Thin Plate Spline, or Projective), the target CRS, the resampling method, and the output file. The GCP table shows each point’s residual, and the status bar shows the mean error. Start Georeferencing writes the rectified raster, and the GCPs can be saved to a .points file.

title: 9  Geocoding and Georeferencing
text:
9.4 Summary

Geocoding assigns coordinates to data that describe a location in another way. Address matching places an address by comparing it with a reference file.
U.S. addresses can be interpolated because house numbers increase along each street, with odd and even numbers on opposite sides.
Reference files range from parcels and address points (most accurate) through street centerlines and ZIP+4 to ZIP Code centroids (least accurate). The same address lands in different places with each.
Linear interpolation places an address along a street segment in proportion to its number within the segment’s range: \(A\% = (A_\# - A_{\text{from}}) / (A_{\text{to}} - A_{\text{from}})\).
Batch geocoding standardizes addresses and scores each candidate. Report the match rate, and review tied and unmatched addresses, which are rarely missing at random.
Georeferencing transforms a raster from file coordinates (rows and columns) to map coordinates, using ground control points that are easy to identify, accurate, stable, and spread across the image.
A first-order (affine) transformation corrects shift, scale, skew, and rotation, and needs at least 3 GCPs. Second- and third-order polynomials bend to fit nonlinear distortion and need 6 and 10. Use the lowest order that fits.
Resampling gives the output cells their values: nearest neighbor for categories, bilinear or cubic for images.
A GCP’s residual is the distance between where the transformation puts it and where it really is. The RMSE combines the residuals into one number. Check it, fix outliers, and report it with the result.

title: 9  Geocoding and Georeferencing
text:
9.5 Exercises

Interpolate. A street segment runs from (100, 200) to (300, 260). Its left side holds 200 to 298 and its right side 201 to 299. Find the coordinates of 250 and 275, and say which side each is on.
Compare reference files. Use the Census Geocoder to geocode your department’s address, or any public building. Then find the same building on a parcel map from NC OneMap or the county GIS website. How far apart are the two points?
Batch geocode. Make a CSV of 20 public addresses in Chapel Hill (schools, libraries, fire stations). Geocode them in batch with the Census Geocoder or in ArcGIS Pro. What is the match rate? Why did any addresses fail?
Georeference a historic map. Download a historic map of Chapel Hill or another North Carolina town from the Library of Congress or the North Carolina Collection’s digital maps. Georeference it in QGIS or ArcGIS Pro with at least 8 GCPs and a first-order transformation. Record the RMSE. Then try a second-order transformation. Did the RMSE fall? Does the image look better or worse away from the GCPs?
Find the bad GCP. In exercise 4, deliberately place one GCP on the wrong intersection. What happens to its residual and to the RMSE? Delete it and compare.
RMSE by hand. Five GCPs have residuals of 2.1, 3.4, 1.8, 2.6, and 9.7 meters. Compute the RMSE. Compute it again without the fifth point. What would you do next?

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.1 Defining data quality
Chapter 8 divided data about people and places into two kinds: authoritative data, made by official agencies to documented standards, and asserted data, contributed by the public. This chapter is about the second kind, and its best-known example, OpenStreetMap.
OpenStreetMap is a free map of the world that anyone can edit. Every street, building, and footpath on the UNC campus in OpenStreetMap was added by a volunteer, some walking with a GPS, most tracing satellite imagery from a desk. The result is used by governments, the largest technology companies, and aid agencies. So how good is it? To answer that, we first need a way to describe the quality of any geographic dataset.

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.1.1 Quality is fitness for use
There is no such thing as a perfect dataset. Every map leaves things out, generalizes shapes, and goes out of date. Spatial data quality is how well a dataset fits the use you have in mind. A road layer that is fine for a tourist map may be dangerous for routing ambulances. A building layer drawn from 2015 imagery may be good enough to estimate a city’s population, and useless for finding houses built since.
Quality questions come from both sides of a dataset:

As a data consumer, how do you judge the quality of data you download?
As a data creator, how do you make data good, and tell others how good it is?

Many things can go wrong. A road may not exist, or may not connect to the road it crosses. An address may be in the wrong place. A building may be labeled a school after it closed. A layer may come with no metadata at all, or in a coordinate system you didn’t expect (Chapter 4).


10.1.2 Seven elements of quality
Van Oort (2006) compared the quality elements used in mapping standards around the world, and found seven that they share (Figure 10.1). They are now written into the international standard ISO 19157, Geographic information: Data quality.






Figure 10.1: The seven elements of spatial data quality, after van Oort (2006).



Take a layer of fire hydrants as an example:

Lineage is the history of the dataset. Who collected the hydrants, with what equipment, and how were the points processed and edited since?
Positional accuracy is how close the coordinates are to the true locations. Is the hydrant where the map says it is, or across the street?
Attribute accuracy is how correct the non-spatial values are. Is the feature labeled a hydrant, with the right flow rate?
Logical consistency is whether the data agree with their own rules. Are hydrants on the water mains they connect to? In a road layer, do roads meet at intersections?
Completeness is “a measure of the absence of data and the presence of excess data” (Oort 2006, 23). Are all the hydrants there, and are there any that were removed long ago?
Temporal quality is whether the dates are right, and the data current. When was each hydrant last checked?
Usage, purpose, and constraints tell users what the data were made for, and what they should not be used for.

The first and last elements are not measurements of the data at all. They are information about the data, which is why metadata matter so much. A dataset with poor positional accuracy can still be useful if its metadata tell you how poor. A dataset with no metadata leaves you guessing.






TipThink about it



Which of the seven elements matters most for each of these uses: (a) routing an ambulance; (b) estimating the number of people in a flood zone from building footprints; (c) a historic map of the town in 1950? Is the answer the same for all three?

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.2 Volunteered geographic information

10.2.1 Anyone can be a data producer
Until the 2000s, almost all map data came from governments and a few companies, made by trained staff to written standards. Three developments changed that:

User-generated content. “Web 2.0” sites let readers create content, not just read it: blogs, wikis, photo sharing, and social networks (O’Reilly 2005).
Cheap GPS. Handheld receivers, and then phones, made it cheap and easy to record a location.
Mobile computing. Fast internet access everywhere let people upload what they recorded, from wherever they were.

Together they produced what Goodchild (2007) called volunteered geographic information (VGI): geographic data created by individuals, most of them not trained in mapping, and shared on the internet. Goodchild described the volunteers as “citizens as sensors,” billions of people able to observe and report on the places around them.
VGI changed the quality question. When a government agency makes a map, you can judge it partly by the agency’s reputation and standards. When anyone can contribute, quality can no longer be assumed from who made the data. It has to be measured.


10.2.2 Types of VGI
VGI comes in three main forms, and the form affects its quality:



Table 10.1: The three main types of VGI.











Type
Examples
How location is recorded
Quality




Location-based social media
Geotagged posts and photos, check-ins
As a by-product: people are not trying to make a map
Very uneven; location may be the phone’s, not the subject’s


Collaborative mapping
OpenStreetMap, Wikimapia
Deliberately: mapping is the goal
Contributors can see and correct each other’s work


Citizen science
eBird, iNaturalist, CoCoRaHS rain gauges, reports of flooded road crossings
By following a protocol set by scientists
Quality control is built into the protocol






Research on VGI has followed several strands. Some studies ask why people volunteer, and who they are. Others measure data quality, as we do below. Others study bias: OpenStreetMap contributors have been mostly young, male, urban, and from Europe and North America, and their interests shape what gets mapped and where. Others study VGI in disasters, the subject of the last part of this chapter.


10.2.3 Big Data
VGI is one source of Big Data, datasets too large, too fast, or too varied for traditional tools. Big Data is usually defined by three Vs (Beyer and Laney 2012):

Volume: from terabytes to petabytes, more than one computer can store or process.
Velocity: data arrive continuously and must be handled in near real time.
Variety: mixed formats, such as text, images, GPS traces, and sensor readings.

OpenStreetMap has all three: billions of nodes, edits arriving every minute, and everything from roads to opening hours. Most of the data from phones, vehicles, and sensors carries a location, so geographic data make up a large share of Big Data.
Some authors add a fourth V, veracity: can the data be trusted? That is this chapter’s question. At this scale, no one can check every feature by hand, so quality checks have to be automated and statistical. More data does not mean better data.


10.2.4 FAIR data
The FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016) say that good scientific data should be:

Findable: data and metadata are easy to find, by people and by computers.
Accessible: once found, users know how to get the data, including any login or permission needed.
Interoperable: the data can be combined with other data, software, and workflows.
Reusable: data and metadata are described well enough to be reused, or combined in new settings.

Many funders and journals now require FAIR data. FAIR doesn’t guarantee that data are accurate, but good metadata let users judge quality for themselves. OpenStreetMap does well on findable, accessible, and reusable: it has an open license and a public API. It is weaker on consistent metadata, because contributors set their own tags.

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.3 OpenStreetMap

10.3.1 A free, editable map of the world
OpenStreetMap (OSM) was founded in 2004 by Steve Coast, then a student in London, to create free, open road data. It now maps far more than streets: buildings, land use, trails, shops, water points, and much more.

Anyone can edit. You can add, change, or delete data, and your edits go live immediately. Each set of edits is saved as a changeset, with the editor’s username and a comment.
The data are open. OSM is published under the Open Database License (ODbL). You can use, change, and share the data for any purpose, including commercial use, as long as you credit “© OpenStreetMap contributors” and share any database you build from it under the same license.
It is big. OSM has more than 10 million registered accounts, and roughly 10 billion nodes. Only a small share of accounts have ever edited, and a much smaller core does most of the work.







NoteDid you know..?



OpenStreetMap began because map data in Britain were expensive. The Ordnance Survey, the national mapping agency, charged for its data, so Steve Coast set out to build a free map from GPS traces he and his friends recorded on foot, by bicycle, and by car. Some of the first OSM mapping parties, in 2006, sent volunteers around a town with GPS receivers to map it in a weekend.




10.3.2 Who uses OpenStreetMap?
OSM is no longer a hobby project:

Governments. The U.S. Census Bureau has compared OSM with its TIGER/Line road files (Chapter 8). Many national and local governments use or contribute to OSM.
Technology companies. Apple, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon all use OSM data. In 2022, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and TomTom founded the Overture Maps Foundation, which builds open map data partly on OSM.
Navigation and logistics. Routing engines, delivery, and ride-hailing apps.
Humanitarian organizations. The Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières use OSM to plan disaster response and health campaigns.
Researchers and students. OSM is free, global, and consistent enough for spatial analysis anywhere.

There is also a public-good argument. Whoever makes the map decides which places exist on it. An open map, which anyone can improve, keeps that power from resting with one or two companies (Wroclawski 2014).


10.3.3 OSM’s data model
OSM’s data model is simple. It has three kinds of element, plus tags (Figure 10.2):

A node is a single point, with a latitude and longitude. A node can stand alone, as a café or a hydrant, or be one of the vertices of a way.
A way is an ordered list of nodes, forming a line such as a road or a stream. A closed way, whose first and last nodes are the same, forms an area, such as a building or a park.
A relation groups elements and describes how they relate, such as all the roads of a bus route, or the outer and inner rings of a lake with islands.
A tag is a key=value pair that describes an element, such as highway=residential or name=Franklin Street. Any element can carry any number of tags.







Figure 10.2: The elements of OpenStreetMap’s data model. The places and tags are examples.



All of the meaning is in the tags, and there is no fixed list of them. Anyone can invent a tag, and the community agrees on conventions and documents them on the OSM Wiki. That flexibility lets OSM map almost anything. It also creates inconsistency, a logical consistency problem in van Oort’s terms: one mapper tags a path highway=footway, another highway=path, a third highway=track. Because the data structure is loose, the community has to define and enforce its own quality standards.

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.4 Measuring the quality of OSM

10.4.1 Extrinsic and intrinsic measures
There are two ways to measure the quality of OSM (Figure 10.3):

Extrinsic measures compare OSM with an authoritative reference dataset, such as the Ordnance Survey’s maps in Britain or TIGER/Line in the United States. You can measure how far OSM roads are from the reference roads (positional accuracy), and what each dataset has that the other lacks (completeness).
Intrinsic measures use only OSM’s own history: how many people edited an area, how many versions each feature has, how recently it was edited, and whether the work was checked by a second mapper.







Figure 10.3: Extrinsic measures compare OSM with an authoritative reference; intrinsic measures use OSM’s own editing history. The values on the right are examples.



The early studies were extrinsic. Haklay (2010) compared OSM’s roads in England with the Ordnance Survey’s. He found them “fairly accurate”: OSM’s roads were, on average, within about 6 meters of the Ordnance Survey’s, and about 80 percent of the motorways overlapped. Completeness was uneven, though. Wealthy and central areas were well mapped, while poorer and rural areas lagged. Later studies found the same in other countries, and found high completeness for building footprints in Munich (Fan et al. 2014).
Extrinsic measures have a limit: they need a trusted reference, and in the places where OSM matters most, there often isn’t one. That is why intrinsic measures are useful. Haklay and colleagues (2010) found that the more people had mapped an area, the more accurate its roads were. This is unique to collaborative data. A traditional dataset has one producer, so there is no crowd to count.






NoteDid you know..?



In open-source software, Linus’s Law says that “given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.” It was named for Linus Torvalds, who created Linux. Haklay and colleagues (2010) tested it on maps. In London, the positional accuracy of OSM roads improved quickly as the first contributors mapped an area, and once about 15 contributors had mapped a square kilometer, the roads were reliably accurate.




10.4.2 Tools for checking OSM
Quality control in OSM happens after edits are made, through software and people:

Osmose and KeepRight run automated checks across the database, flagging problems such as roads that don’t connect, buildings that overlap, and missing or conflicting tags.
OSMCha (OSM Changeset Analyzer) lets experienced mappers review recent changesets, to catch vandalism and mistakes.
MapRoulette turns lists of detected errors into small fix-it tasks that anyone can do in a few minutes.
The HOT Tasking Manager divides a mapping project into small squares. When one mapper finishes a square, a second, experienced mapper validates it.
The ohsome dashboard, from the Heidelberg Institute for Geoinformation Technology (HeiGIT), shows how much was mapped in an area over time, an intrinsic quality signal.

Your GIS also checks data quality. ArcGIS Pro and QGIS can validate geometry and find features that break topology rules (QGIS’s Check Validity and Topology Checker, ArcGIS Pro’s Check Geometry and topology rules).






TipThink about it



Open OpenStreetMap at openstreetmap.org and zoom to a place you know well, such as your hometown or your street. What is mapped, and what is missing? Which of van Oort’s quality elements would you worry about if you used it for a project there?

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.5 Crisis mapping

10.5.1 Haiti, 2010
On 12 January 2010, a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince, Haiti. Before the earthquake, Port-au-Prince was nearly blank in OpenStreetMap. Within days, satellite companies released new imagery, and hundreds of volunteers around the world began tracing roads, buildings, and camps for displaced people. Within weeks, OSM had the most detailed map of the city available anywhere, and aid workers on the ground used it (Zook et al. 2010). It was the first large test of crisis mapping, mapping by volunteers to support disaster response.


10.5.2 The Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team
A small group of OSM mappers had formed the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) in 2009. The Haiti response turned it into a formal organization in 2010. HOT is activated when a disaster or other humanitarian need is declared, and it works with partners such as the Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières. It has an elected board, working groups for activation, communications, training, technology, and more, and local mapping communities in the affected countries.
HOT’s work happens in three steps (Figure 10.4):






Figure 10.4: The three steps of a HOT mapping project, after LearnOSM.




Remote mapping. Volunteers anywhere in the world trace roads and buildings from satellite imagery, using the Tasking Manager so that they don’t overlap. This step is fast and can involve thousands of people. But remote mappers can’t see street names, or what a building is used for.
Field mapping. Local mappers, who know the place, add names, building uses, and evacuation sites, and check the remote work on the ground. This step is also quality control.
Response. Aid organizations use the map to plan routes, count buildings, estimate populations, and deliver help.







NoteDid you know..?



You don’t need a disaster to map for a cause. Missing Maps, founded in 2014 by HOT, the American and British Red Cross, and Médecins Sans Frontières, maps the places most at risk before disasters happen. Many of its volunteers map at mapathons, events where people trace imagery together for a few hours, often on college campuses.




10.5.3 Nepal, 2015
On 25 April 2015, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central Nepal, followed by a magnitude 7.3 aftershock on 12 May. Nearly 9,000 people died, and more than half a million homes were destroyed or damaged. Many of the hardest-hit districts were rural and mountainous, hard to reach, and poorly mapped. Responders needed up-to-date maps of roads, villages, and helicopter landing sites within days.
HOT activated within hours. Kathmandu Living Labs, a civic technology group in Kathmandu, became the local hub, linking remote volunteers with responders in Nepal. HOT called for new volunteers, mapathons, and donations, and the call worked: universities, companies, and community groups around the world held mapathons, and thousands of people created OSM accounts for the first time. Daily edits in Nepal jumped about tenfold after the earthquake, and volunteers edited roads across the central districts in under three weeks.
Parr (2015) counted the contributors who had mapped in Nepal by the year they joined OSM (Figure 10.5). In the ten years before the earthquake, 8,725 people had mapped there. In the 12 days after it, 9,989 more joined. Newcomers suddenly made up more than half of everyone who had ever mapped the country.






Figure 10.5: Contributors to OpenStreetMap in Nepal, by the year they joined. Data from Parr (2015).





10.5.4 The problem of success
The flood of new volunteers created tension within HOT. On its public mailing list, one experienced member wrote in April 2015 that they were “finding totally inexperienced mappers (some with no completed tiles and others with only one or two completed tiles) messing around with validating tiles or unlocking already validated tiles and working on them,” at a time when “people’s lives are at stake.” Another wrote in May: “We need more people. At the same time, we need to adapt in various ways to crowdsourcing as we see various problems arising.”
That is the dilemma of open data in a crisis. The response needed more mappers, not fewer, but beginners make mistakes, and a mistake in a crisis map can send a truck down a road that doesn’t exist.
The newcomers’ work also looked different (Figure 10.6). On average, each newcomer edited about half as many features as an earlier contributor, and changed or deleted far fewer existing ones. Newcomers mostly added new features. Experienced mappers did most of the correcting, and a small core of them did a very large share of it. The quality of the map depended on that core.






Figure 10.6: How contributors who joined before the earthquake compare with those who joined in the 12 days after it. Data from Parr (2015).



HOT’s answer was both social and technical:

Social. HOT improved its training guides at LearnOSM, and asked experienced mappers to review newcomers’ work.
Technical. The Tasking Manager gained a separate validation step, and flags for experienced mappers. A square is marked done only after a second, experienced mapper checks it.

The result was a new layer of data reviewers, the validators. It is a familiar pattern for quality control in open projects: open contribution, followed by expert review. It keeps the door open to beginners while protecting the data that responders rely on.

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.6 Getting involved
OpenStreetMap is one of the few datasets in this book that you can improve yourself:

Use the data. Download extracts for a country, state, or region from Geofabrik (download.geofabrik.de) as shapefiles or in OSM’s own formats. In QGIS, the QuickOSM plugin downloads features for the map’s extent by tag, such as every amenity=hospital in a county.
Join OSM. Create a free account at openstreetmap.org.
Start editing. The iD editor runs in your web browser and needs no installation; it includes a short walkthrough. JOSM is a desktop editor for advanced work.
Map for a cause. Pick a project in the HOT Tasking Manager (tasks.hotosm.org), or join a mapathon.
Meet the community. State of the Map US is held every year, and the OSM community forum is at community.openstreetmap.org.

Whatever you use OSM for, credit it: “© OpenStreetMap contributors.”

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.8 Summary

Spatial data quality is fitness for use. Van Oort’s seven elements are lineage, positional accuracy, attribute accuracy, logical consistency, completeness, temporal quality, and usage, purpose, and constraints.
Volunteered geographic information appeared in the 2000s with Web 2.0, cheap GPS, and mobile internet. It comes as location-based social media, collaborative mapping, and citizen science. Its quality has to be measured, not assumed.
Big Data is defined by volume, velocity, and variety; veracity is the quality question. The FAIR principles call for data that are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.
OpenStreetMap was founded in 2004. It is open under the ODbL, used by governments, technology companies, and aid agencies, and built from nodes, ways, relations, and free-form tags.
Extrinsic measures compare OSM with authoritative data; intrinsic measures use OSM’s own history. OSM’s roads are often accurate, completeness is uneven, and areas with more editors tend to be better mapped.
Tools such as Osmose, OSMCha, MapRoulette, and the HOT Tasking Manager check OSM’s quality after edits are made.
Crisis mapping began in Haiti in 2010 and led to the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team. In Nepal in 2015, newcomers outnumbered all earlier mappers, and validation by experienced mappers protected the map’s quality.

title: 10  OpenStreetMap and Data Quality
text:
10.9 Exercises

Quality elements. Find the metadata for a dataset you have used in this course (for example a TIGER/Line file or a layer from NC OneMap). Which of van Oort’s seven elements does it describe? Which are missing?
Tag a feature. Look up a building and a road you know on openstreetmap.org. Click each (or use the Query features tool) and list its tags. Are any important attributes missing? Look up the recommended tags on the OSM Wiki.
Extrinsic comparison. Download OSM roads for Orange County, NC, from Geofabrik or with QuickOSM, and the TIGER/Line roads for the same county. Display them together and zoom in on three places: downtown Chapel Hill, a new subdivision, and a rural area. Where do they disagree? Which dataset is more complete in each place?
Intrinsic history. Pick a building on the UNC campus in OSM and view its history (View History on the feature page). How many versions does it have? How many different people edited it, and when?
Map something. Create an OSM account and complete the iD walkthrough. Then add or fix one feature near where you live, with a clear changeset comment. Or map one square on a HOT Tasking Manager project.
Crisis mapping. Read the Nepal case in this chapter. Write one paragraph on how you would balance openness and data quality if you ran the next activation.
